News.title: People told 'see a GP' in UK-wide 'flu-like' symptoms summer health warning
News.content:
People told 'see a GP' in UK-wide 'flu-like' symptoms summer health warning

People in the UK have been warned in a new alert issued by a pharmacist about the red-flag signs they need to see a GP

View 3 Images Brits warned horsefly bites can trigger ‘flu-like’ symptoms as warm weather continues (Image: Getty)

With temperatures staying high and horseflies thriving in warm, sunny conditions, pharmacists at Chemist4U are warning that bites from the pesky insect can be far more severe than people realise. As well as causing intense pain, swelling and itching, some sufferers are reporting symptoms that leave them feeling generally unwell, including fatigue, aches, and 'flu-like' symptoms.

‌



Ian Budd, Lead Prescribing Pharmacist at Chemist4U, has explained why horsefly bites can trigger such strong reactions, which symptoms to watch out for, and when a bite could be a sign of infection requiring treatment. He also warns people to 'see a GP' if they notice certain symptoms, saying that "this is usually your body trying to tell you something isn’t right."

‌



He said: "While most insect bites are little more than an irritation, horsefly bites can be a different story, often causing more pain, swelling, and inflammation than people expect. Unlike mosquitoes, which pierce your skin, horseflies actually cut into it with scissor-like mouthparts to feed."

‌



He says that this creates a deeper wound, which is why the bite tends to be immediately painful, can take longer to heal, and carries a greater risk of infection if it’s scratched or not cared for properly. He continued: "In cases where you start to feel generally unwell, experiencing symptoms like aches, fatigue, swollen glands, or even feeling flu-like, it’s typically your body’s immune system reacting to the bite.

"However, it can also be a sign that an infection is developing, particularly if your symptoms are accompanied by spreading redness, increasing pain, heat around the bite, or discharge from the wound. The majority of horsefly bites will improve within a week and can usually be managed at home.

View 3 Images Horseflies prefer to fly in sunlight, avoiding dark and shady areas, and are inactive at night

‌



"A cold compress can help reduce swelling, antihistamines may ease the itching, and hydrocortisone cream can calm any inflammation. The key thing is to avoid scratching, as this significantly increases the risk of infection."

Ian's tips for managing a horsefly bite safely

Cool the area as soon as possible. Apply a cold compress or wrap an ice pack for around 20 minutes to help reduce the swelling and discomfort.

Use antihistamines if itching develops. Antihistamine tablets can help reduce itching and may make bites less tempting to scratch, reducing your risk of infection.

‌



Take painkillers if you’re struggling. Taking paracetamol or ibuprofen (if suitable for you) can also help with pain relief if your bite is particularly painful.

View 3 Images Horse flies are often large and agile in flight, and the females bite animals, including humans, to obtain blood (stock image)

Try not to scratch. As difficult as it might be to avoid scratching, it damages the skin and increases the chance of bacteria getting into the bite.

‌



When should I see a GP, and what are the warning signs?

Ian says: "Watch for signs of infection". While most horsefly bites heal within a week, Ian stresses the importance of keeping an eye out for any signs of infection. "Redness that continues to spread, worsening pain, warmth around the site of the bite, or swollen glands shouldn’t be ignored", he said.

He also recommends: "Listen to your body." For instance, if you develop a temperature, aches, fatigue, or feel generally unwell after a bite, "make sure you seek advice from a GP or pharmacist", he said. "This is usually your body trying to tell you something isn’t right."

He added: "While horsefly bites can be particularly painful and sometimes cause significant swelling, most people recover without any complications. The key is keeping the bite clean, avoiding scratching, and seeking advice if symptoms appear to be getting worse rather than better."

Article continues below

How can I reduce my risk of getting a horsefly bite?

To lower your chances of getting bitten by a horsefly, put on light and loose clothes since horseflies depend on their vision and are drawn to dark, moving objects. When you're around water, in wooded areas, or near tall grass, apply effective insect repellents such as DEET or Picaridin, and try to stay indoors during times when they are most active.

Healthline says: "To prevent future horsefly bites, apply insect repellent before going outdoors. If possible, stick to light-colored clothing. Horseflies are attracted to darker colours, so this may help keep them away."

News.title: 'Gutted' family left stranded at airport gates over passport rule
News.content:
'Gutted' family left stranded at airport gates over passport rule

A family-of-four were about to head off to Portugal for a holiday but one of the kids was told a passport rule meant he could not board the flight forcing them to miss out

View 2 Images Dan and Laura Sharples with their son Sonny (Image: Andrew Teebay Liverpool Echo)

A family planning to jet off to Portugal for a summer holiday were left stranded at the gate in the UK due to a passport rule.

‌



Dan Sharples, 41, and his wife Laura Sharples were due to fly from Liverpool John Lennon Airport with their two sons on June 23, but the family was turned away at the last moment. The dad, from Widnes, said he had booked the getaway at his local travel agent at the start of the year .

‌



He revealed the two parents and their three-year-old son were given the green light to travel but their nine-year-old boy Spencer was told he couldn't go through. The boy's passport hadn't expired but was within three months of going out of date, making it invalid.

‌



View 2 Images Outside John Lennon Airport (Image: Cover/Getty Images)

The family had planned to visit Portugal as part of an annual trip with a group of 24 other people from Dan's former rugby club. Dan claimed he he handed his family's passports over to the travel agent when they were organising the trip for them, according to the Liverpool Echo.

He said: "We booked with Hays Travel and they took all our passports. It was all entered and nothing was ever flagged up. At bag drop they examined our passports and never said anything. But when we went to board the plane, they refused us boarding.

‌



"We were right at the gate and had to wait until everyone else had boarded while we were taken back out. We were just gutted. I was quite angry to be honest. I was asking how we managed to get that far through the process and through the airport without anyone alerting us to the problem."

Entry rules for British passport holders have changed since Brexit, meaning they are now seen as "third-country nationals". To travel to EU countries, passports must be valid for at least three months after your planned return date. Hays Travel said it advises customers to check the most up-to-date guidance for travel documents via the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office website.

Dan said: "Hays Travel had our passports. They checked us in three weeks before we travelled. If they had highlighted the issue at the time, we could have sorted it out. But because it's a child's passport, the quickest you can get a replacement was five days. We lost our holiday basically, so I was annoyed and frustrated."

‌



The dad added: "We had booked it earlier in the year, probably around February. We had it planned for a while. We missed the group trip last year so we decided to go this year, only to end up missing it again.

"Hays Travel had issued us boarding passes with those travel documents and nobody told us anything at all or flagged any concerns. I was annoyed, the kids were upset watching everyone board the plane without us. They walked us back through customs, we collected our bags, and that was early in the morning."

A spokesperson for Hays Travel said: "While we empathise with Mr Sharples, our agents explain to customers at the time of booking that they are responsible for ensuring their travel documents are valid for the destination they are visiting. For this booking, Mr Sharples was advised to check the most up-to-date guidance via the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) website to avoid any issues."

Article continues below

Dan said he contacted Hays Travel in Widnes to explain the situation and claimed they were "were very apologetic" but refused to give him a refund when he called later. He said: "One of the girls from the shop rang us back saying they wouldn't offer us anything, saying it was our fault because we were responsible for the documents.

"We don't get a refund, nothing. My argument is we paid Hays Travel for the service, they offered to check us in so they should have let us know if there was a problem."

The dad added: "I feel very angry. Normally I book these things myself, and I feel if I had done it myself I would have noticed it. But we've been left without a holiday or any form of compensation."

News.title: Man 'unlawfully killed' before his remains found in bin bags in the River Stour
News.content:
Man 'unlawfully killed' before his remains found in bin bags in the River Stour

Two mummified legs and feet and two mummified arms without hands were found by a dog walker in black bin bags in the River Stour at Sudbury

View 3 Images One of the black bin bags contained a white Thing-Me-Bobs carrier bag, containing bricks (Image: Police Handout)

Mummified remains found in weighted bags in a river in Suffolk belong to a man who was unlawfully killed.

‌



Two mummified legs and feet and two mummified arms without hands were found by a dog walker in black bin bags in the River Stour at Sudbury on August 27, 2020. Skull fragments, facial bones and two loose teeth were then found in a thin blue plastic bag by police divers two days later.

‌



The second discovery was made 150 metres further along the river. An inquest in Ipswich today concluded the remains belonged to an unidentified man who was unlawfully killed.

‌



The victim was named the Croft Man for the purposes of the inquest, after the area of Sudbury where his remains were found. Suffolk’s senior coroner Nigel Parsley recorded that the Croft Man died as the result of a "violent assault".

View 3 Images Decorative stones were found within a Boots carrier bag, within a second bin bag (Image: Police Handout)

No matches have been identified after checks were run against national and international databases for missing people and for criminal activity, the coroner said. He said that radiocarbon dating indicated the Croft Man was born before the early 1950s and died in about 2008 to 2012, and it was therefore estimated he was in his late 60s to 70s at the time of his death.

‌



The removal of the man's hands and the injuries to his head and face "appear to have been an attempt to hamper his identification", Mr Parsley said. He concluded it was "more likely than not the Croft Man was unlawfully killed".

The coroner said: "We must remember that the Croft Man was somebody’s son. He lived for 60 to 70 years. He may well have had family, he almost certainly had friends.

"It’s a tragedy we cannot identify him as there must be some loved ones somewhere wondering where their loved one is." In a statement read to the court, dog walker Julie Dunn-Beechin said that she saw two black bin bags in the water on a stretch of the River Stour by water meadows.

‌



Her dogs started sniffing the area, which she said "didn't seem right to me", and so her attention was drawn to the bags. Park ranger Samuel Morgan, whom Ms Dunn-Beechin called, said: "She said she didn’t know if she had been watching too many Midsomer Murders and had a concern about what could be in the bags."

View 3 Images Commercial air freshener blocks - which became obsolete in 2011 - were dumped with the human remains (Image: Police Handout)

He said the bags had rocks and bricks in and "what looked like a toilet Duck soap that had partly dissolved". Mr Morgan said he saw "through a small hole in the bag what I thought looked like mummified skin and bone" and what appeared to be the ball joint of an arm, and he called police.

‌



Superintendent Mike Brown, of Suffolk Police, said it was estimated the bags were deposited between August 13 and August 19. He said a volunteer litter picker who regularly uses a canoe in the area reported the site was clear on August 13.

A first sighting of the bin bags was made on August 19, but this was not reported to the police at the time. A fingertip search of the riverbed was carried out and a dive team found further human remains in a thin blue bag on August 29.

Supt Brown said the "remains from the first deposition site and the second deposition site are the same person" and this was confirmed by DNA testing. The air fresheners in the black bin bags were made in north Wales at a site that closed in early 2012, it was established.

‌



The bricks found in the bags were made in the 1970s, were "very common" and millions were produced, Supt Brown added. The officer said: "The biggest challenge we have is we do not know the identity of our victim so we’re unable to work around the associations they would have had and then look at those wider lines of inquiry."

DNA testing indicated the Croft Man was a white northern European male, likely to have been born with blonde or light hair which may have darkened naturally, and blue or green eyes. Supt Brown said: "The most likely and preferred hypothesis is that there’s a criminal element."

He added that the injuries inflicted on the skull supported this. He said the manner of dismemberment of the body could suggest someone with "skill in butchery".

‌



"Our victim has likely met a violent and unnatural death," he said. Supt Brown continued: "Because of the length of storage, the individual could have been found in a state by somebody who doesn’t want to come to the attention of police and has tried to dispose of them by throwing them away."

Home Office pathologist Dr Ginni Fitzpatrick-Swallow said the limbs in the black bags were mummified but there was no skin on the skull fragments in the blue bag found by police divers. Regarding the skull pieces, the pathologist said there were "at least 14 linear cuts".

These could have been caused by a "heavy weapon with a sharp edge" such as a meat cleaver, axe or machete. She said there had been "multiple blows to the head".

Article continues below

"The appearance is consistent with repeated strikes in rapid succession due to their uniformity," she said. She said it was not known if the skull injuries were inflicted in life as there was no soft tissue remaining.

"To completely destroy a skull like that seems, from a dismemberment point of view, unnecessary," she said. She said that "to remove the hands and destroy the facial features" can be associated with disguising the identity of the deceased.

The pathologist said some of the remains "may have been frozen" and may have been wrapped in plastic for a period of time. She gave the medical cause of death as unascertained.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe died after being hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her Devon home as she ate lunch, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man accused of her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.

Kerry, who prosecutors say was only in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off, the court heard.

The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire, who is charged with murder, later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.

Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.

The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July, and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.

News.title: London-based civil servants offered move to No 10 North in Manchester
News.content:
Civil servants working for government departments based in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move to the North of England, the BBC understands.

It comes as the first details are emerging about the new No 10 North which has already started work, according to sources close to new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The BBC has been told that the Northern branch of Downing Street will be overseen by cabinet minister and ally of Burnham, Louise Haigh.

Haigh, who is the first secretary of state, is thought to have been asked to lead a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC), which will give her control of key decision- making bodies across government.

The OPMC will include No 10, No 10 North and teams within the Cabinet Office.

Announcing the changes,, external which will also include an AI Taskforce, Leader of the House of Lords, Baroness Angela Smith said No 10 North would be a "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

It is understood that the initial location of No 10 North will be Heron House in central Manchester, in the same building which houses offices for the intelligence service GCHQ. Specialist police officers have been seen guarding the building.

It is likely that the longer term base for No 10 North will be at a new government "Digital Campus" which is under construction in the Ancoats area of Manchester. It is not due for completion until 2032.

However, a good indication of what it could look like comes from a new report, released on Tuesday.

The blueprint has been authored, external by the Re:State think tank which Burnham was involved with until he stepped down as mayor of Greater Manchester.

News.title: Parts of the UK move closer to drought
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

In Wales, where just 5% of July rainfall has fallen, Natural Resources Wales has moved the worst affected regions in the north and south-east into "prolonged dry weather status", the first step in its drought plan.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

As the effects of human-induced climate change continue, the Met Office expects our summers to become hotter and drier, external in the future. In fact, by 2070, our summers could be up to 60% drier and 1-6C warmer compared to 1990.

News.title: Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for 10.1 million
News.content:
Thames Water has announced a hosepipe ban affecting 10.1 million customers after an "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The restrictions mean, from Thursday, hosepipes should not be used for watering gardens or allotments, cleaning cars, filling paddling pools or swimming pools, or cleaning windows.

The water company said its region had seen 40% of average rainfall, and more days at or above 34C this year than ever recorded before.

Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources, said: "We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment."

The ban applies to all customers that Thames Water supplies with drinking water and comes into effect on Thursday.

The company provides water to customers across parts of Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Surrey, the Thames Valley, Greater London, and the surrounding areas, external.

It provides water and wastewater services to 16 million customers overall.

It said water use was currently 10% above normal in the Thames Valley and Home Counties and 7% above normal in London, which amounted to an extra 100 million litres of water every day.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months. UK defence sources would not comment on whether the incident might have been timed to coincide with the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they had not been on a "collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

BBC Verify has analysed flight and ship-tracking data which shows the position of HMS Tyne and several British military aircraft operating in and around the Channel near Plymouth on Monday.

Flight data on ADS-B Exchange indicates at least four Royal Air Force and Royal Navy aircraft were flying off the coast of Dorset mostly above the UK's territorial waters, including two Eurofighter Typhoons, a Voyager air refuelling tanker and a Super Lynx helicopter.

A French military H160M GuÃ©pard helicopter also flew out and over the Channel during the afternoon. It is not clear if this is the aircraft which made contact with the Russian warship.

Data on ship-tracking service MarineTraffic shows HMS Tyne began to broadcast its location about 40 miles off Plymouth at 13:57 BST on Monday. It remained in that location for around two hours before departing at 15:56 to return to Plymouth.

HMS Tyne has been tracking Neustrashimy since at least 16 July when both vessels were also captured in the North Sea about 36 miles miles from the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk on a satellite image.

Additional reporting by Ella Kipling, Barbara Metzler, Thomas Spencer and Patrick Jackson

News.title: Argentina's Fernandez defends team after ugly scenes in World Cup final loss to Spain
News.content:
Midfielder Enzo Fernandez has claimed Argentina represented their nation "in the best possible way" during the World Cup, despite ugly scenes during and after their final loss to Spain.

Fernandez was sent off late in normal time for two yellow cards and Spain won 1-0 after extra time on Sunday in New Jersey.

His first booking was for showing dissent towards Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic and Fernandez was later dismissed for catching Pau Cubarsi with a challenge that sent the defender cartwheeling in the air.

But, in a statement on social media, the Chelsea midfielder did not mention the red card and said: "As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result.

"For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn't just about winning; it's about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up.

"It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment."

News.title: Ryanair boss says 'foreign object' may have caused plane window incident
News.content:
An incident on a Ryanair flight which saw a passenger partially sucked out of a plane window may have been caused by "foreign object damage" to an engine, said the airline's boss.

Michael O'Leary said an initial investigation into the incident on 10 July between Greece and Germany suggests "it looks like a foreign object damage to the engine on takeoff at Thessaloniki but ... we can't say that definitively".

He insisted that the engine on the 18-year-old Boeing 737 plane had been fully serviced and overhauled in the past two years.

Serbian national Ljubisa KaroviÄ's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the plane's window, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".

His wife Svetlana GrkoviÄ MaksimoviÄ told BBC Serbia that she and two other passengers held on to his legs for several minutes.

She said: "We pulled him back together. His entire face was deformed and blood was pouring from his nose and mouth."

He was taken to hospital after the plane made an emergency landing.

Passengers told local media they heard "some kind of explosion" on board.

The aircraft was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.

Confirmation that the damage was caused by an external object could affect Ryanair or Boeing's liabilities over the incident.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. O'Leary said that a draft report would be issued in about 28 days.

News.title: Chris Mason: Starmer ally takes swipe at Burnham's first big policy
News.content:
Whenever there is a reshuffle at the top of government, it is worth keeping an eye and an ear on the dislodged, demoted and rejected former ministers. What do they choose to do and say next?

Andy Burnham has started his first full day in the job with a promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from 1 October.

But already â within hours - he is taking flak from a man who just yesterday was in a senior job in Downing Street working alongside Sir Keir Starmer.

On Monday night, the former Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister, Darren Jones, posted a picture on X of him having a beer, external, captioned "thank you and good night. See you September".

If that was meant to suggest a vow of silence it only lasted a little over 12 hours, because at breakfast time this morning came another post, this one unaccompanied by any picture but loaded with political bite.

"Good news that VAT will be cut on electricity bills," wrote Jones.

"It's a simple way for families to save a few quid, and to mechanically help to keep inflation that little bit lower. But the DigitalID program was unfunded. The government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget."

Ouch - that will sting in Downing Street.

News.title: Laos methanol poisoning charges 'slap in face' for families
News.content:
The brother of a British tourist who died in a mass methanol poisoning says the failure to charge anyone over her death is a "slap in the face".

Simone White, 28, was one of six people who died after drinking free shots at the Nana Backpacker Hostel in Vang Vieng, Laos, in November 2024.

Last week authorities in the South-East Asian country said they couldn't determine if the deaths "were caused by the actions of any individual or by any particular cause, because no autopsies were conducted".

Simone's brother, Zak told BBC Newsbeat he found the conclusion "pretty ridiculous", as a death certificate issued in Laos lists "methanol toxicity" as one of her causes of death.

Trainee lawyer Simone and childhood friend Bethany Clarke were among about 100 guests given free shots thought to be tainted with methanol.

They felt unwell the next day and were taken to hospital, where Simone, from Orpington in south-east London, was put on life support before she died.

Two Australians, two Danish citizens and an American also died after drinking the shots.

Medical documents seen by Newsbeat state methanol was found in Bethany's blood in November 2024.

"For them to say there's not really enough evidence, I think for me and my parents, it's a bit of a slap in the face, really," says Zak.

"If you've got a death certificate with that on it, surely there's enough proof?"

Zak previously said his family had braced themselves for an unsatisfying resolution to the case as authorities were "not very forthcoming with trying to speed things along".

The case will remain open for 15 years, but Bethany says she is "not expecting much" from the Laos legal system in future.

"To my mind it's very clear what's happened," she says.

"I don't know why it should take a rocket scientist to come to the conclusion of what's happened here."

News.title: 'Significant hot spots' remain at Cairngorms wildfire
News.content:
Hot spots remain at a wildfire which has burned across 10 square kilometres of land in the Cairngorms over the last week, according to the fire service.

More than 100 firefighters have been involved in the operation to control and extinguish the fire, which started near Ryvoan Bothy, south of Nethy Bridge, last Wednesday.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said on Sunday that they had "surrounded" the large-scale blaze.

However, they say "significant hotspots remain across a large and complex landscape" and crews will stay at the scene until the incident is brought to a safe conclusion.

News.title: Owners of viral TikTok blue lagoon warn people to stay away
News.content:
Owners of a "blue lagoon" that went viral on TikTok during the Covid pandemic have warned people not to enter the site, particularly during the current hot weather.

Brombil Reservoir in Margam in Neath Port Talbot attracted thousands of visitors, which caused traffic problems and littering.

To reach the 30m-deep (100ft) reservoir, visitors must walk up a steep 900m (2,953ft) public footpath.

Leisure Estate Investments Ltd, which bought the secluded site at auction for Â£20,000 in 2024, are now charging Â£2 a visit as "a temporary deterrent" and have installed barriers on its dam face.

It is concerned about people swimming, paddleboarding, littering and damaging structures around the site.

Although the reservoir can be accessed via public footpaths, the barriers were installed to stop people from walking on the dam face - but these have since been removed by trespassers.

The owners said the Â£2 levy was introduced in an effort to manage unauthorised visits and help fund clean-up operations, as part of its efforts to discourage public access because of "inherent safety risks".

A spokesperson for the company said: "We have strictly banned [people] from going there and walking on the face of the dam.

"Our long-term vision has always been to build a sustainable public-private framework so the community can safely enjoy this asset.

"However, managing a critical piece of infrastructure presents immense structural, environmental, and financial challenges that cannot be indefinitely sustained by a private entity alone."

News.title: UK borrows less than expected in June but public finances remain a challenge
News.content:
The government borrowed slightly less than expected in June, according to figures published as new Prime Minister Andy Burnham began setting out measures to cut living costs for households.

Borrowing - the difference between spending and income from taxes - was Â£16bn, about Â£7.9bn lower than a year earlier, although analysts said challenges remained over the UK's public finances.

Other data showed the unemployment rate was unchanged, with the Office for National Statistics (ONS) saying the labour market was "relatively steady".

However, while the borrowing figure was less than forecast, the ONS said total debt was high by historical standards and close to the annual value of the UK economy.

Borrowing for June was slightly below the Â£16.3bn that had been predicted by the government's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said June's figure was "a rare piece of good news" for the new prime minister and his new Chancellor, John Healey.

However, she added: "Overall, there's no escaping the fact that the public finances are fragile and that there is limited scope for extra borrowing."

So far in the current financial year, borrowing has reached a total of Â£57.6bn, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). While this is down Â£3.7bn from the same period last year, it is Â£2.7bn above the OBR's forecast.

James Smith, chief UK economist at ING, told the BBC's Today programme the fact that borrowing was still running ahead of the OBR's projections was "a reminder of the challenges that the new chancellor and the new prime minister face".

He added they would face a "difficult picture" at the autumn Budget, with "lots of tough choices to be made".

Burnham and Healey have both pledged to stick to former chancellor Rachel Reeves' fiscal rules on spending and borrowing, although the new prime minister said on Monday he would use "any flexibility within them" to help with policy changes.

Shortly after Burnham's comments were made public, the yield on 10-year government bonds - effectively the interest rate charged to the UK government for a 10-year loan - rose above 5%.

The yield hit 5.03% late on Monday afternoon. However, when trading began on Tuesday the rate slipped back slightly to 5.01%.

In a statement released on Monday, Healey said "fiscal credibility is the bedrock for economic stability and for national security".

Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said Labour had "maxed out the nation's credit card and sent borrowing soaring".

"If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control," he said.

The new leadership's first major policy announcement was to cut VAT on household electricity bills from 5% to zero from the beginning of October.

Ministers said it would be funded by savings from the cancellation of the digital ID programme, but Labour's Darren Jones, who was sacked as chief secretary to the prime minister on Monday, accused the government of announcing an unfunded tax cut.

News.title: Teenagers jailed for murdering 16-year-old in beach knife attack
News.content:
Three teenagers have been jailed for murdering a 16-year-old boy during a confrontation between rival groups on a beach in North Ayrshire last year.

They were convicted of stabbing apprentice painter and decorator Kayden Moy on Irvine Beach on 17 May 2025.

Cole Turley, 18, who had pleaded guilty to the murder, and Jay Stewart, 19 were given life sentences and told they will serve a minimum of 16 years.

A third teenager - a 15-year-old who cannot be named for legal reasons - will be detained for a minimum of 14 years.

Speaking outside the High Court in Glasgow, Moy's father said his family's grief meant they were themselves enduring a life sentence.

Paul Moy said: "While today's outcome brings a measure of justice, it does not bring peace, it does not bring our son back.

"Kayden was more than a name in the courtroom or a headline in the news, he was our son, he was loved beyond words and had his whole life ahead of him.

"We hope today's sentence sends a clear message that violence has a devastating and irreversible consequences.

"One moment of violence has destroyed so many lives and no family should ever have to endure the pain that we now live with every day."

News.title: Toddler, 3, drowned in swimming pool on family holiday, inquest hears
News.content:
A three-year-old girl drowned in a swimming pool during a family holiday in Majorca, an inquest has heard.

Eleri Ellesmere was discovered unresponsive in the water at their private villa near the town of Pollensa on the evening of 24 June.

The toddler was taken by ambulance to the Spanish island's main hospital, 44 miles (70km) away in the capital, Palma. She died there the following day.

A full inquest will be held in April next year.

The inquest opening on Monday heard Eleri and her family, from New Tredegar in Caerphilly county, were staying at a rented villa with a private pool just under five miles (8km) from Pollensa, in the far north of the island.

It is a popular area with British families for its sandy beaches, and Villa Francisca, a two-bedroom villa, is described on booking websites as "an ideal choice for a family holiday in the sun".

Gwent Coroner's Court heard that family members and later paramedics both attempted CPR before Eleri was taken to the Hospital Universitari Son Espases.

Eleri's body was flown back to the UK and has been formally identified by an undertaker, the inquest heard.

Coroner Rose Farmer said the provisional cause of death was mechanical asphyxiation by drowning and respiratory failure. A full inquest will be held on 13 April 2027.

Eleri's family said she was deeply loved and her parents now face "the most devastating chapter a mother, father and surrounding family can experience".

An online fundraiser has been set up by family member Shannen Hemmings to raise Â£10,000 to pay for Eleri's funeral and to provide financial support for her parents.

It has so far raised more than Â£7,000.

Hemmings wrote that "Eleri was deeply loved, and her loss has left an unimaginable emptiness in all of our lives".

She said the funds raised would help ensure "beautiful Eleri is given the funeral she truly deserves, a farewell filled with dignity, love and respect".

She added it would also allow her parents "the time and space to grieve without the added weight of financial worry, so they can focus on healing and leaning on one another during this heartbreaking time".

News.title: Monkey abandoned in laundry bag on London bus
News.content:
A marmoset monkey has been rescued by animal welfare officers after being found abandoned inside a laundry bag on a bus in north-west London.

The female primate was discovered by a driver on the route 302 bus when it arrived at Kensal Rise on Friday morning, the RSPCA said.

A passenger with a buggy had been unable to move down the bus because the bag was blocking the luggage bay. When the driver moved it, the monkey began chirping and jumping inside.

A spokesperson for the charity said the marmoset was trapped inside a small, metal bird cage wrapped in a chequered plastic bag. She was left with a piece of apple but was stressed and dehydrated.

News.title: Thames Water lenders offer 'golden share' to head off nationalisation
News.content:
Thames Water's main lenders are offering the government a "golden share" and more control for local authorities in a bid to stop the troubled supplier from being nationalised.

The government recently rejected a previous rescue proposal, and the BBC understands the lenders are preparing a legal challenge in case the new Andy Burnham-led government takes the firm into public hands.

The "golden share" would give the government veto powers over major decisions such as mergers.

The lenders are also proposing giving local authorities greater involvement in the firm, similar to the relationship between United Utilities and Greater Manchester agreed when Burnham was the city's mayor.

In his first speech as prime minister on Monday, Burnham said he wanted to see greater public control of "life's essentials".

Sources close to the creditors have told the BBC that in the event of full nationalisation they would pursue payment in full of the outstanding debts, as has happened in previous cases, which could leave the government with a multi-billion-pound bill.

The London & Valley Water (L&VW ) consortium of lenders had already proposed a Â£10bn deal to prevent Thames Water from entering administration. It would involve writing off nearly half of its debt and injecting new cash in return for leniency on future pollution fines.

The deal was rejected by the government in June, with then-environment secretary Emma Reynolds saying it did not do enough for consumers or the environment.

Sources close to the new deal said the creditors had sweetened it with hundreds of millions in new money on top of the existing offer.

A golden share would give the government veto power over major decisions such as mergers and acquisitions. Golden shares are seen as a way for the government to retain a stake in companies of national significance or importance, such as Royal Mail or Rolls Royce.

Any new proposals would have to be reviewed by Ofwat, the regulator.

A government spokesperson said Thames Water "remains financially stable, but we stand ready for all eventualities, including applying for a Special Administration Regime [SAR] if that were to become necessary".

"The government will always act in the national interest on these issues," they added.

An SAR is a form of temporary nationalisation which would allow the government to recoup some taxpayer cash if Thames was sold again to a private buyer.

L&VW said on Tuesday that the new offer had "material improvements" on the old one, and would benefit customers.

A spokesperson said: "We continue to believe that the L&VW plan is by far the fastest and most reliable route to solving Thames Water's complex problems and improving outcomes for customers and the environment."

They said the new deal "achieves this without any government funding or cost to taxpayers".

Fears first emerged three years ago that Thames Water could collapse and it has recently warned it could run out of cash by November.

If the company does go bust, households will still have drinking water and sewerage services.

Thames Water announced a hosepipe ban for all of its customers on Tuesday morning, citing the UK's "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The company, which supplies water and wastewater services for 16 million people across London and parts of southern England, was handed a Â£122.7m fine last year, the biggest ever issued by the industry regulator Ofwat, for breaching rules on sewage spills and shareholder payouts.

Sources close to the creditors have previously told the BBC that in the event of full nationalisation, they would pursue payment in full of the outstanding debts as has happened in previous cases, which could leave the government with a multi-billion-pound bill.

Longtime ESPN broadcaster Karl Ravech is expected to be among the latest layoffs at the network, sources told The Athletic Tuesday.

Ravech, a 31-year ESPN veteran, served as the network’s lead baseball play-by-play announcer and also covered college basketball and anchored SportsCenter. He called the Dodgers-Phillies game Monday before reportedly learning his job was at risk.

When contacted by The Athletic Tuesday morning, Ravech reportedly said he had not yet been informed of his status as ESPN prepared to notify employees.

A memo from ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro to employees Tuesday morning, obtained by The Independent, did not identify those impacted by the layoffs but said the cuts followed a review of the company’s teams, resources and structure after integrating acquired NFL assets.

“Over the past several months, we've made significant progress integrating the NFL assets that we acquired into ESPN. Throughout this process, we have taken the time to carefully evaluate our collective teams, resources and organizational structure to best position us for the future. As a result, we had to make some difficult decisions about job impacts that we will be communicating today,” Pitaro wrote.

open image in gallery Karl Ravech, pictured, is reportedly among those impacted by ESPN’s latest round of layoffs, sources told The Athletic Tuesday ( Getty )

“While most of the job impacts are tied to the acquisition, we will also notify colleagues in other parts of the company today that their positions have been impacted. We are committed to treating employees with compassion and respect and to providing support as they navigate this transition,” the memo continued. “Even in moments like these, the strength of ESPN comes from our people, our teamwork and our shared mission to serve sports fans.”

ESPN declined to provide further comment.

The cuts follow ESPN’s decision Monday to part ways with NFL analyst Ryan Clark, with additional layoffs expected to hit behind-the-scenes staff. Most of the reductions are reportedly coming at NFL Network, including Tom Pelissero, one of the network’s top insiders, per The Athletic.

Wedding suppliers who have turned their hobby into a money-making side hustle are being urged to check their tax obligations.

With the summer wedding season under way, people earning extra income from activities such as selling wedding stationery, filming the first dance or cake making are being reminded that they may need to register for self-assessment and declare their income to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

If someone has earned more than the £1,000 trading allowance from their side hustle in a tax year, they may need to complete a self-assessment tax return.

The £1,000 threshold is a single allowance that covers side hustle income when combined – so someone earning smaller amounts which, when totalled up, are above this threshold could be liable.

Not all extra income is taxable though, for example HMRC said it would not usually expect people to tell it if they are having a wardrobe clear-out and selling unwanted personal belongings.

However, regularly selling goods for profit, or providing a service for payment, is likely to count as trading and may need to be declared, the revenue body said.

The tax year runs from April 6 to April 5 each year.

New entrants to self-assessment should register for the 2025-26 tax year by October 5 2026 and must file their online tax return and pay any tax due by January 31 2027, HMRC said.

It said an online tool on gov.uk can help people earning extra money to check if and when they need to report their additional income.

An Australian woman has given birth to four healthy identical babies following an “extremely” risky pregnancy with “one-in-15 million” odds.

The quadruplets – named Emily, Harriet, Catherine, and Alexa – were delivered prematurely by caesarean section at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital on 14 July. They were born at 28 weeks and four days - more than two months shy of the full term.

Dr Alexa Bendall, who has cared for mother Jenitar Na'amoana, 34, since the start of her surprise pregnancy, said: “We always said that if we could get her to 28 weeks, we would be doing well.”

“So the fact that we've got four beautiful, healthy babies born at 28 weeks and four days is incredible and we're very happy to be a part of it," she added. Dr Bendall said it was a “beautiful tribute” to have one of the girls named after her.

The infants remain in the neonatal intensive care unit, where doctors say they are doing “extremely well”. They are expected to remain until they grow to full term, Dr Bendall said.

open image in gallery The four children were born premature but healthy on 14 July ( Metro North Health )

The rare pregnancy involved a single fertilised egg splitting into four embryos, the hospital noted, making the naturally conceived babies monozygotic, or identical, quadruplets.

Dr Bendall said she had never encountered such a case before.

“This is unheard of. We don’t think it has ever happened in Australia,” the doctor said, according to the news agency AAP.

“There may have been a couple of cases elsewhere in the world. And when I say a couple, literally two.”

Dr Bendall described the pregnancy as extremely high-risk because the four babies shared a single placenta, a situation that could cause complications for both the mother and the children.

“There’s a high risk of mortality and morbidity for these babies and for mum,” she said, according to 7 News.

open image in gallery Jenitar Na’amoana, 34, and her husband already had four children before the surprise pregnancy ( GoFundMe )

Ms Na’amoana was admitted to hospital at 25 weeks so doctors could closely monitor her condition. The medical team had hoped to safely reach 28 weeks of pregnancy.

“When they went along and found out they had four babies instead of one they were quite shocked,” Dr Bendall said.

“We have never seen a spontaneously conceived pregnancy of this type with quads and she’s somehow dodged every complication and risk for both herself and her babies to be here today, with four gorgeous newborn girls.”

Hospital staff said the babies were expected to remain in intensive care until they were closer to full term but had made an encouraging start.

open image in gallery Dr Alexa Bendall, who oversaw Na’amoana’s care, said she had never encountered such a pregnancy before ( GoFundMe )

Ms Na’amoana has started a GoFundMe campaign to help cover the costs of raising the four babies at once, including medical expenses, travel, everyday living costs, and a larger vehicle capable of seating the expanded family.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely,” she wrote on the fundraising page. “While our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges we never could have imagined.”

“We urgently need a larger van with 10 or 12 seats, essential baby equipment, and help with ongoing medical, travel, and everyday living expenses.”

Ms Na’amoana and her husband already had four children before the surprise pregnancy. The older children are between one and 10 years old.

A Boston woman believes toxic blue-green algae poisoning may have claimed the life of her family's 16-year-old dog after a swim at a local park.

Elivia Savadier Sagov said both of her dogs became sick after swimming in the Charles River Friday at Millennium Park in West Roxbury, Massachusetts. She told CBS Boston that the water appeared clean, but she noticed her dog, Dobby, drinking from it before she could stop her.

"It was so beautiful and clear. I saw her drink some water, which I didn't like, but I didn't catch her soon enough," Savadier Sagov said.

Both dogs showed signs of illness within hours of being exposed to the water, according to Savadier Sagov. While both became sick, Dobby, a 16-year-old, experienced more severe symptoms, including muscle stiffness, seizures, weakness and gastrointestinal issues, Savadier Sagov claimed.

Dobby died Sunday, her owner said, leaving her with the belief that the blue-green algae poisoning may have been responsible.

A pet owner believes toxic algae poisoning killed her 16-year-old dog, Dobby, days after she swam at Millennium Park in West Roxbury, Massachusetts ( CBS Boston )

"This year I was very aware [of the algae]. I thought maybe not to let them in the water at all, but it's so tempting,” Savadier Sagov told CBS Boston. “We miss her terribly. It's just been so sudden. Just really miss her.”

The Charles River Watershed Association told WBZ-TV it is unaware of any recent water testing in the section of the Charles River near Millennium Park where the dogs reportedly swam.

However, the river has experienced cyanobacteria, or blue-green algae blooms, nearly every summer over the past decade, with the longest lasting 12 weeks in 2020, according to the organization’s website.

Cyanobacteria can produce toxins that are dangerous to people and animals, with dogs especially at risk because they may drink contaminated water or ingest algae while swimming in rivers, lakes and ponds, according to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine.

Toxic blooms are most common in warm, stagnant, nutrient-rich water, and the toxins can linger for weeks even after the algae is no longer visible.

The toxins can attack the nervous system, liver or skin, causing vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, muscle tremors, seizures, collapse, difficulty breathing and, in severe cases, death.

Symptoms can appear within minutes to hours, and because there is no antidote, owners should seek immediate veterinary care if exposure is suspected, according to Cornell.

Savadier Sagov thinks these warning signs need to be posted at local spots.

"I almost feel there should be permanent notices here that state it very strongly: July and August there is likely to be algae,” she told CBS Boston. “If there's rain, you may not even see the scum, but spores are still in the water. And once the dog get this, the vets say there's nothing that can be done.”

The Independent has contacted the Charles River Watershed Association for comment.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe ‘struck with hammer 21 times’, court hears
News.content:

The man charged with murdering former MP Ann Widdecombe is accused of hitting her 21 times with a hammer and taking her wallet, a court heard.

Joshua Kerry, 28, is alleged to have arrived at the Reform UK spokeswoman’s remote bungalow in Haytor, Devon, shortly after midday on Wednesday 8 July.

A doorbell camera captured the suspect’s red Vauxhall Corsa pulling up outside the property, Westminster Magistrates’ Court heard.

A camera positioned in the hallway showed the 78-year-old politician sitting down eating lunch in the kitchen before the defendant allegedly entered via the front door and asked her: “Don’t suppose you have bank cards and ID?”

He is then alleged to have struck her 21 times on the head with the hammer before tipping her out of her chair and on to the floor.

open image in gallery Ms Widdecombe was found dead at her home ( PA Archive )

Ms Widdecombe was discovered face-down on the kitchen floor the following day by a gardener, who had been asked to check on the former Conservative prisons minister after she missed an interview scheduled with Channel 5.

A provisional cause of death was given as a “blunt force injury to the head”, the court heard.

Kerry, who was arrested days later at his home 265 miles away in Rotherham, South Yorkshire, appeared wearing a grey prison-issue tracksuit. He sat with his arms folded and spoke only to confirm his name , date of birth and address during the brief hearing.

A hammer and black gloves - on which Ms Widdecombe’s DNA was found - was recovered during a search of bins outside his property, prosecutor Kashir Malik said.

Chief magistrate Paul Goldspring told the defendant: “You are charged with an offence of murder which can only be tried in the crown court.”

At a hearing at the Old Bailey on Tuesday afternoon, Kerry was remanded in custody by Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb.

He was told to appear at the same court on 9 October for a case management hearing, with a further plea and trial preparation hearing on 20 November.

A provisional trial date was listed for 8 June 2027.

open image in gallery Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court ( PA )

Announcing the charges on Monday, Counter Terrorism Policing head Laurence Taylor said that establishing whether the attack was politically motivated remains an “active avenue of investigation”.

“I want to make it very clear that our investigation into this individual, determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing,” he said in a statement delivered outside Scotland Yard.

“Given Ann Widdecombe's profile and the targeted nature of the attack, determining the motivation, including any possible political motivation, remains an active avenue of investigation for our detectives. And as with all murder investigations, understanding the why is a key part of our inquiries.”

News.title: California city manager arrested on burglary charges after being on the job for less than three weeks
News.content:

A newly appointed California city official was arrested on burglary charges after being found on board someone else’s yacht over the weekend, less than three weeks after taking over the municipality’s top administrative role.

Elaine Forbes, the 53-year-old city manager of Sausalito, was taken into custody shortly before 7 a.m. on Saturday by the Marin County Sheriff’s Office, the Marin Independent Journal first reported. Forbes, who previously spent nine years running the Port of San Francisco, faces felony charges following an incident at a local dock.

According to sheriff's deputies, Forbes allegedly boarded at least two vessels docked near a local restaurant, including a boat named the Lisa Marie.

A yacht captain, Bill Aubrey, was moored nearby and first noticed the disturbance when he heard a boat horn blaring at around 5:30 a.m., according to The San Francisco Standard. Aubrey said he had found Forbes inside the wheelhouse, where she looked at him and replied, “Good morning!” pleasantly, after he had boarded the vessel and told her to get off.

Investigators stated that she appeared to try to start one of the vessels by manipulating its switches and control levers. Authorities also noted that alcohol bottles on board the vessels had been opened and either consumed or poured out.

open image in gallery Elaine Forbes, the 53-year-old city manager of Sausalito, California, was arrested on Saturday after reportedly attempting to steal a yacht, fewer than three weeks after starting her role ( City of Sausalito )

Residents reported hearing a disturbance at the harbor early Saturday morning. Michael Lappert, a witness at the scene, told ABC7 San Francisco that a boat horn was sounded continuously for nearly two hours before police intervened.

“She was honking the horn, all these large yachts have a very loud horn because you’re out in the ocean and you gotta be heard so when you honk that thing I think most people have heard what those sound like,” Lappert said.

The arrest comes amid recent adjustments to Forbes’ employment status, as reported by the Los Angeles Times. On Thursday, the Sausalito City Council held a closed-door session and approved an immediate leave of absence for the city manager, though local officials declined to provide specific reasons for the decision at the time.

The Sausalito City Council voted unanimously in May to hire Forbes, according to a city news release. She officially started her job on July 1 with a base salary of $275,000, the LA Times reported.

“Elaine has proven to be a strong executive and it's important for this community to have a strong executive to help us sort through the many issues that we face,” Mayor Steven Woodside said at the time, according to the city news release.

“People from around the world save money and dream of coming to Sausalito for very good reasons. I'm incredibly honored to join this community,” Forbes said at the City Council meeting in which she was appointed.

Following her arrest, the City of Sausalito released a statement acknowledging the situation.

“This is a difficult development for our City staff and our community,” the statement read, adding that the municipality would withhold further comment due to the active criminal investigation.

A representative for Forbes’ family, public relations executive Sam Singer, issued a statement asking the public not to rush to judgment.

“Elaine is experiencing a mental health crisis,” Singer wrote. “As the facts become clearer and Elaine obtains legal and healthcare counsel in the coming hours and days, we hope people will respond with compassion, patience and respect for her and her family during an extraordinarily difficult time.”

Forbes remained in custody as of late Sunday afternoon, according to booking records.

News.title: Naval crews beat each other with oars as Philippine and Chinese vessels clash over disputed territory
News.content:
Naval crews from China and the Philippines appeared to beat each other with oars in a clash over a disputed territory, leaving one Filipino sailor injured.

Footage from Monday (20 July) shows several boats passing by one another in the Second Thomas Shoal, a submerged reef that is claimed by both Beijing and Manila.

Philippine officials said one of its navy personnel was struck on the head by a wooden baton; however, Beijing said Manila provoked the incident by ramming one of its patrol vehicles.

The Second Thomas Shoal, where a grounded Philippine navy ship has served as a territorial outpost since 1999, is within the 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone of the Philippines. It is about 1,300km from mainland China, which refers to it as the Renai Reef.

News.title: The best cat food, recommended by a vet – including new online cat food delivery services
News.content:
As a cat carer for over 50 years and a vet for nearly 40, I understand the importance of finding the best cat food. It isn’t always easy to get it right. Cats need a complete and balanced diet providing protein, carbohydrate, fats, minerals, vitamins and fibre, as well as some specific nutrients such as taurine and essential fatty acids.

With such a huge range of products available, selecting the right one can be a real challenge. The aim of this article is to offer guidance on how to select the optimal diet for your feline friend. You can read my full reviews of the current best cat foods further down, followed by a comprehensive guide to cat nutrition, where you’ll learn how much and how often to feed your cat, among other things. But if you’re in a hurry, here’s a quick look at my top five:

The best cat foods: At a glance

Are cat food delivery services better than shopping in pet stores?

There are pros and cons to both. News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

News.title: How to have the perfect holiday in France’s gastronomic capital
News.content:
Calling all bon vivants. This is your city. Within seconds of tucking into a traditional andouillette (tripe sausage) or modern vegetarian cuisine in a jam-packed bistro, admiring fine art in a Renaissance abbey, or getting delightfully lost in a traboule (secret passageway) used by 19th-century silk weavers, you’ll quickly realise that Lyon is a city that knows how to live well.

Enthralling, cinematic and richly storied, after living here for 10 years, I still find myself being surprised by a walled garden I never knew, a fresque (wall mural) suddenly popping up on a riverfront wall, a new museum or river boat route.

Street-smart Romans first spotted the city’s extraordinary topography, founding Lugdunum (Lyon’s predecessor) in 43BC on the sunny slopes of Fourvière. And to this day, this basilica-crowned hill above Lyon’s quaint Unesco-listed Old Town (Vieux Lyon) is the perfect perch for clocking the mighty Rhône and Saône rivers that wend their way so gracefully through the centre.

The city’s quays, landscaped with peaceful water gardens and floating bars, buzz night and day – while culture lovers can explore a bounty of museums. Then there’s the gastronomy: among France’s finest, thanks to the unfaltering creativity and sass of city chefs, both past and present.

Sports.title: ‘Football is suffering’ – Gianni Infantino told to resign over radical plot to make World Cup even bigger
Sports.content:
GIANNI INFANTINO has been told to QUIT by furious LaLiga boss Javier Tebas over a plot to expand the World Cup to 64 countries.

The Spanish football chief lost his rag as the dust settled on this summer’s already-bloated 48-nation tournament that was plagued with controversy.



It included a personal intervention by Donald Trump to overturn a USA red card, a 27-minute half-time in the final and hydration breaks in air-conditioned stadiums.

And when asked directly if Infantino should pack his bags after 10 years at the helm, Tebas, 63, did not hold back.



He said: “In my opinion, yes, I think he has had his day.

“But he has the support of the system, of the federations. There is no opposition candidate, no-one wants to present themselves to lose.



“This is the system and it’s one that’s sick at the source.

“I don’t know if silence or complicity is worse because those who are silent are perfectly aware of the damage that football is suffering.”

There are growing fears that the radical move to pack extra countries into the 2030 tournament to be staged in Spain, Portugal and Morocco — as well as games in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay — will push domestic leagues to breaking point.

Fifa are to stage three opening matches in the South American nations to mark 100 years since their participation in the first World Cup held in Uruguay.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Tebas fumed: “Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense. The football industry is not just the World Cup, which is the most important event.

“But not everything can revolve around the World Cup. It’s national competitions that support this sport.”

The LaLiga chief claims the relentless expansion of international fixtures is putting thousands of ordinary club jobs at risk across Europe.

He barked: “They are destroying the industry, the one that generates tens of thousands of jobs.



“And for what? An event that lasts 40 days and to which the minority of players go.

“We need fewer national teams and more protection for national football, at all levels. They don’t realise but they decide irresponsibly.”

Infantino, 56, is still poised to be re-elected for a fourth term at Fifa’s March congress.

But Tebas also believes the under-fire president should have already been brought down by the Folarin Balogun affair.

The USA striker’s one-match ban after being sent off against Bosnia and Herzegovina was controversially suspended by Fifa’s disciplinary committee after Infantino received a personal call from American president Donald Trump.



That decision allowed Balogun to play in their last-16 tie with Belgium.

Tebas said: “The suspension of the American player’s disqualification is something of absolute gravity.

“They were lucky Belgium eliminated the USA because otherwise a case could have been created that could have cost Infantino his job.



“Since Belgium won, they managed to bury the thing. But these things are only the tip of the iceberg.

“Fifa fixes things as it wants, for what it wants, for its interests, certainly not for football.”

The Spanish boss also took a swipe at TV  breaks during games in America, labelling them a total corporate scam.

Tebas claims greedy television bosses are using fake hydration breaks to cash in.

He added: “If they need a 27-minute interval to suit their interests, they just do it. These hydration breaks are a lie.



“We have them in LaLiga, but only when it’s really hot.

“Over in America, the stadiums in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Atlanta had full air conditioning. I actually had to put on a sweater in the stands!

“The heat was a total lie. It was just an excuse for an advertising break.”
