Donald Trump has threatened to blow Iran "off the face of the earth" if it attacks US ships trying to reopen the blocked Strait of Hormuz, pushing the region back to the edge of full-scale war.

The threats came as the US launched its "Project Freedom" operation on Monday to help hundreds of ships and their crews get moving again after months of being stuck in the Gulf. Over 800 ships and around 20,000 crew members are still stranded in the region.

Iran hit back hard, warning it would strike any US ship approaching the strait. Iran's military claimed it had already fired two missiles at a US warship in the area. The US military said it destroyed six Iranian boats and shot down Iranian missiles and drones, though Iran denied this.

Trump called the US naval effort "one of the greatest military maneuvers ever done" in an interview with Fox News on Monday. He also said Iranian officials had been "far more open" in recent talks than before, suggesting a deal could still happen.

Trump's threats echo comments he made in April when he warned that a "whole civilisation will die" if Iran did not comply with his demands. Those comments drew criticism from around the world.

The fragile ceasefire brokered by Pakistan last month has stopped the bombing but failed to reopen the strait, which normally carries about one fifth of the world's oil supplies.

The US military said it had redirected 50 ships on Monday as part of the ongoing operation.

Image source: File

Trump launches 'Project Freedom' to get ships out of blocked oil route

Donald Trump has announced a new operation called "Project Freedom" to help hundreds of trapped ships get out of the Strait of Hormuz, as he claimed peace talks with Iran were going well.

More than 900 ships are stuck in the Gulf with crews who may be running low on food and basic supplies after months of being blocked in. Trump said US forces would start moving vessels to safety from Monday.

"We will use best efforts to get their ships and crews safely out of the strait," he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump called the operation a "humanitarian" gesture, saying the crews had suffered enough. He also said his team were having "very positive discussions" with Iran that could lead to something good for everyone.

But Iran gave little away. Its foreign minister said Tehran had sent Washington a 14-point peace plan, and that the US had already written back through Pakistani mediators. Iran's spokesman said they were looking at the response and would act when ready.

Peace talks have been stuck since the ceasefire began on April 8, with only one round of face-to-face talks held so far.

The blocked strait has pushed oil prices up by about 50 percent since the war began in February. Germany's foreign minister has demanded the route be reopened immediately, saying Iran must give up nuclear weapons and unblock it now.

Both sides are still hitting each other where it hurts, with Iran cutting off oil and gas to the world and the US blocking Iranian ports.

Image source: File

Trump jokes he will not wear a bulletproof vest because he does not want to look fat

Donald Trump has said he refuses to wear a bulletproof vest despite surviving multiple assassination attempts, joking that he does not want to look 20 pounds heavier.

Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump told journalists he had been asked about wearing protection but was not keen. "I don't know if I can handle looking 20 pounds heavier," he said. "In one way, you don't like to do it because you're giving in to a bad element."

The comments came days after a man armed with guns and knives tried to storm the White House Correspondents' dinner in what prosecutors say was a plot to kill Trump. Cole Tomas Allen was taken into custody and agreed on Thursday to remain behind bars while awaiting trial. A Secret Service officer was shot during the incident but survived because he was wearing a bulletproof vest.

In other news from the Oval Office, Trump said he would lift tariffs on Scottish whisky, crediting King Charles and Queen Camilla's state visit to the White House with changing his mind. "The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do," he said. Buckingham Palace said the King "will be raising a dram to the President's thoughtfulness."

Image source: File

Trump considers sending troops into Iran

Oil prices have shot up to $125 a barrel as Donald Trump weighs new military options against Iran, including sending ground troops into the country.

Trump is expected to be briefed on Thursday by US military commanders on a range of options to break the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz. These include a fresh wave of strikes on Iranian infrastructure, deploying ground forces to take control of part of the strait, and using special forces to seize Iran's stockpile of enriched uranium.

Oil was trading at around $70 a barrel before the war began in late February. It has now nearly doubled in price, pushing up the cost of fuel for ordinary people around the world.

Trump renamed the Strait of Hormuz the "Strait of Trump" in a social media post on Thursday, urging Iran to sign a deal. "Iran can't get their act together. They better get smart soon," he wrote.

The US military said it had turned away 42 ships trying to pass its blockade of Iranian ports, blocking Iran from selling an estimated $6-billion worth of oil.

The war has so far cost the US military $25-billion, according to a senior Pentagon official. Most of that money has been spent on weapons.

Trump also claimed that Russian president Vladimir Putin offered to help deal with Iran's enriched uranium. "He told me he'd like to be involved with the enrichment," Trump said.

The US is also trying to build a coalition of countries to help reopen the strait to shipping.

Image source: File

Trump's face is going on American passports

The United States will release a limited number of passports featuring a portrait of Donald Trump, the White House has confirmed.

The passports will be available to any American citizen who applies for one when they go on sale, but only at the Washington Passport Agency and only for as long as stocks last. They will be released as part of celebrations marking 250 years since the US Declaration of Independence in July.

The new passport shows Trump's image surrounded by the text of the Declaration of Independence and the American flag, with his signature printed in gold. Current US passports feature historical scenes such as the Moon landing and the Statue of Liberty.

It is not yet clear whether Americans will be able to choose not to receive the special edition.

The Trump passport is the latest in a long line of moves to put the president's name and face on public buildings and government programmes. The US Mint is planning a gold coin featuring Trump as part of the same anniversary celebrations. Trump is also set to become the first sitting US president to have his signature printed on US banknotes.

A performing arts centre in Washington previously known as the Kennedy Center has been renamed the Trump-Kennedy Center, a move condemned by members of the Kennedy family.

Plans have also been approved for a 76-metre victory arch in Washington called the "Arc de Trump." The White House is also being sued after construction of a new ballroom began before the proper plans were filed.

Image source: @WhiteHouse

America tells South Africa it wants to kiss and make up

The United States has signalled that it may be willing to repair its relationship with South Africa, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio sending a public message of goodwill on Freedom Day.

"We remain open to constructive engagement where our interests align," Rubio said in a statement on Monday, marking the 32nd anniversary of South Africa's first democratic elections on 27 April 1994.

It was the first formal public outreach from the US to South Africa in months, coming after a long period of bad blood between the two countries.

Trump has repeatedly claimed without evidence that white Afrikaners are being systematically killed in South Africa. He ambushed President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office last year, playing a video repeating those claims.

The US boycotted the G20 summit hosted by South Africa in Johannesburg, with Trump saying the South African government refused to address what he called human rights abuses against Afrikaners. The US State Department later said it wanted to remove South Africa from the G20 altogether and replace it with Poland.

South Africa was dealt another blow this month when Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana was blocked from attending a G20 finance meeting in Washington.

Despite Rubio's message, it is not yet clear whether relations between the two countries are genuinely improving.

Image source: File

Iran says it will make America regret the war

Several senior Iranian officials have pushed back hard against Donald Trump's claim that Iran's leadership is falling apart, saying the country stands together as "one soul."

Iran's president, foreign minister and parliament speaker all posted the same message on X on Thursday. "We are all Iranian and revolutionary, and with the iron unity of the nation and government, we will make the aggressor criminal regret his actions," they wrote.

Trump has spent the past week claiming that Iran's leaders are fighting among themselves and do not know who is in charge. He used this to justify extending the ceasefire, saying Iran needed more time to sort itself out.

Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi fired back. "The battlefield and diplomacy are fully coordinated fronts in the same war. Iranians are all united, more than ever before," he wrote.

Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who took power after his father was killed in US strikes in February, has not been seen in public since. US officials say he was wounded in the same strike. The New York Times reported he is gravely wounded but still mentally sharp.

Trump made clear on Thursday he was in no hurry to end the war. "A deal will only be made when it is appropriate and good for the United States," he posted. He also warned that US forces would shoot and kill Iranians laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Israel added to the pressure, with its defence minister saying the military was locked, loaded and waiting for Trump's go-ahead to strike Iran again.

Image source: File

Trump asks Fifa to replace Iran with Italy at the World Cup

A close ally of Donald Trump has asked Fifa to replace Iran with Italy at this summer's World Cup, the Financial Times has reported.

Paolo Zampolli, a US special envoy, confirmed the request. "I confirm I have suggested to Trump and Fifa president Gianni Infantino that Italy replace Iran at the World Cup," he told the FT. "I'm an Italian native and it would be a dream to see the Azzurri at a US-hosted tournament."

The move is reportedly an attempt to repair relations between Trump and Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni after the two fell out over Trump's attacks on Pope Leo XIV during the Iran war.

Italy failed to qualify for the World Cup for the third time in a row after losing a playoff final to Bosnia and Herzegovina on penalties in March.

Iran issued a statement on Wednesday saying it was prepared for the tournament and planned to participate, according to the FT.

Iran had previously said it would only decide whether to send its team once Fifa responded to its request to move its matches from the US to Mexico.

Image source: File

Trump extends Iran ceasefire

Donald Trump has extended the ceasefire with Iran without setting a new deadline, saying the US military will hold off its planned attack until Iran puts forward a plan to end the war.

Trump made the announcement on Tuesday in a social media post, just hours after saying he was against extending the truce. The ceasefire had been due to expire on Wednesday.

Trump said he was extending it at the request of Pakistan's prime minister and army chief, who are helping to broker peace between the two sides. He said Iran's government was "seriously fractured" and needed more time to come up with a unified response.

But Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi rejected that claim and called the US blockade of Iranian ports an "act of war." "Iran knows how to resist bullying," he wrote.

A reporter for Al Jazeera in Tehran said Trump's claim about divisions in Iran's leadership was likely wrong, saying the country has been united under its new leadership since the killing of former supreme leader Ali Khamenei.

The two sides remain far apart. The US wants Iran to shut down its nuclear programme completely. Iran says it has the right to enrich uranium and will not give up its weapons or its support for groups like Hezbollah.

Pakistan's prime minister Shehbaz Sharif welcomed the extension. "I sincerely hope that both sides will continue to observe the ceasefire," he said.

Image source: File

Trump is hurting his own peace talks

Peace talks between the US and Iran were thrown into confusion this week after Donald Trump made a series of claims on social media and to reporters that Iranian officials quickly rejected.

Trump told several news outlets on Friday that Iran had agreed to key demands, including handing over its enriched uranium and suspending its nuclear programme. Iran denied this, saying it had not agreed to those things. Some Trump officials privately told CNN that the president's public comments were hurting the talks.

"The Iranians didn't appreciate the president negotiating through social media and making it appear as if they had signed off on issues they hadn't yet agreed to," one person familiar with the talks told CNN.

Trump also gave confusing and contradictory information about whether Vice-President JD Vance would lead the US delegation to the next round of talks in Pakistan. At one point Trump told reporters Vance would not be going, while two senior government officials said on television that he would. Vance is now expected to travel to Islamabad on Tuesday, with talks set to begin on Wednesday.

The two-week ceasefire between the US and Iran is also due to expire soon. Trump has given different answers about whether he would extend it, at one point saying "if there's no deal, fighting resumes," and at another saying he would extend it if needed. He told Bloomberg the ceasefire ends Wednesday evening Washington time.

The two sides remain far apart on key issues. The US wants Iran to stop enriching uranium and hand over its stockpile. Iran wants to keep control of the Strait of Hormuz and have US sanctions lifted. Proposals on how long any pause on enrichment should last have ranged from five to twenty years, with neither side yet agreeing.

Trump said on Monday he was "under no pressure whatsoever" to reach a deal.

Image source: File

Trump says again that white people are being killed in South Africa

Donald Trump has again claimed that white people are being persecuted and killed in South Africa, calling it "a genocide."

Trump has made this claim before and used it to justify offering white South Africans refugee status in the United States. He repeated it on Friday at a Turning Point USA rally in Phoenix, Arizona.

"They kill people if they're white. If you're a white person in South Africa, they kill white farmers. Terrible, terrible. We can't let it go on," he told the crowd.

Trump said his administration had suspended all refugee resettlement except for white South Africans. "You come into our country, and we let you come in. You get a green card and a passport. You can stay in our country," he said.

President Cyril Ramaphosa's spokesperson Vincent Magwenya pushed back. "We appreciate our present moment. We are defining our future, owning our truth as we own our destiny. We are rational and undeterred," he said.

ANC secretary-general Fikile Mbalula said Trump's claims were racist. "The racist trope that we are uncivilised and animal-like as a race is what Afriforum has peddled, and now Trump is reinforcing his messaging," he said.

Mbalula said there is no genocide against white people in South Africa, and that black people have historically suffered the most.

The DA's Ryan Coetzee also said there is no white genocide in South Africa. "There is, however, an epidemic of violent crime that affects all communities," he said.

Image source: File

Trump says Iran war is going 'swimmingly'

Donald Trump has said the war against Iran is going "swimmingly" and should be ending soon.

"The war in Iran is going along swimmingly. It should be ending pretty soon," Trump told a crowd in Las Vegas on Thursday. He has made similar predictions about the war ending since the US and Israel began bombing Iran in late February.

Trump made the comments at an event promoting his policy to remove federal income tax on tips for workers in tipped jobs such as waiters and hotel staff.

Earlier on Thursday, Trump said a second round of face-to-face talks between US and Iranian officials could happen "probably, maybe, next weekend."

Trump also said Israel and Lebanon had agreed to a 10-day ceasefire. Iran has complained about Israel continuing to strike Lebanon during the current ceasefire between the US and Iran.

The two-week ceasefire between the US and Iran is due to expire next week. Both sides are in talks about extending it.

Image source: File

Trump posts image of Jesus hugging him

Donald Trump has shared another image showing Jesus embracing him, days after deleting a similar post that drew criticism from church leaders and his own supporters.

Trump posted the new image on Truth Social on Wednesday, writing: "The Radical Left Lunatics might not like this, but I think it is quite nice!!!"

The post comes as Trump has continued to attack Pope Leo XIV, the first American-born pope, who has called for an end to the US-Israeli war on Iran. Trump described the pope last Sunday as "weak on crime" and "terrible for foreign policy."

Trump also shared old social media posts from before the pope's election, when he was still known as Cardinal Robert Prevost, which showed him criticising Trump and Vice-President JD Vance. "Not good!!!" Trump wrote.

Vance also went after the pope at a conservative event in Georgia, telling him to "be careful when he talks about matters of theology." The US Conference of Catholic Bishops pushed back, saying the pope was not offering opinions but "preaching the Gospel."

Pope Leo said on Monday he had "no fear" of the Trump administration. "Too many innocent people are being killed. Someone has to stand up and say there's a better way," he said.

Vance said Trump's original Jesus image, which he deleted on Monday, was meant to be a joke. "He recognised that a lot of people weren't understanding his humour," Vance told Fox News.

Trump also posted that someone should "tell Pope Leo" that Iran had killed tens of thousands of protesters and that it was "absolutely unacceptable" for Iran to develop a nuclear weapon.

Image source: @realDonaldTrump

South Africa names new ambassador to the US after more than a year without one

South Africa has appointed veteran political negotiator Roelf Meyer as its new ambassador to the United States, the Presidency has confirmed.

Meyer, 78, takes over from Ebrahim Rasool, who was thrown out of the US in March last year after suggesting there was a "supremacist instinct" in US politics. South Africa has not had an ambassador in Washington since then.

Relations between the two countries have been difficult since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025. Trump has claimed South Africa is persecuting white farmers and seizing their land, and his administration granted refugee status to white Afrikaners.

The fallout has spread to international events. Trump reportedly tried to block South Africa from taking part in the G20 summit in Miami, and President Cyril Ramaphosa was uninvited from the G7 in France after Trump objected to his presence.

Meyer is best known for his role in helping South Africa move from apartheid to democracy. He served as a constitutional affairs minister during the apartheid era and was one of the key people who helped negotiate the country's democratic transition. He now runs an organisation that promotes democracy and peace in other countries.

Ramaphosa had delayed naming a new ambassador after Rasool was removed.

Image source: @USAmbRSA

Trump deletes Jesus image after even his own supporters say he went too far

Donald Trump has deleted an AI-generated image of himself dressed as a Jesus-like figure after people on all sides, including some of his own supporters, said he crossed a line.

Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Sunday. It showed him in a white robe placing his hand on a man's head in a scene that looked like a healing. He deleted it on Monday. Trump later told reporters the image showed him "as a doctor" linked to the Red Cross, calling criticism "fake news."

The post came after Trump attacked Pope Leo XIV on social media, calling him "weak on crime" and "terrible for foreign policy." Trump said he did not want "a Pope who criticises the President of the United States."

Pope Leo, the first US-born pope, said he was not looking for a debate with Trump. "Too many people are suffering in the world today. Too many innocent people are being killed. And I think someone has to stand up and say there's a better way," he said.

Senior Catholic leaders in the US spoke out. Archbishop Paul Coakley, head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said he was hurt by Trump's words. "Pope Leo is not his rival," he said.

Conservative figures also turned on Trump. Fox News host Riley Gaines wrote: "A little humility would serve him well." Conservative columnist Megan Basham called it "outrageous blasphemy." Senator Bernie Sanders called Trump's behaviour "deranged."

Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, one of Trump's closest allies in Europe, also said his attack on the pope was "unacceptable."

Trump won strong support from Christian voters in 2024, including a majority of Catholics. Last year he also shared an image of himself dressed as pope after the death of Pope Francis.

Image source: File

Trump orders US Navy to block key oil route after Iran peace talks fail

US president Donald Trump has ordered the US Navy to blockade the Strait of Hormuz after peace talks with Iran in Pakistan ended without a deal.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of water through which about one fifth of the world's oil normally passes. Iran has largely controlled it since the US and Israel began bombing the country in February.

Trump announced the blockade on Sunday in a post on Truth Social. He said most issues at the talks had been agreed, but that Iran refused to deal on its nuclear programme. "The only point that really mattered, NUCLEAR, was not," he wrote.

Trump said the US Navy would stop any ship trying to enter or leave the strait. He also said US forces would hunt down ships that had paid Iran to pass through, and would clear mines he says Iran placed in the water. He warned that any Iranian forces who fired on US ships or "peaceful vessels" would be "blown to hell."

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said civilian ships could still cross the strait if they followed its rules. It warned that military vessels approaching would be "dealt with severely."

Oil prices jumped above $103 a barrel after Trump's announcement.

Oman's foreign minister urged both sides to keep talking. "I urge that the ceasefire be extended and talks continue," he said. "Success may require everyone to make painful concessions."

Some US politicians pushed back. Senator Mark Warner said he did not understand how blockading the strait would push Iran into opening it.

The two-week ceasefire between the US and Iran agreed last week is now in serious doubt.

Image source: File

Trump accuses Iran of breaking ceasefire deal

US president Donald Trump has accused Iran of doing a "very poor job" managing oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, saying it was "not the agreement we have."

Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran appeared to be charging fees to ships passing through the strait. "They better not be and, if they are, they better stop now," he wrote. The strait is a narrow stretch of water through which about one fifth of the world's oil normally passes.

The ceasefire between the US and Iran, agreed earlier this week, has been shaky from the start. Iran and Pakistan said the deal included Lebanon. The US and Israel said it did not.

After Israeli strikes continued in Lebanon on Thursday, Iran said Israel was breaking the ceasefire. Iran then partly blocked the strait again and threatened further strikes.

Trump told NBC News he had spoken to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and asked him to ease off. "I spoke with Bibi and he's going to low-key it," Trump said.

Israel and Lebanon are set to begin direct talks in Washington next week, focused on disarming Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group, and building peaceful relations between the two countries. Lebanon's president had called for a ceasefire before any talks begin. Netanyahu said: "There is no ceasefire in Lebanon."

Israeli strikes on Thursday were among the heaviest since the conflict began six weeks ago. At least 303 people were killed and 1,150 wounded on Wednesday alone, according to Lebanon's health ministry. More than 1.2 million people have been forced to leave their homes.

The head of the World Health Organisation warned that two major hospitals in Beirut, treating around 450 patients, were in an evacuation zone with nowhere to send patients.

Image source: File

Don't criticise your hosts, Ramaphosa tells ambassadors

South African president Cyril Ramaphosa has said ambassadors should never publicly criticise the countries they are sent to, in remarks made in front of the US ambassador to South Africa, Leo Brent Bozell III.

Ramaphosa made the comments on Wednesday after receiving credentials from 20 new ambassadors at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guesthouse in Pretoria. "Ambassadors should never criticise their hosts," he said.

Bozell was called in by the South African government last month after publicly criticising South Africa's policies at a business conference. He later apologised for his comments.

Ramaphosa said ambassadors should always raise concerns privately and in a constructive way, not publicly or in a confrontational manner. "It is this approach that I believe builds strong relationships between nations," he said.

South Africa has not had its own ambassador in Washington since March 2025, when the Trump administration expelled Ebrahim Rasool and gave him one week to leave the US.

Both leaders welcomed the two-week ceasefire agreed between the US and Iran on Tuesday.

Bozell said the ceasefire was "a good thing" but warned that Iran needed to stick to the agreement. Ramaphosa called for dialogue to bring about a permanent end to the conflict.

Image source: File

Trump backs down and agrees ceasefire with Iran

The United States and Iran have agreed to a two-week ceasefire after weeks of war, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the key route through which a large share of the world's oil passes.

Trump had threatened to bomb Iran's power plants and bridges if the strait was not reopened. He pulled back from those threats after Pakistan's prime minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir brokered the deal.

"I agree to suspend the bombing and attack of Iran for a period of two weeks," Trump said in a White House statement. He said the US had already met all its military goals and was close to a long-term peace agreement.

Iran's foreign minister said Iranian forces would stop fighting if US attacks halted. He said ships could pass through the strait for two weeks, with coordination from Iran's military.

Iran claimed it had won a "historic victory." Trump called that claim "fake news." CNN said it had obtained the Iranian statement directly from official Iranian spokespeople.

Analysts said the ceasefire gave Iran more control over the strait than it had before the war started.

Oil prices, which had climbed to nearly $150 a barrel, fell after the announcement. Stock markets rose and bond markets rallied. Fuel prices had been rising around the world, including in South Africa.

However, Iran continued to strike Israel, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar in the hours after the ceasefire was announced. Analysts said this was likely because the news had not yet reached Iranian forces on the ground.

Image source: File

Trump warns he can take out Iran 'in one night'

US president Donald Trump has warned that the whole of Iran could be "taken out in one night" if it does not reach a deal before his deadline to reopen a key oil route.

The deadline is set for 20:00 Washington DC time on Tuesday. Trump wants Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of water through which a large share of the world's oil normally passes. Iran has largely blocked it since the US and Israel began bombing the country in February.

"The entire country can be taken out in one night -- and that night might be tomorrow night," Trump said at a White House news conference on Monday. He warned Iran would have "no bridges" and "no power plants" if the deadline passed.

Despite the threats, Trump said he believed Iran's leaders were negotiating in "good faith." Iran has rejected a temporary ceasefire and is calling for a permanent end to the war and the lifting of all sanctions against it.

A regional official close to the talks told the BBC that progress is slow because of a communications blackout inside Iran. "To convey messages to Iran, getting a response in a reasonable time is not possible," the official said.

Legal experts warned that bombing Iran's power plants and bridges could be a war crime. "Those kinds of things are all flatly illegal," former US national security legal adviser Tess Bridgeman told CBS News.

Trump also hit out again at the UK, Nato and South Korea for not helping the US in the war. "That's a mark on Nato that will never disappear," he said. The US military said it has carried out more than 13,000 strikes on Iran since the war began.

Image source: File

Open the oil route or we bomb your power plants, Trump warns Iran

US president Donald Trump has threatened to bomb bridges and power plants inside Iran if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened by Monday.

Trump made the threat in a social media post on Truth Social on Sunday, using strong language to warn Iran of what was coming. "Tuesday will be Power Plant Day, and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one, in Iran. There will be nothing like it," he wrote.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of water through which a large share of the world's oil normally passes. Iran has largely blocked it since the US and Israel began bombing the country on 28 February.

Trump told Fox News on Sunday that Iran was currently negotiating with the US and that he believed a deal could be reached before the deadline. Iran has denied this, saying it is not seeking to end the war.

Iran's mission to the United Nations condemned Trump's threats, saying they amounted to war crimes. "The international community must act now. Tomorrow is too late," it said.

An Iranian government official said the strait would only be reopened once Iran had been paid for war damages, possibly through fees charged to ships passing through.

Asked if he was worried about the effect of bombing bridges and power plants on ordinary Iranian people, Trump told the Wall Street Journal: "No, they want us to do it."

The US also confirmed it had rescued the crew member of an F-15 fighter jet shot down over Iran on Friday.

Image source: File

Tiger Woods told police he was on the phone with Trump after crash

Golf legend Tiger Woods told a police officer he had just spoken to US president Donald Trump on the phone, shortly after being arrested for drunk driving in Florida last week.

Bodycam footage obtained and published by TMZ on Thursday shows Woods walking back to the crash scene and telling the officer: "I was just talking to the president." Woods then told his manager that Trump "was very apologetic for what he did last night."

Woods, 50, was charged with driving under the influence after his Land Rover SUV clipped a truck's trailer in Jupiter, Florida on Friday. He was found with two opioid pills in his pants and showed signs of intoxication, according to police documents. He has pleaded not guilty.

Trump called Woods "a very close friend" shortly after the crash. "I feel so bad. He's got some difficulty," Trump told reporters.

The evening before the crash, Trump said during a Fox News interview that Woods would not be playing in the upcoming Masters golf tournament. Woods had not publicly ruled out playing before the crash.

On Tuesday, Woods said he was "stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health."

Woods is dating Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Trump's son Donald Trump Jr. This is not Woods's first run-in with the law. He was arrested for drunk driving in Florida in 2017 and was seriously injured in a car crash in California in 2021.

Image source: White House
