What the AAA Rating Means

HR Ratings, one of Mexico’s primary credit agencies, awarded the HR AAA grade, its maximum national quality category. It signals the municipality has the highest capacity to meet financial obligations on time.

The upgrade from HR AA+ followed a 9.1% primary balance surplus relative to total income at the close of 2025. Analysts had initially forecast a 3% deficit, making the result a striking turnaround that caught market watchers by surprise.

Why Fiscal Health Matters to Foreigners

A strong Merida credit rating directly supports stable property taxes and predictable public service fees. For expats and retirees on fixed incomes, that predictability removes a major financial worry and makes long-term budgeting far easier.

Low municipal debt also means less pressure for future tax hikes. It frees up public funds for infrastructure, parks, and security, all priorities for the growing international community that has made Merida its home.

Culture as a Quiet Anchor

While no new Maya museums opened alongside the rating, Yucatan‘s cultural depth remains a primary draw. The region is anchored by world-famous sites like Chichén Itzá and a living Maya heritage visible in daily language, food, and craft.

Merida itself offers a rich colonial center, a celebrated Yucatecan culinary scene, and year-round warm climate. These cultural layers give foreign residents a sense of place that goes far beyond cost savings, rooting daily life in centuries of tradition.

A Broader Safe-Haven Picture

The city is consistently ranked among the safest in Mexico, a decisive factor for North American and European retirees. Affordable private healthcare and a large, established expat network ease the transition for newcomers arriving with limited local knowledge.

The AAA rating adds a financial dimension to that safety. It tells investors and homebuyers that the local government manages money as carefully as they do, reducing the perceived risk of putting down roots in a foreign country.

Only about ten municipalities across Mexico hold a triple-A rating, which puts Merida in rare company. The city sits alongside far larger metros despite its modest size.

For newcomers weighing where to settle, the rating is one more signal that the local government is on stable financial ground.

What This Means for Property Investors

A top-tier credit rating can strengthen demand for residential real estate by signaling institutional stability. Foreign buyers often view such upgrades as a green light, especially in a market where property titles and municipal permits depend on a well-run local government.

While the rating does not guarantee price appreciation, it removes a layer of uncertainty that can deter cautious investors. For those considering a second home or rental property, Merida’s fiscal discipline offers a compelling piece of the due-diligence puzzle.

What Happens Next

Mayor Cecilia Patrón Laviada confirmed the rating on July 20, 2026, but the municipality has not yet detailed how it will use its improved credit profile. Future steps could include refinancing existing obligations at lower rates or funding new public works without taking on heavy debt.

For foreign residents and prospective expats, the key watchpoint is whether the surplus-driven discipline continues. Sustaining an HR AAA rating requires consistent fiscal performance, and any shift back toward deficits would likely trigger a review by HR Ratings.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the Merida credit rating upgrade mean for property owners?

It suggests stable municipal finances, which can keep property taxes predictable and support consistent public services. For homeowners, this reduces the risk of sudden fee increases and helps preserve the value of their investment over time.

Did new Maya museums open in Yucatan in 2026?

Available sources do not confirm any new museum openings. The region’s appeal still rests on its deep existing Maya heritage and colonial culture, which continue to attract visitors and new residents without the need for fresh institutional attractions.

Why do expats choose Merida over other Mexican cities?

Expats cite safety, lower cost of living, quality healthcare, and a strong sense of community, now backed by top-tier fiscal credibility. The AAA credit rating adds a layer of financial reassurance that complements the city’s well-established cultural and practical advantages.

World.title: Flooding Shuts Route 32 and Cuts Route 4 in Costa Rica’s Caribbean
World.content:
If you are driving to the Caribbean coast or the Northern Zone today, plan for trouble. The main highway between San José and Limón, Route 32, closed overnight after mud and rock slid onto the road, and there is no guarantee it will stay open once you set out. Days of rain from tropical wave 24 have soaked the region, and officials have placed the entire Caribbean slope, the Northern Zone, and the canton of Turrialba under a yellow alert.

Here is why the closures keep happening. After days of rain, the steep ground above Route 32 is 80 to 95 percent saturated, which means it cannot soak up any more water. Every new downpour sends loose soil, rock, and whole trees sliding onto the highway, and crews have to shut the road to clear it. When more rain falls before they finish, the material comes down again. That cycle is why a road can reopen in the morning and close by afternoon, so the status you saw last night tells you almost nothing about the status right now.

As of early Tuesday, Route 32 was closed and had not reopened. Your most reliable alternative for any vehicle is Route 10, which runs through Turrialba between Siquirres and Turrialba; crews cleared a landslide there and reopened it. The Vara Blanca route (Route 126) is open only to light vehicles. Route 4 was cut entirely at the El Tigre straightaway, where water ran across the road. Check conditions right before you leave rather than the night before, because the picture changes by the hour.

The worst damage so far is in Guácimo, in Limón province, where the Parismina River overflowed into several communities. A washed-out crossing at La Perla is closed, and a landslide has weakened the Guacimito bridge. In Sarapiquí, the Tigre, Sarapiquí, Puerto Viejo and Sucio rivers all climbed, forcing preventive evacuations from Naranjal 1, Álamo, Oropel, Carretones and El Tigre, and crews were still moving families out of Los Ángeles de Nogal and Pénjamo.

By Monday night, five shelters were housing evacuated residents; the National Emergency Commission counted 220 people, while later reporting put the figure closer to 254 as more communities were cleared. Officials expect the number to rise. A temporary shelter has opened in Santa Rosa.

More rain is coming. Forecasters expect another 60 to 80 millimeters (2.4 to 3.1 inches) across Limón and the Northern Zone through Tuesday, with some areas nearing 100 millimeters (3.9 inches), and the heaviest bursts arriving in the afternoon, at night, and again before dawn. The unsettled pattern holds through Wednesday. Strong trade winds are a second hazard, with gusts capable of bringing down branches, signs and power lines.

If you can postpone a trip to the Caribbean or the Northern Zone, do it. If you have to go, take Route 10, carry enough fuel and water to wait out a long closure, and never drive through water sitting on the road. You cannot see whether the surface beneath it has washed away, and moving water hides how deep it really is. Stay well back from swollen rivers and quebradas, and if you live near one, decide now where you would go if the water rises. The emergency line is 9-1-1.

World.title: Historic UCR Music School Faces Possible Closure
World.content:
The historic building that houses the University of Costa Rica’s School of Musical Arts could lose its operating permit after health inspectors found infrastructure and sanitation problems, including openings that allow raccoons to enter the facility. The Ministry of Health gave the university until Monday, July 20, to comply with a sanitary order issued after an inspection in April. The order requires the university to address the building’s structural problems, eliminate areas where animals can shelter and improve waste-management practices.

Failure to comply could lead to penalties ranging from a temporary closure to the cancellation of the school’s sanitary operating permit. One of the most visible problems involves raccoons entering through openings near the building’s roof and exterior eaves. The animals have reportedly gained access to classrooms, offices and other interior spaces.

The School of Musical Arts has responded with cleaning and disinfection, more frequent garbage collection and efforts to seal entry points. However, administrators say those measures have reduced the problem without providing a permanent solution. University officials say the aging building requires broader structural work that the music school cannot complete with its own budget. The UCR rector’s office submitted a corrective plan to health authorities in June and requested additional time to carry out the repairs.

The university has said that concerns about the building’s condition were raised internally as early as 2023. Since then, the school has sought technical support and funding for repairs. The building contains classrooms, rehearsal rooms, administrative offices, a music library and spaces used for concerts and academic research. A closure would disrupt lessons, rehearsals and other activities while the university looks for temporary locations or completes the required work.

The School of Musical Arts is now waiting for the Ministry of Health to decide whether to approve the corrective plan and extend the deadline. No closure had been officially announced as of Monday morning.

World.title: Costa Rica turned out for the 2026 World Cup final
World.content:
By early afternoon on Sunday, the concert grounds at Parque Metropolitano La Sabana had turned into an open-air stadium of their own. Families, groups of friends and visitors filled the space in front of a giant screen, faces painted, red Spanish shirts mixing with the sky blue and white of Argentina, waiting for a match that would crown a new world champion. When Ferran Torres struck in the second half of extra time, one half of the crowd erupted and the other fell quiet, and the afternoon tipped over into celebration.

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at the stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, to lift the trophy for the second time in the country’s history and the first since 2010. Torres, a substitute, scored the only goal in the 106th minute against an Argentine side reduced to ten men after Enzo Fernández was sent off late in regulation. For Lionel Messi, at 39, it was most likely a final World Cup appearance, and it ended without the trophy.

None of that happened in Costa Rica, and yet the country spent the day living it. San José was the center of it. The municipality turned La Sabana into the heart of its “San José Te Quiere Aquí” mid-year holiday festival, with the final shown free on a large screen, food markets, a craft fair and children’s activities across the weekend. National acts including Tapón and Luis Rosal warmed up the crowd, and the Colombian group Piso 21 closed the night with a free concert once the football was over. Organizers had projected space for a large capacity at the venue, and by kickoff the grounds were packed, though a confirmed attendance figure was not released.

The party was not limited to the capital. Municipalities set up fan zones with giant screens in Turrialba, at Parque Ignacio Pérez in Esparza, in Grecia and elsewhere, many of them pairing the broadcast with markets meant to draw people out and lift local business during the holiday week. Shopping centers joined in too, with venues such as Lincoln Plaza in Moravia installing screens for families who wanted somewhere to watch outside the house. For anyone who stayed home, the match aired free on Teletica and on subscription through FOX Sports and Tigo Sports, with kickoff at 1 p.m. local time.

The pull is easy to explain. This World Cup was co-hosted across the United States, Mexico and Canada, closer to Costa Rica than any tournament in memory, and it has been front of mind here for weeks even though the national team did not qualify. Costa Rica also has deep and personal ties to both finalists, through a large resident Spanish community and a steady Argentine presence, and both turned out. At La Sabana, dozens of Spanish fans, joined by Costa Ricans backing La Roja, celebrated the title with flags, hugs and chants once the final whistle blew. Argentine supporters, on the losing side, stayed to applaud their team and promised to be back for the next one.

That mix of heartbreak and pride played out on a far larger scale in Buenos Aires, where crowds gathered at the Obelisk with fireworks and flags to salute the runners-up, and where President Javier Milei said the squad could name a day to celebrate the second-place finish that would then be declared a national holiday. Coach Lionel Scaloni, who guided Argentina to the 2022 title, broke down in tears and cut short his post-match press conference, leaving his own future with the team an open question.

By early afternoon on Sunday, the concert grounds at Parque Metropolitano La Sabana had turned into an open-air stadium of their own. Families, groups of friends and visitors filled the space in front of a giant screen, faces painted, red Spanish shirts mixing with the sky blue and white of Argentina, waiting for a match that would crown a new world champion. When Ferran Torres struck in the second half of extra time, one half of the crowd erupted and the other fell quiet, and the afternoon tipped over into celebration.

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at the stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, to lift the trophy for the second time in the Spain’s history and the first since 2010. Torres, a substitute, scored the only goal in the 106th minute against an Argentine side reduced to ten men after Enzo Fernández was sent off late in regulation. For Lionel Messi, at 39, it was most likely a final World Cup appearance, and it ended without the trophy.

None of that happened in Costa Rica, and yet the country spent the day living it. San José was the center of it. The municipality turned La Sabana into the heart of its “San José Te Quiere Aquí” mid-year holiday festival, with the final shown free on a large screen, food markets, a craft fair and children’s activities across the weekend. National acts including Tapón and Luis Rosal warmed up the crowd, and the Colombian group Piso 21 closed the night with a free concert once the football was over. Organizers had projected space for a large capacity at the venue, and by kickoff the grounds were packed, though a confirmed attendance figure was not released.

The party was not limited to the capital. Municipalities set up fan zones with giant screens in Turrialba, at Parque Ignacio Pérez in Esparza, in Grecia and elsewhere, many of them pairing the broadcast with markets meant to draw people out and lift local business during the holiday week. Shopping centers joined in too, with venues such as Lincoln Plaza in Moravia installing screens for families who wanted somewhere to watch outside the house. For anyone who stayed home, the match aired free on Teletica and on subscription through FOX Sports and Tigo Sports, with kickoff at 1 p.m. local time.

The pull is easy to explain. This World Cup was co-hosted across the United States, Mexico and Canada, closer to Costa Rica than any tournament in memory, and it has been front of mind here for weeks even though the national team did not qualify. Costa Rica also has deep and personal ties to both finalists, through a large resident Spanish community and a steady Argentine presence, and both turned out. At La Sabana, dozens of Spanish fans, joined by Costa Ricans backing La Roja, celebrated the title with flags, hugs and chants once the final whistle blew. Argentine supporters, on the losing side, stayed to applaud their team and promised to be back for the next one.

That mix of heartbreak and pride played out on a far larger scale in Buenos Aires, where crowds gathered at the Obelisk with fireworks and flags to salute the runners-up, and where President Javier Milei said the squad could name a day to celebrate the second-place finish that would then be declared a national holiday. Coach Lionel Scaloni, who guided Argentina to the 2022 title, broke down in tears and cut short his post-match press conference, leaving his own future with the team an open question.

After a summer of watching a World Cup on the doorstep, Sunday was the last chapter, and Costa Rica watched it together, in a park, in a mall and in front of the television, the way most of the world did.

World.title: International News: U.S. State Department issues worldwide caution due to tensions in Middle East
World.content:
International News: U.S. State Department issues worldwide caution due to tensions in Middle East

By Zoila Palma: On July 20, 2026, the U.S. State Department issued a worldwide caution due to heightened tensions in the Middle East.

“The security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation.

Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions. Please monitor embassy and consular security alerts, local authorities, and the news for breaking developments. Americans outside the Middle East should reconsider travel to and through the region,” the alert said.

In addition, the U.S. State Department informed that U.S. diplomatic facilities, including outside the Middle East, have been targeted.

“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world,” the U.S. State Department added.

World.title: International News: Tropical Storm Bertha nears Northern U.S. Gulf coast
World.content:
International News: Tropical Storm Bertha nears Northern U.S. Gulf coast

By Zoila Palma: Tropical Storm Bertha is moving toward the northern Gulf Coast, where tropical storm watches and warnings remain in effect for parts of the region.

As of this morning, the storm was located about 100 miles (165 km) south-southwest of Panama City, Florida, and 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Mobile, Alabama. Bertha was moving northwest at about 5 mph (7 km/h), with a turn toward the west expected by the middle of the week.

The storm is packing maximum sustained winds of 50 mph (85 km/h), with higher gusts, and a NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft is currently investigating the system.

Forecasters say slight strengthening is possible later today, followed by gradual weakening through the middle of the week. Tropical storm conditions are expected along portions of the northern Gulf Coast from late Tuesday through Wednesday, while tropical storm conditions remain possible in parts of the Florida Panhandle and Louisiana.

Bertha is also expected to produce storm surge and coastal flooding, with the highest water levels occurring near the immediate coastline.

Surge could reach 2 to 4 feet from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Alabama-Florida border, while areas including parts of Florida, Louisiana and Lake Pontchartrain could see 1 to 3 feet of surge.

Residents in affected coastal areas are urged to monitor updates from local National Weather Service offices as conditions develop.

World.title: Trial against Rupert Codd concludes in one day; accused of raping woman on picnic table near KHMH
World.content:
Trial against Rupert Codd concludes in one day; accused of raping woman on picnic table near KHMH

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The rape trial of Rupert Codd wrapped up in a single day today before High Court Justice Derick Sylvester, leaving the Belize City man awaiting a verdict late this September.

The allegations stem from an incident on April 2, 2023. According to court testimony, the 31-year-old victim was walking toward the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH) at around 4:00 a.m. to seek medical attention when a man—whom she later identified as Codd—began following her. She testified via video link that Codd held her at knifepoint, forced her onto a nearby picnic table just steps from the hospital, and raped her.

The Crown, represented by Crown Counsel from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), presented 11 witnesses in total. Three witnesses took the stand in person: the victim, the arresting officer, and a forensic analyst. Statements for the remaining eight witnesses were formally agreed upon by both sides and read directly into evidence before the prosecution rested its case.

Taking the stand in his defense alongside his attorney, Michael Peyrefitte, Codd offered a sworn statement denying the assault entirely. He claimed that the woman had stolen his phone and wallet, and maintained that he only placed her onto the picnic table to recover his missing belongings.

“No sex, no rape occurred,” Codd testified.

Following the swift proceedings, Justice Sylvester reserved his verdict until September 29, 2026, when oral submissions will also be heard in open court. Both the Crown and defense counsel have been ordered to file their written closing arguments by July 31, 2026.

If convicted of rape, Codd faces a penalty ranging from a minimum of eight years to life imprisonment.

World.title: Belize City woman slapped with cyberbullying charged over alleged Facebook Live attack on police officer
World.content:
Belize City woman slapped with cyberbullying charged over alleged Facebook Live attack on police officer

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 34-year-old Belize City woman was arraigned on Monday on a cybercrime charge arising from statements allegedly made about a female police officer during a Facebook Live broadcast.

Amika Shanee Chanel Betran, a housewife of Partridge Street, appeared before a Senior Magistrate and pleaded not guilty to using a computer system to disseminate a statement she allegedly knew to be false with the intention of harming another person’s reputation.

Police allege that on July 11, 2026, Betran made insulting and sexually suggestive remarks about a 28-year-old police constable during a livestream posted under the Facebook account “Yanzie Chayqnnel Betran.”

The officer reportedly learned about the broadcast from her sister and later viewed and screen-recorded the video. She told investigators that the comments left her feeling embarrassed and insulted and caused harm to her reputation.

Betran was detained on July 18 and formally charged the following day.

The prosecution did not object to bail, and Betran was granted bail in the sum of $1,500 with one surety of the same amount. She was ordered not to contact the complainant or her relatives, interfere with prosecution witnesses or make any social media posts concerning the officer or the case.

The Magistrate warned that any breach of the conditions could result in her bail being revoked.

Before securing bail, Betran was also required to settle an outstanding fine of $75. Her case was adjourned until September 7, 2026.

World.title: Miguelito Encalada gets two life sentences for murdering wife and brother
World.content:
Miguelito Encalada gets two life sentences for murdering wife and brother

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Miguelito Encalada was sentenced on Monday to two concurrent life sentences for the murders of his wife, Desiree Elizabeth Gonzalez, and his younger brother, George Vincent Rochester.

Justice Candace Nanton ordered that Encalada must serve at least 40 years before becoming eligible for parole. The sentences were backdated to April 24, 2023, when he was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Encalada was found guilty on May 22, 2026, of two counts of murder in connection with the fatal shootings, which occurred on April 20, 2023, at a restaurant and residence on Scissors Tail Street in the New Site area of Ladyville.

Justice Nanton began with a minimum term of 42 years, citing the use of a firearm, the close-range nature of the killings, the deaths of two close relatives and the fact that the murders occurred inside the victims’ home and business.

She deducted two years after considering Encalada’s good conduct while on remand, his completion of rehabilitation programmes, his lack of prison infractions and favourable accounts of his work mentoring young men in Ladyville and his role as a father.

Before being sentenced, Encalada offered condolences to both families but continued to maintain his innocence.

“I am not behind this crime. I am not the shooter,” he told the court, claiming the real killers remained in the community.

During his trial, Encalada said armed men entered the establishment, forced him to the ground and stole approximately $8,000. He claimed he later found Gonzalez and Rochester lying on the floor and denied having any involvement in their deaths.

Encalada was represented by attorney Hurl Hamilton, while Crown Counsel Glenfield Dennison appeared for the prosecution.

World.title: Juan Carlos Novelo acquitted of murdering common-law wife Leslie Verde
World.content:
Juan Carlos Novelo acquitted of murdering common-law wife Leslie Verde

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Juan Carlos Novelo was found not guilty on Monday of the November 2023 murder of his common-law wife, Leslie Margarita Verde, in Caye Caulker.

Justice Candace Nanton announced the verdict shortly before 2:40 p.m. on Monday, freeing Novelo of the murder charge. The judge said her reasons for the acquittal will be provided in a written decision at a later date.

“It feels good because I never killed my common-law wife,” Novelo said after leaving court. “I just want to say to the family, from my heart, I never did what they think I did. I am so happy with this verdict.”

Verde, a mother of two, was found motionless inside her home in the Bahia area of Caye Caulker during the early hours of November 4, 2023. She was taken to the Caye Caulker Health Clinic, where she was pronounced dead.

A post-mortem examination conducted by a doctor determined that Verde died from asphyxia caused by compression of the neck. He classified the death as a homicide, saying the injuries were not self-inflicted or accidental.

The prosecution’s case relied largely on circumstantial evidence, including surveillance footage showing Novelo entering and leaving Verde’s home around the time of her death.

Verde’s then-13-year-old daughter also testified that she awoke and saw Novelo shaking her mother’s motionless body. However, the child said she had been between sleeping and waking and later went back to sleep.

Novelo’s attorney, Leeroy Banner, argued that there were no eyewitnesses or reliable evidence proving that his client killed Verde. The defence maintained that Verde was alive when Novelo left the home and urged the court to acquit him.

World.title: Kenton Young critically injured in Belize River Valley shooting; two detained
World.content:
Kenton Young critically injured in Belize River Valley shooting; two detained

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting near the Mussel Creek Bridge that left 29-year-old Kenton Young of Bermudian Landing Village critically injured.

The shooting occurred at around 10:25 p.m. on Saturday, July 18, 2026.

Police said Young was travelling in his SUV when he was confronted by a man riding a motorcycle. The motorcyclist reportedly fired several shots at the vehicle, injuring Young.

Young was transported for medical treatment and was listed in a critical but stable condition at the time of the police briefing.

Investigators believe the shooting may be connected to an ongoing dispute involving individuals from Bermudian Landing and Lemonal villages. Two persons have been detained for questioning, while police are searching for a third individual.

Initial public reports described the incident as a shooting in the Burrell Boom area before police clarified that it occurred near Mussel Creek Bridge.

Young is also known within Belize’s cricket community and has previously been publicly identified as captain of the Belize National Cricket Team.

World.title: Santa Elena resident charged after police find four rounds of 9mm ammunition
World.content:
Santa Elena resident charged after police find four rounds of 9mm ammunition

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged 37-year-old Simon Bateman of Santa Elena Town with keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

Bateman’s arrest followed an intelligence-led operation conducted at his residence on Friday, July 17, 2026, as police searched for illegal firearms and ammunition.

Police said a search of Bateman’s person resulted in the discovery of four live rounds of 9mm ammunition.

Investigators determined that Bateman was not the holder of a gun license, and he was subsequently charged.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Sweltering heat threatens egg industry
World.content:
President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association Mark Campbell on his egg farm in Trelawny on Monday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association (JEFA) Mark Campbell is urging members to protect their flock from an ongoing heatwave that is taking a toll on the industry, even as it recovers from the double whammy of hurricanes Beryl and Melissa.

Speaking with reporters on his farm in Trelawny Monday afternoon, Campbell noted that prolonged high temperatures have been especially hard on farmers along the island’s south coast, where laying hens have died from heat stress. He said farmers have reported losses of hundreds of birds, representing millions of dollars in replacement costs, plus income lost from reduced egg production.

“This year, 2026, the egg industry has come under sweltering heat, and a number of farmers, particularly those on the south side of the island — St Elizabeth, and Clarendon — they have suffered heavy losses. One farmer over there told me that he has lost over 700 chickens because of the heat that is on the land. And another farmer on the same south side of the island lost over 600 chickens. Now, those two figures run into millions of dollars just in the cost to purchase these chickens. And then the opportunity that has been lost is significant,” said Campbell, who is also operator of Campbell’s Egg Farm Limited in Trelawny.

He explained that laying hens perform best at temperatures between 60 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit and become increasingly vulnerable as temperatures approach about 106 degrees Fahrenheit, which is their body temperature.

The JEFA president is recommending that farmers install irrigation systems or lawn sprinklers on the roofs of bird houses to help reduce temperatures during the hottest part of the day, between 10:00 am and 2:00 pm.

“The heat that radiates off these roofs and goes down to the chickens is what really hurts them. Once the temperature comes up to the body temperature of the chicken, the bird is going to die,” he explained.

Campbell pointed out that while temperature-controlled poultry houses provide greater protection, many local producers may not be able to afford them. To compensate, he encouraged farmers constructing new poultry houses to incorporate adequate roof height and insulation.

Other advice provided by the JEFA president involve feeding birds during cooler hours of the morning, adjusting lighting schedules to encourage earlier feeding, and providing vitamin supplements to help maintain feed intake.

“We have to start looking at how we are going to prepare for periods of elevated heat because laying birds cannot deal with heat at all,” he urged.

Campbell said chickens experiencing heat stress often reduce their feed intake, resulting in lower egg production. He added that production losses could range from 50 to 70 per cent if birds remain exposed to excessive heat. He said farmers in cooler, mountainous areas have not reported similar levels of losses because of lower temperatures and stronger winds.

Despite the challenges being faced by some farmers, Campbell cautiously said he does not expect any scarcity of eggs this year as replacement birds are entering production.

“I hate to make forecasts about production because so many I have made in the past have been wrong. But this is the period between now and the end of the year where a significant number of new birds are going in the field, and if the farmers pay attention to good practices, I do not see a shortage because of the heat at the moment,” he said.

World.title: Supporting acts, fireworks fuel A Taste of Sumfest
World.content:
A section of the Sumfest crowd at Plantation Cove in St Ann.(Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Although thousands of patrons from across Jamaica and the Diaspora travelled to Plantation Cove in St Ann to witness the highly anticipated reunion of dancehall rivals Vybz Kartel and Mavado on the same stage at A Taste of Sumfest, the night’s supporting acts proved they were more than capable of delivering memorable moments of their own.

From explosive pyrotechnics and dazzling fireworks to energetic choreography and crowd-pleasing performances, the annual Reggae Sumfest warm-up event transformed Plantation Cove into a pulsating celebration of dancehall culture long before the night’s main attraction.

The night’s entertainment included music from selectors Code Red Sound, C Note Sound, DJ Mac and Baba, Boom Boom, DJ Ashile, DJ Tom & Reavers, and Ricky Platinum, who kept the energy high with a carefully curated mix of dancehall anthems that had patrons dancing from the early hours of the evening.

One of the standout performances came from Ayetian, whose appearance was especially significant as it followed his impressive seven Caribbean Music Awards nominations. Clearly determined to celebrate the milestone with fans, the artiste delivered an energetic set featuring crowd favourites Wah Yo Deh Pon, Tip, and Balance, with the audience enthusiastically singing along to every word.

Recording artiste Marcy Chin also commanded the stage with a bold and unapologetic performance that reaffirmed her place among dancehall’s elite. Addressing critics who questioned her repeated appearances at Sumfest, Chin declared that, “Sumfest is my home,” before reminding patrons that, “It nuh tek bwoy fi do music,” earning loud cheers for her statement celebrating women’s place in the male-dominated genre.

Dressed in a striking red velvet, long-sleeved monokini emblazoned with her name on the sleeves, sheer fishnet stockings, and thigh-high boots, Chin captivated audiences from the moment she stepped onstage. She was joined by a dancer from France and a male performer during Gimme More, creating one of the night’s most visually engaging performances. She also drew laughter and applause after delivering a cheeky freestyle playfully addressing long-standing rumours linking her romantically to Downsound Entertainment CEO Joe Bogdanovich.

Dancehall artiste Shawn Storm was equally well received, earning several pull-ups for his hit Itch Scratch, originally released in December 2025. The humorous track, which marked a departure from his usual catalogue centred on women and relationships, has grown into a fan favourite, with patrons repeatedly demanding rewinds.

He also performed songs including Empire and My Life, while encouraging fans to continue representing Gaza, reaffirming his unwavering loyalty to the movement that has defined much of his career.

Shauna Controlla, Youngwildapache, and Jamal each maintained the night’s momentum, delivering energetic sets that kept patrons engaged.

Veteran deejay Harry Toddler delivered one of the night’s most emotional moments as he paid tribute to late reggae artiste Fantan Mojah, who died on July 14 at age 49. The heartfelt tribute prompted patrons to observe a moment of silence, creating a touching contrast to the night’s otherwise high-octane energy. It marked the first of two tributes to the late singer during the event.

Another memorable appearance came from cultural icon Queen Ifrica, who explained why she was included on a show centred on Gaza founder Vybz Kartel.

Reflecting on the height of the infamous Gully-Gaza rivalry, she reminded the audience of the role she played in promoting peace.

“Me a the bravest fi stand up inna the middle of the war and tell dem fi look out fi the children, and we still a dweet in 2026,” she said, drawing loud applause from sections of the crowd.

The event attracted visitors from several countries, many of whom described the experience as unlike anything they had witnessed before.

“I flew from Toronto just for Sumfest, and every performer gave us a reason to dance. The energy, the music, the fireworks — it wasn’t just a concert; it was a celebration of who we are,” one patron told the Jamaica Observer.

First-time visitor Marcus Bennett from London, England, said the event exceeded his expectations.

“I’ve watched dancehall online for years, but nothing compares to seeing it in Jamaica. The passion of the performers and the connection they have with the crowd is incredible. This culture is alive, authentic and unforgettable,” he added.

World.title: World Cup champs Spain get heroes’ welcome home
World.content:
Spain fans pack Cibeles Square in Madrid on July 20, 2026, as they await the arrival of Spain’s players one day after the national football team won their second FIFA World Cup title with a 1-0 victory against Argentina. Spain’s World Cup winners come back home to a heroes’ welcome in Madrid where a reported one million fans showed up to greet them after a night of raucous celebrations across the country. (Photo: AFP)

MADRID, Spain (AFP) — New World Cup champions Spain began their celebration parade on an open-top bus through the streets of Madrid on Monday, early evening.

Local authorities told AFP that a jubilant crowd of over a million people turned out to celebrate.

The players, some shirtless, others holding drinks, set off on their procession under a blazing sun, along the main arteries in the city centre where a sea of fans in red and yellow were waiting, with the destination Cibeles square.

After flying back from the United States to Madrid, the players were received by King Felipe VI and the royal family, and then Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, before kicking off the parade.

Players passed around the gleaming World Cup trophy and waved to a sea of delighted Spain fans in red and yellow, the day after defeating Argentina 1-0 in extra-time in New Jersey.

Ferran Torres’s strike in extra-time was enough to bring Spain their second World Cup, following a first victory in 2010.

“You have shown your grit, your resilience and your courage, always backed by your technical skill, your control and command of the game, combining head and heart,” the king told La Roja’s stars, who were dressed in suits but changed to more casual clothing for their parade on a hot summer’s day.

“Kings of the world” ran the words on the front of their vehicle, with fans chanting “champions” to their heroes.

Spain captain Rodri held the World Cup trophy aloft at the top of the stairs as he descended from the Iberia plane that flew the team home after clinching their second star.

Later at Moncloa, Rodri said this was the crowning achievement of his career.

“I’ve always said it, winning with your country is the most beautiful thing there is, above all a World Cup,” he said.

“This generation grew up watching [Iker] Casillas and [Andres] Iniesta lift the cup and that we can do it today is the biggest thing you can do in football.”

Many younger supporters were not yet born when Iniesta’s extra-time goal against the Netherlands secured Spain’s first World Cup in South Africa 16 years ago.

Match-winner Torres joked he was “flying, literally” after the team returned from the United States after beating Argentina in New Jersey.

“I’m very happy to see how excited all of the children are… [and] to have the parade and celebrate with all of the Spaniards,” he said.

Spain’s World Cup winners bus parade started at Moncloa before heading towards Cibeles square, where hordes of fans had reserved their spots hours in advance.

A ceremony involving the players and a concert will then be held at the square, the traditional gathering point for celebrations by the Spanish national team and its supporters. Over 120,000 people were estimated to be waiting there.

Spain’s women’s side won the World Cup in 2023, meaning for the first time a country has both trophies at the same time.

In 2030, Spain will defend their crown on home soil, as one of the World Cup hosts along with Portugal and Morocco.

“It’s two for two,” said Prime Minister Sanchez, of Spain’s record in World Cup finals. “Why not dream of a third in 2030, especially with Spain as hosts?”

The Spanish press was running out of superlatives to describe its heroes after they overcame favourites France in the semi-finals before downing Argentina.

“The kings of all-time!” wrote Marca, celebrating a “second star that will now be stitched onto the Spanish jersey after yet another masterclass in collective play”.

Argentina, despite the presence of all-time great Lionel Messi, failed to create clear chances against Spain’s well-organised and more positive side in the final.

Messi had a sensational World Cup but drifted through the final like a ghost, shedding tears at the end.

“The pain is immense, and it’s going to be hard for this wound to heal,” Messi wrote on Instagram.

In Madrid, tears also flowed on Monday night, but they were tears of joy.

World.title: A host of concerns
World.content:
An architectural design of the National Stadium redevelopment project unveiled by the Sports Ministry in 2025.

DESPITE FIFA expressing concerns about Jamaica’s readiness to host matches at the Women’s World Cup in 2031, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts says he’s confident the country will secure hosting rights, with an official announcement expected in November.

Last October, Jamaica joined the USA, Mexico, and Costa Rica in launching a joint bid to host the 2031 tournament, which would mark the first time a FIFA World Cup would be staged across four countries.

A FIFA delegation visited the island in February, inspecting facilities including the National Stadium and meeting with representatives of the Jamaica Football Federation and the Government. Hosts were initially expected to be confirmed at the FIFA Congress in Canada in April, but the world governing body postponed the announcement until November 23.

Despite the delay, Sports Minister Olivia Grange told Parliament last month that Jamaica had been selected as one of the hosts, although FIFA has yet to officially confirm the successful bid.

FIFA Consultant and Women’s Football Division Advisor Jose Andres Portabella told the Jamaica Observer that while FIFA is enthusiastic about Jamaica hosting matches, there is no guarantee the country will be selected.

“I couldn’t be more excited about the possibility of the World Cup coming to Jamaica in 2031,” he said. “FIFA wants to see football all over the world. Next year, the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup will be held in Brazil, which shows the first time ever that the World Cup goes to South America. It’s going to be a fantastic performance by players, by fans, incredible stadiums, so why not Jamaica in 2031 with the US, and Mexico, and Costa Rica?”

“There’s a lot of work to be done, let’s be clear. We have had a delegation that’s come here to visit already [so] you (Jamaica) know what you need to do. The infrastructure is a key component of hosting the Women’s World Cup so we’re hopeful, we’re excited, and we’re looking forward to seeing what Jamaica does to bring this tournament to the island.”

It’s understood that USA and Mexico are almost guaranteed to host the tournament given their established infrastructure, some of which was on display during the recently concluded FIFA Men’s World Cup. Costa Rica is also reportedly well positioned, having hosted FIFA youth tournaments including the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in 2022.

Jamaica has never hosted a FIFA tournament but it has staged several Concacaf competitions, most notably the 2019 Concacaf Gold Cup, becoming the first Caribbean nation to do so.

Although the country faces a nervous four-month wait for the Women’s World Cup decision, Ricketts told the

Observer he’s optimistic Jamaica will host matches after seeing the level of work and commitment that has gone into the bid.

“When the FIFA team came here we had intense discussions with the contractors who would be doing the renovation and the refurbishing of the National Stadium, and they would have done a presentation which, based on the body language from the FIFA reps, we’re pretty satisfied and pretty confident that we will be in a position to host the Women’s World Cup in 2031,” he said.

“Minister Grange did make an announcement in Parliament. She was pretty confident and so am I, and I want to believe that we will be one of the four countries that will be hosting the 2031 Women’s World Cup.”

The redevelopment of the National Stadium, which is intended to meet FIFA standards, is expected to begin in July or August 2027, with United Kingdom-based Ryder Architecture and global consulting firm CAA Icon currently completing the detailed design phase, after the feasibility study and concept design.

Last summer Grange said the redevelopment would be completed in 2029. However, during World Athletics President Seb Coe’s visit to Jamaica in January she said she could not provide a completion date, although she was “conscious that we have to be finished by a particular time”.

Ricketts says FIFA would still allow Jamaica to host the World Cup even if the National Stadium’s full upgrade isn’t completed by 2031.

“I would want to think that even if — and I’m hoping that it doesn’t happen — the stadium is not completely refurbished we still would be in a position to host,” he said. “Of course our stadium is, maybe, archaic but when you look at some other stadiums around Concacaf, it is still not the worst. And I would think if we can’t get it fully refurbished and we can do minor repairs and minor adjustments, we still would be in a position to host the World Cup.

“It’s unfortunate that we really do not have options like some countries do but this is our main stadium — and, of course, it’s probably the only stadium that could really host a World Cup game — but it’s not that bad. And I don’t think FIFA would come down [hard, even though] they would not be totally happy if the stadium was not refurbished and ready, because they were given some kind of a guarantee from the contractors.

“It’s out of the hands of the JFF and out of the hands of even Concacaf but the Government has given an indication. And, having had discussions with the contractors who did a presentation to the FIFA group in the presence of the IPL [Independence Park Limited] personnel, persons representing Minister Grange’s office, the JFF and Concacaf… we are pretty confident that we will host this major tournament — probably the biggest thing ever to happen in local football, maybe in local sport.”

World.title: More Than Practice: Why Your Wedding Rehearsal Matters
World.content:
More than a run-through, the wedding rehearsal is a chance to gather loved ones and savour the moments before “I do.”

When couples think about wedding planning they often focus on the venue, flowers, menu, music, and décor. The wedding rehearsal, however, is sometimes treated as an optional extra or simply another item to check off the list. In reality, it is one of the most meaningful moments of the entire wedding journey.

A wedding rehearsal is about much more than practising how to walk down the aisle. It is an opportunity to slow down, gather the people who matter most, and prepare emotionally and practically for one of life’s biggest milestones.

For many couples the rehearsal is the first time everything begins to feel real. The ceremony space is set, family and friends have arrived, and suddenly the months — or even years — of planning come together. It becomes a quiet pause before the excitement of the wedding day. As you stand where you will exchange your vows, the reality often sinks in: Tomorrow, you begin a brand-new chapter together as husband and wife.

It is also a rare opportunity to spend quality time with your closest family members and wedding party before the celebrations become a whirlwind. Wedding days move incredibly quickly. From hair and make-up appointments to photography, greeting guests, speeches, dancing, and countless other moments, couples often find they have very little uninterrupted time with the people they love most.

The rehearsal creates a more intimate setting in which conversations are unhurried, laughter comes naturally, and emotions can be shared without the pressure of a full schedule. Parents offer words of wisdom, siblings share stories, lifelong friends toast the journey ahead, and everyone has the chance to simply be present together before the festivities begin.

Beyond the emotional value, a rehearsal is essential for ensuring your ceremony runs smoothly.

Every member of the wedding party should know exactly where to be, when to move, and where to stand. From the procession order to the recessional, everyone should understand their role. This eliminates uncertainty and helps avoid awkward pauses, confusion, or unnecessary delays during the ceremony.

The rehearsal also allows everyone to become familiar with the venue. Questions such as where parents will be seated, how the bridal party will enter, where the officiant will stand, how bouquets will be handed off, and where readers or musicians will be positioned can all be answered ahead of time.

For couples who are nervous about speaking in front of a crowd, rehearsing provides confidence. Walking through the ceremony once beforehand helps reduce anxiety because the setting already feels familiar. Instead of wondering what comes next, you can focus on the moment itself.

Your wedding planner and officiant also benefit from the rehearsal. It gives them the opportunity to coordinate timing, fine-tune logistics, answer last-minute questions, and identify any adjustments before guests arrive. A small issue discovered during rehearsal is far easier to resolve than one encountered during the ceremony.

One of the simplest pieces of advice I give every wedding party is this: Please pay attention during the rehearsal.

It may seem obvious, but conversations, mobile phones, and side discussions can easily distract everyone. The more focused the group is during those 30 to 60 minutes, the more relaxed and seamless the ceremony will feel the following day. Listen carefully, ask questions if you’re unsure, and remember where you’re meant to stand and when you’re meant to move. Those few moments of attention make an enormous difference.

If you’re planning a destination wedding, rehearsals become even more valuable. Many guests and members of the wedding party may be unfamiliar with the venue, so walking through the ceremony helps everyone feel comfortable and confident in the space.

When the wedding day finally arrives, you’ll be grateful you took the time to rehearse. Everyone knows where to go, transitions happen naturally, and the ceremony flows effortlessly. Instead of worrying about logistics, you can focus on what truly matters — looking into the eyes of the person you’re about to marry and embracing one of the most unforgettable moments of your life.

A wedding rehearsal is not simply a practice session. It is the bridge between planning a wedding and beginning a marriage — a chance to reflect, connect, prepare, and fully appreciate the incredible journey that starts the very next day.

World.title: Jamaica received more than 1,300 deportees in 2025, says PIOJ
World.content:
The majority of the deportees, also referred to as involuntary returned migrants (IRMs), came from the United States.

The survey also found that the total number of voluntary returned migrants (VRMs) stood at 852 in 2025, an increase of 52.1 per cent when compared with the 560 who returned home in 2024.

VRMs are individuals who choose to return to their home country or place of origin due to personal decisions, economic opportunities or family reasons.

Conversely, IRMs are those who are forcibly returned or repatriated to their country of origin due to legal reasons such as immigration violations or criminal activities.

In the meantime, the number of Commonwealth Citizens who migrated to Jamaica in 2025 decreased by 3.8 per cent to 3,491 from 3,630 in 2024.

The PIOJ said there was also an increase in the number of aliens registered in 2025, with the figure jumping to 11,029 when compared to the 2024 figure, which stood at 10,146, an 8.7 per cent increase.

The planning institute said that at 49.0 per cent, Asians accounted for the largest share of individuals who requested extension of stay beyond six months, followed by Caribbean nationals at 19.4 per cent, and Africans at 11.4 per cent.

World.title: 27 dead, 83 missing from capsized Guyana ferry, says PM
World.content:
Handout picture released by NCN Guyana showing President Irfaan Ali (L) attending a meeting with some of the survivors and relatives of those still missing after a ferry carrying more than 100 people capsized off the coast of the country, in Mabaruma, Region One, Guyana, on July 20, 2026. The ageing ferry MV Barima capsized off the coast of Guyana late on July 18 during a trip from the capital Georgetown to Port Kaituma. Rescue teams saved 67 people, officials said, as the search continues into July 20. (Photo by Handout / NCN Guyana / AFP)

GEORGETOWN, Guyana (AFP) — At least 27 people died after a ferry capsized off the coast of Guyana, Prime Minister Mark Phillips said Monday, as the small South American nation mourned the tragedy.

Sixty-nine people aboard the MV Barima have been rescued since the vessel flipped over on Saturday night, Phillips told reporters, adding that 83 more remained missing.

“Our focus again is on finding people,” he said, having raised the death toll from a previous 10. “We still have hope.”

READ: Death toll rises as more bodies found following boating tragedy

The aging ferry was traveling from the capital Georgetown to Guyana’s inland Essequibo region when it overturned.

Phillips said he was now “confident” that 179 people were aboard, following uncertainty about the numbers involved in the disaster.

Public Works Minister Juan Edghill earlier stated that the ship’s passenger manifest listing 133 people on board was inaccurate.

Authorities earlier Monday expanded the size of the area being searched from 400 to 1,070 square kilometers (154 to 413 square miles), while local fishermen joined recovery efforts.

The French army also sent 12 divers, two doctors and a mechanic from nearby French Guiana to aid the search-and-rescue operation, the presidency said.

Two crewmembers aboard the aging ferry tested positive for marijuana after the incident, Phillips had told reporters Sunday, adding that an investigation was underway.

The ship began its journey in mid-afternoon and a distress call was received about eight hours later, Edghill earlier said.

The ferry was built in 1939, according to the shipping website VesselFinder.

Boats typically travel by sea before reaching a river to arrive at Port Kaituma, which is located in the depths of a dense rainforest.

World.title: Natural gas prices surge as violence in Middle East flares again
World.content:
A digital display shows the price of petrol at an Aral petrol station in Berlin on July 19, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

Traders fear that they’re going to need to permanently price in instability in the Strait of Hormuz as shortages loom and Asian demand heats up.

BRUSSELS — European natural gas prices shot to a four-month high as renewed violence around the Strait of Hormuz triggered concerns about the feasibility of transporting energy through the world’s most vital energy chokepoint.

The benchmark European natural gas price — known as the Dutch TTF — briefly crossed €60 per megawatt-hour on Monday, the highest level since mid-March, and settled at €59 per megawatt-hour on Tuesday after the United States launched a tenth consecutive night of strikes against Iran. Tehran responded by targeting U.S. allies in the region and tankers in the Persian Gulf.

Before a ceasefire was struck in June, gas prices had consistently stayed below €50 per megawatt-hour, with traders wary of placing big bets during a war that had become impossible to predict.

World.title: French environment minister to resign after passage of controversial farm bill
World.content:
Barbut was against the pesticide and water storage proposals, both of which were added late in the legislative process to ensure the bill’s passage in the conservative-majority Senate. She made her opposition clear over the weekend in an interview published by Sunday newspaper La Tribune Dimanche.

“This government bill, which was intended to address an emergency situation facing our farmers, has — since the Senate’s amendments — significantly altered the policy governing the allocation of water resources in our country,” she said.

Annie Genevard, France’s conservative agriculture minister, directly opposed her colleague at the Ministry of Ecological Transition, warning that “allowing this bill to fail — whether out of ideology, self-interest or fear — would push farmers to the brink of despair,” in an interview with another Sunday publication, Le Journal du Dimanche.

Balancing farming and the environment

The debate over the legislation has highlighted the tensions between calls to protect the environment and efforts to keep French agriculture economically viable.

It has also exposed serious rifts among Macron’s centrists, most notably between Lecornu and Gabriel Attal, the head of Macron’s centrist Renaissance party and a candidate in next year’s presidential election in France.

Attal and Lecornu both supported reintroducing the pesticide in question, acetamiprid, under exceptional circumstances, but in a parliamentary debate Monday night the centrist lawmaker nonetheless expressed frustration that the government allowed the provision to be introduced at such a late stage.

World.title: EU farming support contributing to pricier healthy food, says UN
World.content:
This amounts to “indirect taxation,” said David Laborde, one of the authors behind the report and the FAO’s lead director of agrifood economics.

The EU’s direct farm subsidies from the Common Agricultural Policy, which Europe has paid since the 1960s, is partly to blame. Europe's agricultural subsidies (CAP) form one of the largest EU funding programs.

But, the lack of investment into research to bring down the costs of producing fruit and vegetables, which tend to be labor-intensive, has had an even bigger effect on the affordability of healthy foods in Europe, Laborde said.

“This has increased productivity in some sectors. But we have done nothing for pulses and beans,” Laborde told POLITICO.

For the average European citizen, that means that the cost of buying a meal every day that meets the minimum requirements for a healthy diet — the right balance of nutrients, calories and variation — rose by $1 between 2021 and 2025, to $3.97. The European price surge is higher than the world average of a 25 percent increase, the FAO report found.

For every healthy meal, vegetables, fruit and legumes eat up nearly 60 percent of the total price, while starchy crops like wheat or rice take up just 13 percent. Still, most farm subsidies worldwide end up in grain, sugar, dairy, beef and oil crops for animal feed.

World.title: Hamish Falconer appointed UK’s new Brexit minister
World.content:
Unlike his predecessor, who was based solely in the Cabinet Office, Falconer’s new job will be a joint role shared between that department and the FDCO. He will attend Cabinet meetings.

One Whitehall official, granted anonymity to discuss the changes, suggested the appointment was a sign that the EU reset would be brought back within the grip of the FCDO and away from the Cabinet Office.

Falconer has a long history in the U.K.’s foreign affairs department, having worked as a diplomat before becoming an MP.

The son of Labour grandee Charlie Falconer, he takes over at a crucial time for discussions between London and Brussels.

Summit prep

Before Starmer’s resignation, a U.K.-EU summit had been scheduled for Wednesday July 22 to round off talks on issues like an agri-food agreement, youth mobility scheme, and emissions trading deal.

Starmer had also planned to use the meeting as a launchpad for a closer relationship with the bloc.

World.title: Burnham Day 2: After the purge, the splurge
World.content:
The Andy Burnham era is under way, and the new prime minister is kicking off with a bang – cutting VAT on electricity bills.

He promised the country some “breathing space” on the cost of living, but with prices still rising will anyone actually feel better off? And is it properly funded?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine what the announcement shows about Burnham’s direction of travel in government, as his new cabinet gathers for the first time.

Plus, the duo unpack the biggest cabinet appointments – from John Healey as chancellor to Wes Streeting as defence secretary – after many Starmer loyalists were shown the door.

World.title: Turkey holds up NATO’s €27B fuel pipeline revamp deal
World.content:
At this month’s NATO leaders’ summit in Ankara, alliance Secretary-General Mark Rutte hailed a deal as imminent.

“Allies are taking a historic step to enhance NATO's fuel supply chain to ensure our forces have the energy supplies they need,” he told reporters. “While allies continue to finalize the details, we know that this €27 billion investment will modernize our existing fuel storage and distribution infrastructure.”

Despite that, Ankara has indicated it still wouldn’t green-light the proposal unless the 21 projects on Turkish territory are considered for fast-tracked funding, the diplomats said. Ankara's push reflects the fact the largest share of funding will be disbursed in the first five years of the overhaul.

“They just want their projects brought forward, to the detriment of more mature plans in other allies,” said one of the diplomats. “Of course, Russia is the one happiest with these delays.”

NATO countries had previously disagreed over the high costs of the agreement — touted by diplomats as the alliance’s most expensive commonly funded project ever — while some fretted over the fact it would lock in fuel projects for decades. Capitals later agreed to drop their opposition to the scheme as eastern flank states in particular lobby hard for a rapid agreement.

Ankara's move risks delaying an agreement on the pipeline extension until September, when NATO ambassadors will reconvene after the summer break, one of the diplomats said.

Turkey’s permanent representation to the alliance declined to comment. NATO referred POLITICO to Rutte’s remarks on the fuel pipeline agreement earlier this month at the summit.

World.title: GKV-Reform: Wer jetzt um Therapieplätze bangt
World.content:
Psychische Erkrankungen sind die häufigste Ursache für Krankschreibungen, doch die GKV-Reform bremst Psychotherapeuten künftig durch feste Budgets aus. POLITICO-Gesundheitsexperte Louis Westendarp erklärt, warum Patienten droht, noch länger auf freie Behandlungsplätze zu warten.

World.title: Merz turns resignation of party bigwig to his advantage
World.content:
The reshuffle is attractive to Merz because Spahn was sometimes an obstacle to him: The 46-year-old former health minister was not only an internal party rival who at times pushed back against his plans, but was also disliked by the more left-wing politicians amid his coalition partners in the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

With Spahn gone, Merz can choose a new CDU parliamentary leader to settle down the coalition. A cabinet reshuffle also allows him to make a political reset before crucial regional elections in the fall, in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is expected to perform well and could even secure an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt in September.

Merz’s spokesman Stefan Kornelius said the chancellor was now weighing his next move.

“There are always possibilities — that is, they exist, or they are seized upon, or they are not seized upon — and once a decision has been made, I think [the chancellor] will let us know,” Kornelius told reporters. “The process is underway.”

Merz and fellow high-ranking conservatives are expected to come up with a concrete proposal over the coming days.

Following a CDU leadership meeting on Monday, conservative lawmakers were asked to prepare for a gathering in the Bundestag on Wednesday next week — despite the ongoing summer recess — to elect a new parliamentary group leader, according to a message sent to lawmakers and seen by POLITICO.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.
