World.title: Germany: Mass shooting suspect found dead in prison
World.content:
A man suspected of carrying out one of the worst mass shootings in recent German history was found dead in his cell after an apparent suicide.

The Justice Ministry of Germany's state of Lower Saxony confirmed on Tuesday that the man suspected of killing six people at a youth and womens' shelter in the town of Stade last month had died by suicide.

Identified as Fatih Khan G. due to Germany's privacy laws, the ministry said there was "no indication of third-party involvement" in his death.

What happened in Stade?

G. is believed to have opened fire at the center for mothers and children, killing six welfare workers.

According to authorities, his three-month older daughter and her 34-year-old month were residing there. He had been in a custody dispute with his former partner over the baby, who showed signs of shaken baby syndrome.

He had reportedly previously threatened a doctor at a medical practice where his daughter had been seen.

He came to the shelter on June 29 to allegedly discuss accusations he had physically abused the baby. G. attempted to flee in a car but was caught shortly thereafter by police.

World.title: China narrows AI gap, challenges US influence
World.content:
At the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, Beijing showcased advances in AI while promoting its vision of open-source development and global governance.

As China narrows the artificial intelligence (AI) gap with the United States, Beijing is promoting a narrative centered on "open source" and "inclusive AI" as an argument for its vision of global governance.

During his keynote speech at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai on Friday, Chinese President Xi Jinping expressed China's ambition to take a leading role in setting global standards in AI. He criticized what he described as the "overextension of the concept of national security."

Xi did not openly reference the United States. However, Beijing's effort to position itself as an advocate of a new AI order and challenge US dominance was unmistakable.

This year's Shanghai summit sent several important signals, says Rogier Creemers, assistant professor at Leiden University specializing in China's digital technology policy. The WAIC indicates that artificial intelligence is now one of Beijing's political priorities, and that China intends to compete with the United States by supporting open-source AI models and promoting AI-driven industrialization, Creemers told DW. He also noted China hopes to win support from countries in the Global South for this effort.

Beijing closing the AI gap

China is steadily narrowing the gap with the United States in AI model development, and its efforts at AI application in industrial processes are slowly maturing.

China's President Xi Jinping said artificial intelligence should not be dominated by a single country Image: Ng Han Guan/REUTERS

Chinese AI model developers have continued to keep pace on the global stage, largely by training open-weight models on limited but advanced computer hardware, Paul Triolo, senior vice president for China and tech policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, told DW.

Triolo believes deployment of AI across Chinese enterprises may be progressing faster than in the United States.

In addition, there is less fear of AI among the Chinese population than there is in the US, facilitating more rapid uptake of AI applications at the consumer level.

Earlier this year, Chinese state media claimed that the performance gap between Chinese and US AI models had "largely disappeared."

Several experts broadly agreed with this assessment, saying that certain benchmark tests of China's large language models (LLMs) such as GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 showed the gap narrowing or even fully closing.

For most applications, Triolo noted, China's leading open-weight AI models are cheaper to run and more than capable of handling most tasks.

At the same time, advanced proprietary models from leading US companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google still retain advantages in areas such as security and scalability.

Has the US 'AI firewall' worked?

In January 2025, the US Commerce Department expanded AI-related export controls through its "Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion," covering advanced computing chips, certain AI model weights and access to large-scale AI computing infrastructure.

The US also boosted export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment intended for China.

Laila Khawaja, research director at Gavekal Research, told DW that the US has been partially successful.

The controls have indeed impacted China's ability to manufacture chips domestically, cheaply, and at scale.

As for export controls on advanced AI chips, however, Khawaja notes that a significant amount of chips is still entering China through the gray market, while Chinese firms can still access computing resources through overseas cloud services.

According to Triolo, the evidence so far suggests the US strategy of slowing down China's advanced AI development has failed at many levels. At the same time, it caused massive collateral damage to US companies, especially to to their budgets for research and development and their supply chains, such as those delivering rare earths.

China's open-source AI push

In his keynote speech, Xi emphasized the importance of "encouraging open-source development."

Humanoid robots prepared meals inside the WAIC and directed traffic at intersections outside the exhibition halls Image: China News Service/VCG/IMAGO

Chinese state media has likewise promoted the message that China "does not pursue technological blockades."

Analysts say Beijing is increasingly framing "open source" and "inclusive AI" as its own narrative to counter the United States' largely closed-source AI ecosystem.

Chinese AI models are largely open-weight, with leading offerings such as DeepSeek, Zhipu's GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3 released under MIT licenses that allow users to download, deploy, modify, distribute and commercialize them.

Creemers noted that, for the time being, Chinese AI models are quite open in weight, but slightly less open in source.

According to Creemers, China hopes to encourage the rest of the world to adopt Chinese AI models, thereby creating overseas markets for Chinese technology and ensuring that China remains part of the next wave of technological development.

China's WAICO challenges Pax Silica

In Shanghai, Xi also announced that the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), an initiative launched by China, has already attracted 29 member countries.

He described the organization as "an important milestone in the history of AI development" and said it responds to calls from Global South countries for a greater role in AI governance.

Can Europe keep up with the US, China in the high-tech race? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

WAICO is seen as an initiative to counter the US-led Pax Silica international initiative which aims to secure ​global AI and critical mineral supply chains.

The real competition, according to Triolo, lies in which parts of the US and Chinese AI technology stacks are ultimately adopted by countries in the Global South.

He believes China holds a significant advantage due to lower costs and the extensive digital infrastructure already built by Chinese companies such as Huawei across many developing countries.

Looking ahead

Overall, experts believe that the US will continue to lead in AI hardware design and compute capacity, while China could seize the lead on model innovation and will come to lead on AI diffusion.

Creemers argued that China's biggest structural disadvantage remains the lack of trust from countries in the Global North.

At the same time, US export controls continue to leave Chinese companies facing shortages of advanced AI computing hardware, limiting their ability to rapidly scale inference capacity to meet growing demand.

Looking ahead, Creemers argues that the rise of China's AI sector represents a broader historical shift.

"We need to understand that we are now facing, for the first time in modern history, a non-Western technological superpower," he said.

In his view, the future will not be defined by a singular global technological sphere, but rather by "a complex of overlapping technological networks and processes."

World.title: Is Germany investing in the right weapons?
World.content:
Germany wants to build up its army and pour hundreds of millions of euros into its defenses. But in a world where the battlefield is increasingly dominated by cheap drones, how many expensive tanks does the country need?

The German government's efforts to modernize and expand its military, the Bundeswehr, is in danger of being derailed by the country's slow procurement processes, according to critics.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran have shown that drones costing just tens of thousands can be an effective against weapons that devoured countless millions to develop and manufacture. Ukrainian air defenses, for example, have shown that they are able to hold their own against Russian attacks despite the fact that the Ukraine air force has only a fraction of the number of fighter jets and bombers.

Meanwhile, Germany has massively boosted its defense spending in the past few years. On top of the €100 billion ($114 billion) "special fund" announced following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the state has been rapidly raising its regular defense spending: From €62.4 billion in 2025 to €82.7 billion in 2026, with plans to raise that to €152 billion by 2029.

But critics are wondering whether these vast sums are being spent in the best way, not least since FCAS Franco-German fighter jet, which cost over €100 billion, was scrapped in June.

Respected defense analyst Nico Lange, who once worked for the German Defense Ministry, gave a scathing verdict on the current strategy. "It's the same dysfunctional system as before. They're just pouring significantly more money into it," he told the news portal Web.de. "The point is: Unless you actually change the structures of military planning and procurement, nothing better will come of it."

Drone warfare: German startup draws on Ukraine's experience To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany learning its procurement lessons

Germany is currently climbing a steep learning curve, according to some politicians. Andreas Schwarz, Social Democrat member of the Bundestag defense committee, said the war in Ukraine is "completely changing how war is being fought."

On a visit to Ukraine earlier this month, Schwarz found that the debates that had dominated German politics in the first year of the war — about whether Germany should send Taurus rockets or Leopard tanks to help Ukraine — had become entirely irrelevant.

"When I was in Ukraine last week and visited the Defense Ministry, no one asked me about a Taurus cruise missile or a Leopard tank," he told DW. "What they need is help with drones, with ammunition, with modernizing their IT sector, with satellites and communication."

Can an army still fight with 'legacy' weapons?

But the Ukrainian experience doesn't mean that heavy weapons systems — often called "legacy systems" have become obsolete, as some analysts have been arguing in recent months. Max Becker, policy fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) , said that the Ukrainian war had shown, on the contrary, that tanks or artillery systems were still important to capture and hold territory, as well as for long-range strikes.

"It's about having the right mix of legacy systems, which you still need, and drone technology," he told DW. "That is a dilemma, because on the one hand you still need to invest in very expensive systems like combat tanks, which take a long time from order to delivery, but you also have to invest in systems like drones and loitering munitions."

The Ukrainian military, Becker added, had only developed its drone-based strategy partly out of necessity, because of its lack of conventional artillery and combat tanks. "I think the scenarios that Germany and NATO are preparing for are very different from those of the war between Russia and Ukraine, because NATO has very different equipment."

Andreas Schwarz also thinks that the Bundeswehr still needs the old weapons. "I don't want to say that we don't need tanks anymore — not at all, we're always going to need them," he said. "But the question is: Do we still need them in that quantity? And could I not complement or even optimize them with smaller, more flexible units?"

Drones are not only becoming more sophisticated, but also easier and cheaper to control — whereas expensive special computer systems were vital in the past, some military drones can now be steered with apps on a smartphone. Schwarz believes that though the German government and defense industry has grasped this new reality, but it still needs some time to implement the necessary measures to deal with it.

Why Germany struggles to recruit women soldiers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The procurement problem

The devil is in the detail — or, as so often, in the bureaucracy. Defense procurement is notoriously slow and complicated, and has proved especially so in a country where the arms industry is dominated by major companies like Rheinmetall that have made a lot of money building tanks and submarines for the world's militaries.

"We have an arms industry that for decades has relied on certain tried-and-tested technologies," said Schwarz. "Of course, we also have an army that has spent decades preparing for scenarios that are no longer very likely today. And of course, it’s difficult to establish this new way of thinking when we’ve been operating on the basis of different scenarios up until now — which requires those in charge to be willing to rethink their approach."

In an attempt to speed things up, the German government introduced a new law at the beginning of the year, whose name is as self-explanatory as it is unwieldy: the Bundeswehrbeschaffungsbeschleunigungsgesetz — or, the Military Procurement Acceleration Law.

This measure hopes to decentralize procurement by raising price thresholds so that certain purchases can be made without extra decision-makers being looped in, and removing paperwork for defense procurements between governments.

These are all good things, said Becker, because they help to change the received logic of defense procurement: In a world where drones and weapons can become obsolete within weeks, it makes no sense to make an order and then stockpile weapons that will be outdated in months.

"You create this new logic by agreeing innovation clauses in the procurement process, which obligate the companies to update their systems," Becker said. Seeing that the German government had grasped that such innovations were important had given him hope, he said.

What Germany should be concentrating on, he said, was setting up a new manufacturing infrastructure that can react quickly to new orders. "I can't buy a million drones," he said. "I need a stockpile of drones for training, and for exercise purposes, but I also need the industrial capacities so that the production of a mass of drones can be set up within four to six weeks."

The German military is also in the middle of a massive recruitment drive that is proving unpopular among young people — but, despite the increased automation of warfare, Schwarz believes that new human recruits are still essential. "We still need those people as drone pilots for example, but we also need people who can work with this technology," he said. Not only that, he added, new recruits were necessary to strengthen the reserve army to protect German territory for the worse case scenario.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

World.title: Ozempic maker sues US rival over ad campaign
World.content:
Novo Nordisk has claimed that Eli Lilly is using bad data to compare the companies' weight-loss and diabetes products in its ads.

Denmark pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk announced on Tuesday that it is suing its main competitor, the US-based Eli Lilly for "false and misleading" s.

Novo Nordisk says that its rival is using "intentionally selected outdated studies" that compare higher doses of its popular GLP-1 agonist drugs Wegovy and Ozempic to lower doses of Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound.

The American firm's ads are "deceptively (presented) those results as proof of broad, product-level superiority while burying or omitting critical clinical context," the Danish group said.

"As new and more effective treatment options become available, people deserve accurate information that reflects the latest scientific evidence and helps them make informed care decisions," the company's general counsel John F. Kuckelman said.

Weight-loss drugs Wegovy, Ozempic, Mounjaro boom in UK To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the heart of the suit is a Eli Lilly campaign that Novo Nordisk claims "aired during recent, widely viewed global sporting broadcasts and on TikTok and Facebook, causing widespread confusion."

The lawsuit has been launched in a US district court in New Jersey, specifically alleging breaches of fair competition laws and federal false advertising statutes.

What is a GLP-1?

These medications mimic the body's natural GLP-1 hormone, which is produced by your body after you eat, using it to control apetite.

Both Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly have developed seperate synthetic GLP-1 molecules.

They can be used to treat type 2 diabetes as well as a weight loss drug, the popularity of the latter creating massive windfalls for both companies.

World.title: How India's youth-led 'Cockroach' movement challenges Modi
World.content:
What started as a satirical protest against exam leaks in India has grown into a wider movement voicing young Indians' anger over jobs and education.

Riot police fired tear gas and used batons in New Delhi as tens of thousands of supporters of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) marched towards India's Parliament on Monday (July 20).

Police in the Indian capital said 60 protesters and 118 police officers were injured in the clashes between demonstrators and security forces. Mobile internet was suspended in parts of the city, including around the Jantar Mantar protest site, during the violence.

Protesters are demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Earlier this year, authorities canceled the high-stakes NEET medical entrance exam over a leaked question paper, affecting millions of students and sparking outrage across India.

What is India's Cockroach Janta Party?

The CJP began as an online campaign in May and rapidly evolved into a Gen Z street movement, giving a voice to a generation frustrated by unemployment, shrinking opportunities and a failing education system.

The protesters attempted to march toward India's Parliament Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

The youth-led "Cockroach" party is now posing an unexpected challenge for Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, prompting a response that combines political outreach with police action.

Modi's rivals have also tried to step in and take advantage of the youth's frustrations.

"Is this how a government behaves? Using tear gas and baton charges against students? This is a worthless government," Renuka Chowdhury, an MP from India's opposition Congress party, told DW.

Lessons from earlier protests in India

The CJP movement gained fresh momentum over the weekend after veteran reform activist Sonam Wangchuk, whose three-week hunger strike has become a symbol of the protests, was forcibly taken to a hospital by police.

It is not the first time India has experienced major protest movements. Hunger strikes, famously used by Mahatma Gandhi, remain a common and peaceful form of protest in India.

India Against Corruption (IAC) led by veteran activist Anna Hazare, managed to mobilize millions in 2011 and reshape the country's political landscape. A decade later, yearlong farmers' protests forced Modi to repeal controversial farm laws. However, a 2023 Olympic wrestlers' protest over allegations of sexual harassment achieved few of their goals, despite widespread sympathy.

Analysts say the CJP lacks a nationwide organizational network, which the farmers had at their disposal. Yet like the IAC movement, it has tapped into a broader public mood.

"This protest is different because it reflects a much broader cross-section of Indian society," said Yamini Aiyar, an analyst and senior visiting fellow at Brown University. "They are expressing their frustration with a country whose long-atrophied education system has left them with very little hope of a better future."

"Like the IAC movement, it has drawn the middle class onto the streets," Aiyar told DW. "But this is a far more coercive political environment. From the anti-citizenship protests to the farmers' movement, citizens have increasingly looked beyond political parties to hold governments to account."

Police response sparks backlash among Indian protesters

This week's clashes have done little to quell the anger among India's Gen Z.

"Like many young people across India, I am angry about a lack of jobs and an education system that crushes my aspirations. Even though my family supports the BJP, I managed to get away," Rukmini Singh, a student from Meerut, told DW.

"This was an attack against our children. I saw many young boys and girls hurt and bleeding. They will never forget it but the courage these people displayed gives me hope," Vasundara Singh, a teacher from Bihar, told DW.

As during the farmers' protests, leftist parties and student organizations have become visible on the ground, helping mobilize supporters and giving the movement organizational backing.

"After 50 years, youth have occupied the road to parliament," political activist Yogendra Yadav told DW. "This energy by the students shows that the path to parliament goes through the streets. It is remarkable."

Can CJP mobilize India's villages as easily as its cities?

The surge in protest numbers forced the government to engage with the movement after weeks of dismissing it.

Alongside the police action, senior ministers opened talks with CJP leaders. Home Minister Amit Shah met cabinet colleagues while Health Minister J P Nadda held discussions with representatives of the movement.

"We will decide on how best to address the students' demands," a senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP, told DW on condition of anonymity.

Most CJP support appears to come from students and India's urban middle class. The BJP's strongest electoral base remains in rural India and smaller towns, where the CJP has yet to prove that its message resonates with young voters.

However, some experts believe that the CJP will do just fine beyond India's urban centers.

"This movement is likely to resonate beyond India's cities because the aspirations of young people in small towns and villages are no different," political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan told DW.

India's 'cockroach' protests meet with batons and tear gas To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"For a generation that saw education as the route to a better life, the failure of the education system has become a deeply political issue," she said.

"Young people in rural India no longer see farming or traditional occupations as their only future. Whether the CJP itself survives is another matter, but the anger and frustration it has tapped into have the potential to reshape politics."

'The anger is now directed at the government'

A movement focused on India's cities may generate headlines without altering the BJP's political fortunes. But if the CJP spreads to rural youth, it could become a much broader political challenge.

"I don't think this will remain an urban movement," said commentator Apoorvanand.

"People constantly move between villages and cities, and those who witnessed the police action will carry those experiences home," Apoorvanand told DW.

"The anger is now directed at the government. Whether it becomes a broader political movement depends on the CJP's ability to widen its appeal."

For now, the CJP has already achieved something unusual. It has transformed satire into sustained street mobilization, forced the government into talks, and ensured that the concerns of India's young people remain firmly in the national spotlight.

"This is a long fight. We will have to engage in a very long struggle for this. Because you have to change an entire system, the nexus of that system is very deep-rooted," said Saurav Das, CJP's chief spokesperson.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Italy: Protests in Bologna over death of immigrant in police custody
World.content:
Demonstrators are demanding answers over the death of 42-year-old Abderrahim Fakir. Local authorities have urged calm while the investigation is underway.

A day after police and protestors clashed in the northern Italian city of Bologna, local authorities on Tuesday urged residents to remain calm and await the results of an official investigation into the death of Abderrahim Fakir.

"They killed my brother in cold blood, I want justice," Fakir's sister Khadija told reporters following his death in the city's Pilastro neighborhood on Sunday.

What do we know about the death of Abderrahim Fakir?

According to Italian media, Fakir came to Italy from Morocco as a child with his family, and they settled in Bologna. He ran a cleaning business and was a legal permanent resident of Italy. He was in Pilastro visiting friends, family members reported.

Bologna Police have said that they were called to the neighborhood on Sunday morning, responding to a call about a man causing damage to a vehicle.

Officers said that it was some 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) when they arrived, and that they tried to subdue Fakir with pepper spray before holding him down and handcuffing him when he continued to be aggressive.

In a video widely circulated online, Fakir can be seen repeatedly calling for help and struggling to breathe before he stops moving. His family told Italian media that he had a history of asthma and heart problems, that he was married and not known to have any previous run-ins with authorities.

Protests in central Bologna

On Monday, a demonstration was held in Bologna's famous Piazza del Nettuno. Italian news agency ANSA reported that some protestors chanted anti-police slogans and one threw a firecracker, but that demonstrators were largely peaceful.

ANSA added police responded with tear gas and water cannons.

Italy's two main police unions have accused activists of using social media to conduct online witch hunts against police based on incomplete footage of the event and said that dozens of officers were injured in clashes with protestors.

Local authorities have urged calm, saying a thorough inquiry is being carried out. Bologna Police have said they plan to release the bodycam footage in full to investigators.

Bologna health authorities have said they are also launching an investigation into how long it took to arrive on the scene.

Police released smoke canisters to disperse protestors Image: Michele Lapini/REUTERS

How have lawmakers responded?

Mayor Matteo Lepore of the center-left Democratic Party (PD) also urged residents to await the full picture, but said you could tell that "something clearly went wrong."

"You cannot die like this," he said, appearing alongside some of Fakir's loved ones. At the same time he expressed his confidence in the rule of law in the city and that the truth would be borne out.

He thanked a niece of Fakir for calling for "respect, truth, and justice, not revenge."

Italy's far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has also called for the full truth to come to light, but accused online agitators of fomenting "hatred against the police."

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: Why the youth jobs crisis is becoming global
World.content:
Young people in much of the world face growing competition for entry-level jobs as graduate numbers rise, hiring slows and AI-driven disruption adds uncertainty to career prospects.

The youth job crisis that first became obvious in China points to major economic and social problems that governments and businesses need to address.

Last year, unemployment, weak job prospects and a general lack of economic opportunities drove young people onto the streets in Kenya, Peru, Nepal, Indonesia and the Philippines.

This year, concerns about youth unemployment have added fuel to protests in South Africa and Morocco. In India, they helped give rise to the Cockroach Janta Party, a movement that started as a satirical social media project but quickly gained national attention.

China's youth unemployment problem

Youth unemployment refers to the share of young people, typically aged 15 to 24, who are actively seeking work but cannot find it. The rate is usually higher than overall unemployment because young people have less experience and networking opportunities, but that gap is widening in a growing number of countries.

China became an early example of the problem as university enrolment and graduate numbers grew faster than job creation, contributing to anxiety, long job searches and underemployment during a period of weaker economic growth.

In May, the official unemployment rate among ​urban 16-to 24-year-olds in ‌China was ​15.6%, according to Reuters news agency based on National Bureau of Statistics data.

While this represents the lowest level ⁠in 11 ​months, it remains three times higher than the overall unemployment rate of around 5%. Since 2023, the Chinese youth unemployment figures exclude the millions of university students, making comparisons with older data harder.

Is AI reshaping entry-level job opportunities?

China is not the only country with weak growth, slowing upward mobility, or a sense of intergenerational inequality.

In other countries, technology, sluggish hiring and rising competition have also weakened the link between a university degree and a secure white-collar career.



Besides the growing number of graduates, another factor eating away at confidence is the fear that artificial intelligence (AI) could turn into a massive entry-level job destroyer. Experts are not yet clear about its impact.

A decade after Brexit, youth in Britain want the EU back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"In the UK, new postings for graduate jobs have fallen faster than for non-graduate jobs, and many of these roles are highly exposed to AI," said Golo Henseke, an associate professor in applied economics at University College London.

His research has shown that "where firms have taken up AI faster, employment of 15-to 24-year-olds has grown more slowly, while prime-age employment holds up." But for now, the AI-effect is small compared to the regular business cycle.

Sara Elder, a youth employment expert at the Geneva-based International Labour Organization (ILO), agrees. AI may be one of the current drivers of stagnating youth employment, but she considers other factors more important.

Right now, economies are not dynamic and job creation is just not keeping pace with the number of young people seeking jobs, says Elder.

"This is then exacerbated by the tendency of employers to raise hiring criteria in ways that make it more difficult for young people with little job experience to get their foot in the door," said Elder.

What type of jobs are impacted where?

Without these entry-level jobs, young people may never get the experience they need for better jobs. Consequences could be lower consumption, lower home ownership rates and delayed family formation — not to mention widespread frustration.

Currently across Europe, there is no broad youth jobs crisis, says Henseke, who specializes in education, labor markets and human resources.

Since 2022, the share of young people not in employment, education, or training has increased in only a handful of European countries like Austria and Germany and fallen in much of southern Europe.

"Youth unemployment is not new to Europe either," said Henseke. "It was severe after the financial crisis, and the biggest improvements since have been in the countries that struggled most then."

Youth employment growth is strong in Latin America, South Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, even if the quality of jobs is low, says the ILO's Sara Elder Image: Stefan Sauer/dpa/picture alliance

But the ILO found that between 2023 and 2025 youth unemployment rates rose in eight of the world's 11 regions, like East Asia, North America (the US and Canada), Southeast Asia and the Pacific.

Opportunities for young people have declined in manufacturing, construction and the service sectors, in particular.

"Jobs for young people in high-skilled knowledge-based technical areas, like science, engineering, health and information and communication technologies, have fared better, showing continued growth in most countries," said Elder.

Dream job abroad? It could be a trafficking trap To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What can be done about entry-level jobs?

In Germany, a survey this spring by consultancy EY found that students are much less optimistic about finding suitable work after graduation than they were two years ago. Job security now also ranks ahead of salary as their top priority when choosing an employer.

This leaves lots of room for improvement. Policymakers and employers will need to make big investments to create decent jobs and "support young people's school-to-work transitions," said Elder.

Golo Henseke is cautious about blaming young people's skills. "It is very unlikely that today's graduates are less capable than those who left education just a few years ago, and the skills employers want have not changed overnight."

"More than anything, what would help is economic growth," concluded Henseke.

Edited by: Andreas Becker

World.title: China, Philippines clash in South China Sea ahead of ASEAN meeting
World.content:
China and the Philippines traded accusations after a violent altercation between navy personnel in the disputed South China Sea. The incident heightened tensions ahead of a major diplomatic summit in Manila.

Sailors from the Chinese and Philippine navies faced off with oars and batons in the disputed South China Sea, with Philippine officials saying that one of its sailors suffered a head injury as a result of the altercation.

What did Beijing, Manila say about the South China Sea confrontation?

The latest confrontation took place on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, a contested area where the two countries haverepeatedly clashed before. The Philippines keeps a military presence in the area aboard the grounded warship BRP Sierra Madre.

Manila said that Chinese Coast Guard personnel had assaulted Filipino sailors as they approached the outpost.

China quickly rejected this narrative. Beijing's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the "Philippine side provoked the incident first," by approaching the Chinese vessel in small rubber boats, but then "turned around ​and made counter-accusations, distorted the facts and engaged in malicious ​hype."

On Tuesday, China summoned the Philippine ambassador in Beijing to lodge its complaints, with the Philippines quickly following suit with the Chinese counterpart in Manila.

Disputed South China Sea remains a flashpoint

The Second Thomas Shoal is part of the Spratly islands, a disputed archipelago in the South China Sea.

The Spratlys are key to Beijing's claim of the entire South China Sea, a key global trade route. Beijing maintains its claim to the waterway despite a 2016 ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague that there is no legal basis to its argument.

China has repeatedly demanded the removal of the outpost on the BRP Sierra Madre, and surrounded the atoll with its ships in a tense territorial standoff that has dragged on for years.



Philippine island on edge amid fear of China-Taiwan conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US, Australia condemn China ahead of ASEAN gathering

The incident came just ahead of a meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) which was set to begin on Tuesday with foreign ministers of the eleven member states and external partners.

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who was in Manila for the summit, denounced Beijing on Tuesday for what she called "destabilizing and dangerous conduct" during the standoff.

Wong, during a visit to the headquarters of the Philippine Coast Guard, also announced a support package for the agency totaling 10 million Australian dollars ($6.7 million) for drone technology.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Manila on Tuesday morning ahead of the ASEAN summit Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

The US State Department also issued a statement criticizing China's actions, saying its "troubling pattern of provocations against the Philippines' legitimate maritime operations undermines regional peace and stability."

"We stand with our Ally, the Philippines, and commend the professionalism and restraint shown by Philippine navy personnel in this incident," the statement read.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in the Philippine capital on Tuesday morning, and has indicated he was open to meeting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who is also attending the ASEAN summit.

Edited by: Rana Taha
