World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.title: China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.content:
China’s first regulations on AI companion services have taken effect, setting new limits on chatbots designed to simulate emotional bonds with users and barring platforms from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors.

The rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other government departments in April, came into force July 15. They cover AI products designed to mimic human personalities, emotions, and communication styles.

The measures come after years of growing use of AI companion apps in China, where users have created virtual lovers modeled on TV characters, recreated deceased relatives through customized voices and personalities, and treated chatbots as long-term emotional confidants.

Regulators and state media have warned that such apps carry security and compliance risks, including emotional dependence, sexually suggestive content, and weak protections for minors.

As such, the new regulations prohibit AI apps from generating content for minors that may incite unsafe behavior, trigger extreme emotions, or foster habits that could harm their physical or mental health. They also should not excessively cater to users in ways that induce emotional dependence or addiction and damage their real-life relationships; manipulate users’ emotions to push them toward unreasonable decisions that harm their legitimate rights and interests; and act as virtual relatives or virtual partners to minors.

If a user is believed to be overly reliant on or addicted to a service, the platform must send them a reminder about overuse every two hours.

Zhang Linghan, dean of the Institute of Artificial Intelligence Law at China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media outlet China News Weekly that the emotional investment offered by anthropomorphic interactive services can easily lead to psychological dependence in users, resulting in a decline in real-world social skills, particularly a weakening of the ability to resolve emotional conflicts and build deep relationships.

The new regulations apply to any services deemed as designed to foster emotional connection and interaction. Other AI chatbot functions, such as intelligent customer service, knowledge-sharing tools, and workplace assistants, are not affected.

The same day the regulations went into effect, tech giants ByteDance and Alibaba discontinued their AI companion features on Doubao and Qianwen, respectively. Qianwen shut its companion service down immediately, while Doubao is offering users a three-month grace period to migrate their data to its sister app, Maoxiang, before it is permanently deleted on Oct. 15.

Tech companies had already begun increasing regulations of their chatbots and companion services, primarily due to findings of suggestive content in their chats. On June 30, Tencent removed its AI companion service from its chatbot Yuanbao.

In April 2023, leading Chinese AI model developer MiniMax removed its AI companion product, Glow, from multiple app stores due to pornographic content. Its product manager told domestic media that “80% of users would engage in suggestive or sexually explicit conversations with the AI companions they created within Glow.”

In June 2025, AI chat app Zhumengdao was summoned to appear before the Shanghai Municipal Cyberspace Administration for generating vulgar and suggestive content that harmed minors.

After the new regulations took effect, several other AI chatbots reported an influx of users migrating from Doubao and Qianwen, and began requiring ID verification before use.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Malte Mueller/Getty Creative/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.title: Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.content:
GUANGDONG, South China — Above a dialysis clinic in Guangzhou, southern China’s Guangdong province, 67 kidney patients sew, iron and finish garments for customers in China and overseas. Many once worked as chefs, truck drivers or machine technicians before illness pushed them out of their jobs. Three times a week, they leave the factory floor for four hours of dialysis, then return to work.

The workshop was opened in 2023 by Xie Qiang, a retired oncologist who wanted patients to earn an income without hiding their condition. It offers routine, independence and a community of people living with the same illness. But it is also a business struggling to survive. Dialysis interrupts production, inexperienced workers make costly mistakes, and delayed orders threaten already narrow margins.

In June, Sixth Tone followed the workers, managers and Xie as they tried to keep the factory running. Their daily routines show how difficult it is to meet deadlines and maintain quality while making room for dialysis, fatigue and medical complications.

Additional reporting: Jiang Xinyi; story editors: Qi Ya and Apurva; script editors: Apurva and Wu Huiyuan.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018796/Chinese Tech Firms Pitch AI Agents as the Future of Smartphones
World.title: Chinese Tech Firms Pitch AI Agents as the Future of Smartphones
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018796/Chinese Tech Firms Pitch AI Agents as the Future of Smartphones
World.content:
SHANGHAI — From finding EV chargers and ordering food to booking trips and making payments, Chinese smartphone makers and AI companies are racing to bring “agentic” AI phones to market.

At this year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, domestic companies including StepFun, Nubia, and Honor showcased phones designed to understand user intent, break requests into steps, and coordinate tasks across services.

At the booth of Tencent-backed AI startup StepFun, a staffer asked the company’s new StepX Neo smartphone to find the nearest EV charging station and have his usual coffee delivered to his home when the charging session was nearly done.

Within seconds, the phone generated two service cards: one for the charging station, the other for the coffee order. The coffee card displayed an expected delivery time after the order was placed, leaving final confirmation with the user. It was unclear whether the phone completed a charging reservation.

StepFun said the phone’s built-in AI agent, Amoo, treated the two requests as connected. Drawing on stored preferences, it selected a charging station based on the driver’s vehicle model, preferred charging speed, usual charging time, and charger availability. It also used the user’s favorite coffee brand, usual order, and home address to arrange the order around the charging session.

StepFun, valued at $10 billion, also demonstrated how its AI agent could assist with workplace tasks and travel planning. To support those functions, the company said Step AOS, an Android-compatible operating system built for AI agents, has been integrated with major services including Alipay for payments, Trip.com for travel bookings, Didi Chuxing for ride-hailing, and Meituan for food delivery and other on-demand services.

The company has not disclosed the release date or price of the StepX Neo.

Other tech firms at the conference staked out similar territory, though the products on display showed how loosely the new category is still being defined.

Smartphone brand Nubia showcased the NaviX Ultra, which it described as the world’s first mass-produced AI agent phone. The device’s agent architecture is built around Doubao, China’s most popular AI assistant, developed by TikTok parent ByteDance, enabling users to manage schedules, search for information, and control multiple apps through voice or text commands.

The latest model was not available for hands-on testing at the event, and Nubia has not released official information on its launch date or price. But a previous prototype unveiled last December could handle natural-language requests, including planning trips and booking tickets and hotels.

Handset maker Honor introduced its RobotPhone, which features a built-in mechanical gimbal that allows its camera to move independently, track users’ movements, and respond to music through physical gestures.

The company said the device, based on its agentic mobile operating system, represents a shift from smartphones that respond mainly to touch commands toward devices that can interact with users more naturally. The company has not announced a launch date, delivery timeline, or price for the phone.

At a conference panel discussion, Huang Fei, Honor’s chief AI scientist, said agentic operating systems must be able to understand what users want, break complex goals into smaller tasks, and call on the right tools to complete them.

“The essence of an agentic OS isn’t adding an AI assistant to an operating system,” Huang said. “It’s rebuilding the operating system around users’ intentions and tasks.”

Even if an AI agent can plan and reason, completing real-world tasks requires access to third-party apps, payment systems, travel platforms, delivery services, and other parts of the mobile ecosystem.

“An agentic operating system cannot be built by any single company alone,” Xu Zhuhong, vice president of Alibaba Group, said at the conference.

“It requires an open ecosystem and shared standards rather than a closed product,” Xu added. “Companies across the industry chain, from foundation models to platforms and applications, must work together.”

(Header image: A man interacts with the Honor’s RobotPhone at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, July 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018788/China-Proposed Global AI Organization Launched at WAIC
World.title: China-Proposed Global AI Organization Launched at WAIC
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018788/China-Proposed Global AI Organization Launched at WAIC
World.content:
SHANGHAI – China’s World AI Conference (WAIC) kicked off on Friday in Shanghai, one day after 29 countries agreed to establish a global organization dedicated to collaborating on AI innovation, development, and governance.

Termed the “World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization,” or WAICO, China first proposed the initiative at last year’s WAIC. Signatories include Kazakhstan, Laos, Pakistan, Russia, and Indonesia.

The annual conference, held this year from July 17 to 20, was founded in 2018 by multiple national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government to connect AI companies, researchers, and developers.

This year’s event featured a keynote speech by Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well as over 1,100 international AI companies showcasing more than 3,000 cutting-edge products and technologies, including over 300 global debuts, such as an agentic AI smartphone, which can operate autonomously rather than simply responding to users’ commands.

The event also welcomed other world leaders, including United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

In his keynote speech at the conference’s opening, Xi said that AI is emerging as a new engine of economic growth and is moving from the “digital world” into the “physical world.”

“We should seize this opportunity to promote open collaboration, accelerate innovation, and expand real-world applications so that AI can empower industries across the economy,” Xi said.

He also called for enhanced alignment and coordination to develop a consensus-based global AI governance framework that better benefits humanity.

Wang Tianchan, an AI research fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies (SIIS), told Sixth Tone that Xi’s attendance reflects that the event aligns with the country’s broader national priorities.

Xi also announced that China will invite 5,000 individuals from developing countries to partake in AI training opportunities over the next five years. China will also establish international AI application cooperation centers with regional organizations, including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Arab League, the African Union, and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States.

The AI race has moved beyond models and chatbots, Gu Jiawei, founder and CEO of AI startup Ling.ai, told Sixth Tone.

“The next breakthrough will happen in the real world — whether AI can understand its environment, proceed through successive situations, and work reliably under complex constraints,” he said. “What matters most at WAIC is seeing intelligence move from demonstration into daily life.”

With AI becoming a strategic technology shaping economic growth and global competition, WAIC has also expanded beyond technology showcases to include discussions on AI governance, international cooperation, and the industry’s future. Beginning in 2024, the conference has been held alongside the country’s “High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance,” a platform for global AI dialogue.

“As AI reshapes the global landscape, the way we approach these conversations matters,” Wang, the SIIS research fellow, said. “An open, cooperative, and pragmatic approach is essential to answering one of the most critical questions today: where should AI go next?”



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A visitor interacts with an AI-powered companion robot at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, July 17, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018783/Deliver Rider Wins China’s Top Literary Prize for Poetry
World.title: Deliver Rider Wins China’s Top Literary Prize for Poetry
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018783/Deliver Rider Wins China’s Top Literary Prize for Poetry
World.content:
Food delivery rider and poet Wang Jibing has won one of China’s highest literary honors, the Lu Xun Literary Prize, for his poetry collection “Low Flight.”

The prize, announced July 15 and in its ninth edition, honored 35 works across seven categories. The award was established in 1996 in memory of the renowned Chinese writer Lu Xun and is given every four years.

Wang, a 57-year-old from the eastern Jiangsu province, is known as “a delivery rider by day and a poet by night.” Since becoming a food delivery rider in 2019 in the province’s Kunshan city, he has logged over 150,000 kilometers on the road and written more than 6,000 poems inspired by his deliveries and life.

In recent years, grassroots writers like Wang have gained increasing recognition in China. They include former miner Chen Nianxi, whose poetry and nonfiction stories document the lives of Chinese workers; Yu Xiuhua, a former farmer whose candid poems dissect subjects such as love, desire, and living with cerebral palsy; and Hu Anyan, a former courier whose book, “I Deliver Parcels in Beijing,” details the strain of gig-economy work.

Another outlet is the Picun Literature Group, a collective of migrant worker writers based in an urban village on the outskirts of Beijing. In 2017, group member Fan Yusu’s autobiography, “I Am Fan Yusu,” became a nationwide hit.

“I made deliveries yesterday, and as long as I live in Kunshan, I’ll keep delivering food,” Wang said after receiving the award. He has previously said that food delivery had since become his “side hustle,” alongside literary events and book royalties.

“Low Flight” is Wang’s third published collection. For it, he interviewed more than 140 delivery riders in hopes that readers “would better understand the challenges they face.”

“Literature used to be like a pyramid, with everyone’s attention fixed on the few people at the top,” Wang told domestic media. “Now it’s turning its focus to the base, giving voice to the silent majority.”

Born into a rural family, Wang dropped out of middle school and worked as a construction laborer and trash collector, among other jobs, before becoming a delivery rider. A father of three, he now also runs a small grocery store with his wife.

Wang began publishing literary works in magazines in the 1990s before self-publishing on social media. In July 2022, his poem “Man in a Hurry” went viral on microblogging platform Weibo. His first poetry collection, “Man in a Hurry: Poems of a Food Delivery Rider,” was published the following year.

“Man in a Hurry” was inspired by a delivery in 2019, in which a customer entered the wrong address. Wang had to rush from the address entered in the app to the correct one, delaying his other deliveries and resulting in a financial penalty from the platform.

Wang has also said that he believes the positive reception sometimes stems from his label as a “delivery rider poet” rather than the poems themselves.

“Now, every type of publicity is tied to my identity,” he said in an earlier interview. “People automatically see your writing as coming from the bottom of society. They tend to read it with sympathy, or even pity. I’m grateful for the praise, but I take it cautiously because much of it isn’t purely about the literature. I know I still have a long way to go as a writer.”

An English translation of “Low Flight” is scheduled to be published by U.S.-based Chax Press this December.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Wang Jibing alongside copies of his poetry collection “Low Flight” in Suzhou, Jiangsu province, Feb. 26, 2025. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018774/China’s AI Summer Camps Tap Into Parents’ Worries
World.title: China’s AI Summer Camps Tap Into Parents’ Worries
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018774/China’s AI Summer Camps Tap Into Parents’ Worries
World.content:
An increasing number of Chinese summer camps promising parents that their children can master AI and become “venture capitalists” within a week, and charging thousands of yuan to do so, have appeared in recent months.

As parents’ fears about their children being left behind in the AI era grow, companies are capitalizing on their anxieties, claiming they can teach kids how to use AI for business and finance in weeklong “study tours” or camps. But these summer programs often offer little more than unqualified instructors and a photo opportunity at a tech company, according to a recent report by domestic media outlet China Newsweek.

The rise of AI camps comes amid a national push to merge AI with education. Released in June, China’s national education plan integrates AI across all educational levels. In 2024, the Ministry of Education also stated that by 2030, AI education must be “basically universal” in primary and secondary schools.

And the market is lucrative. A report by domestic analytics firm Changjiang Securities projected that China’s AI education market will reach 160 billion yuan ($22 billion) by 2027 and nearly 180 billion yuan by 2030.

One Beijing AI study tour company claims it can teach children to “launch an AI startup in six days.” Priced at nearly 13,000 yuan ($2,000), the live-in program covers “AI basics, business skills, and financial thinking.”

“Many college students can’t create a business model template, yet our campers can present one on stage after just six days,” an anonymous company staff member told China Newsweek.

Prices for multi-day AI study camps in Beijing and Shanghai typically start at around 6,000 yuan. Equivalent courses in Hong Kong generally cost more than 10,000 yuan, and overseas courses can cost up to 30,000 yuan.

Official rules require study tour companies to hold three licenses: a business registration, a travel permit, and an educational service certification. But according to China Newsweek, many AI camp organizers are media firms or one-person companies.

A study tour industry insider with 10 years of experience said that STEM camps have overtaken traditional outdoor programs. Her children’s AI camp at the Harbin Institute of Technology (HIT) in the northeastern Heilongjiang province sold out after advertising exclusive access to a chip lab and AI courses.

The insider said, however, that many companies double their prices despite only offering visits to tech organizations, rather than actual coursework. “As long as kids snap a photo at HIT, the trip is deemed ‘meaningful’ (by parents),” she said.

Dong Ling, the mother of a 5-year-old in Shanghai, views AI as a tool. “AI amplifies (children’s) existing strengths,” she told Sixth Tone. “For their generation, AI is their native environment.”

She believes parents’ focus should be on integrating AI into daily learning. “We are entering an era of human-AI collaboration,” she said. “Instead of chasing hype, parents should focus on teaching kids how to use these tools responsibly and creatively in their daily lives.”

Song, the parent of a fifth-grader and a third-grader in the southern city of Guangzhou, told Sixth Tone that she plans to enroll her children in AI camps once they reach middle school. When choosing camps, she says she will prioritize interaction, hands-on experiences, and small classes.

“I hope my kids make diverse friends, learn about others, see their own differences, and gain real knowledge through firsthand experiences (at AI camp),” Song said.

But surging demand has also created a shortage of qualified AI instructors, with many programs relying on hastily trained graduate students or basic programming tutors to lead classes.

Outside first-tier cities, qualified teachers are hard to find, an anonymous edtech recruiter told domestic media. Her company interviewed music and sports majors for an AI course, and ended up hiring a flight attendant. “A few days of training is standard,” she said.

Fu Lin, co-founder of Kaichuangli, an edtech company based in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen dedicated to equipping children with AI literacy and programming skills, said that AI education in China suffers from inconsistent standards. The goal, he said, is to teach children AI as though it is their native language, and not to take shortcuts.

An 11-year-old surnamed Xu told Sixth Tone that she spent five days this July at an AI camp at the tech giant Alibaba’s headquarters in the eastern city of Hangzhou.

Xu toured the corporate campus and participated in hands-on coding sessions. She described how instructors guided students in using Alibaba’s large language model, Qwen, to generate a business plan template for a simulated online store and craft compelling product descriptions on the company’s e-commerce platform Taobao.

“I learned so much that isn’t in our textbooks,” Xu said.

But despite AI’s rapid rise, Song, the mother in Guangzhou, isn’t anxious.

“Some human qualities can’t be replaced,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A STEM camp in Beijing, June 2026. VCG)

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Hearsay? Defense questions Matibag’s knowledge of Sara Duterte’s ‘threats’
World.content:
MATIBAG. National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag testifies in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 21, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – The defense team of Sara Duterte centered its cross-examination on Tuesday, July 21, by pounding on National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag’s lack of personal knowledge of some aspects of the NBI’s probe into the Vice President’s alleged grave threats.

During his cross-examination, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan laid out the NBI director’s lack of personal knowledge by asking him a series of queries. First, Vinluan asked Matibag about the 10 subpoenas issued to the personalities who attended Duterte’s 2024 press conference, where she allegedly threatened President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Each time Matibag said he lacked personal knowledge of a specific document flashed on the screen, the defense put an “X” emoji on it.

The NBI director said he was also not the signatory to the NBI subpoenas because he was not yet appointed at the time.

“The witness already testified that he has no personal knowledge about the first investigation. And all his testimonies will be based only on the records existing in the NBI,” lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro interjected during the trial.

Matibag explained on Tuesday that the NBI probe has two parts. The first was the investigation right after the November 2024 press conference under a different NBI head. The second probe, meanwhile, refers to the special task force created by Matibag’s Administrative Order No. 11 last April.

Vinluan later went straight to his point: witnesses can only testify to the information they have personal knowledge of. During the trial, he asked Matibag about the rule on the limitations of testimony, stating Section 22 of Rule 130 of the amended rules on evidence.

“A witness can testify only to those facts which he or she knows of his or her personal knowledge; that is, which are derived from his or her own perception,” the provision stated.

The defense’s point was that Matibag only has personal knowledge so far as the second probe is concerned.

“Ang sinasabi natin is, pagdating do’n sa unang investigation na wala siyang personal knowledge, ‘yon po ay tinatawag nating hearsay. So, ibig sabihin, wala kang personal na kaalaman kasi hindi ka na-involve doon sa investigasyon na ‘yon,” defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa told reporters in a briefing.

(What we are saying is, in terms of the first investigation, which he has no personal knowledge of, that’s hearsay. This means a person has no personal knowledge because that person was not involved in the investigation.)

Play Video

Testing Matibag’s credibility, ‘bias’

Similar to past impeachment trials, the defense team cast doubt on Matibag by testing his credibility and supposed bias.

“Ang point namin talaga is to test the credibility, test kung may bias man o wala,” Poa said. “We were really just testing the credibility at kung may personal bias ‘yong witness because that will, syempre, affect ‘yong integrity ng kaniyang mga naging testimonya or at least ‘yong pagsasagawa ng imbestigasyon.”

(Our point is to test the credibility, test if there’s bias or none. We were really just testing the credibility, and if the witness has personal bias, that will affect the integrity of his testimony or his conduct of investigation.)

The defense also touched on Matibag’s personal life, specifically on his incident with friend Mel Sabio.

Last May, Matibag was in hot water after his conversation with his friend leaked. In the viral video, Matibag was arguing with Sabio over the phone, and, at one point, the NBI director could be heard allegedly threatening to harm his friend.

However, Matibag and Sabio have already reconciled after the incident.

As to the alleged bias, the defense also highlighted that Matibag’s wife, Laguna 1st District Representative Ann Matibag, is among the lawmakers who backed the articles of impeachment against Duterte.

Vinluan also presented Matibag’s opinion article, “Inday Sara, The Bratinella,” which depicted the Vice President as a brat.

“Yes, my wife is one of the endorsers of the impeachment,” Matibag said during the trial.

“My decision to be a witness is by virtue of a subpoena issued by the honorable court and by invitation of the committee on justice, the prosecution. However, the job of my wife as a legislator is totally detached from me being the director of the National Bureau of Investigation,” he further explained.

Play Video

“We meant no offense, and I hope none was taken by Director Matibag. We respect that, except that in cross-examinations, you really have to test not just the credibility but also bias,” Poa said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Objecting to Lascañas’ affidavit

The prosecution asked Matibag to read portions of self-confessed Davao Death Squad member Arturo Lascañas’ affidavit, which mentioned the Vice President. This affidavit has been submitted to the International Criminal Court as part of the crimes against humanity case against Duterte’s father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Lascañas named the Vice President over five times in his affidavit. There, he claimed that they had allegedly received kill orders from the former president, then later, from Sara as Davao City mayor.

In another instance, Lascañas claimed that an abduction operation allegedly ordered by Sara had been relayed to him at one point.

For the defense, Matibag’s reading of the document during the trial was “highly improper.”

“We already allowed the witness [to] at least identify this document. But as to the fact that he is allowed to read even portions thereof, he’s not the author of this affidavit. And as to the truth or falsity thereof, [he’s] incompetent to testify on that. And it…already violates the rights of our client because she’s being prejudiced by the reading of this affidavit,” Vinluan explained.

The impeachment court allowed the defense’s motion to continue its cross-examination of Matibag on Wednesday, July 22, to give them more time to study the Lascañas document. – Rappler.com

World.title: Barangay health workers appeal to Marcos: Revive Magna Carta as priority bill
World.content:
LONG-STANDING PLEA. Barangay health workers submit an appeal letter to Malacañang to seek the passage of their own Magna Carta, July 21, 2026.

They hope President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. would include the proposed Magna Carta of Barangay Health Workers in his upcoming State of the Nation Address on July 27

MANILA, Philippines – Barangay health workers (BHWs) from various cities in Metro Manila submitted an appeal letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Tuesday, July 21, to reiterate their calls for a Magna Carta ahead of his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA).

Representatives of the National Confederation of Barangay Health Workers of the Philippines (NCBHWP) and labor group UNI Global Union–Philippine Liaison Council personally delivered their letter to Malacañang, calling for the proposed Magna Carta of BHWs to be restored as a priority legislative measure.

“For more than four decades, BHWs have waited for the enactment of a Magna Carta that would uphold and protect our rights,” they wrote in the letter.

APPEAL. The first page of the National Confederation of Barangay Health Workers of the Philippines and UNI Global Union–Philippine Liaison Council’s appeal letter addressed to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Photo by Eirene Manatlao/Rappler

Myrna Gaite, a barangay health worker and president of the BHW Federation of the National Capital Region, recounted how some of her colleagues have died without ever receiving better compensation.

“Ako, 40 years in service na ako. Boluntaryo ako, nagsimula sa wala…. Pinapanalangin ng bawat barangay health worker na magkaroon ng katugunan ang Magna Carta dahil doon napapaloob ang lahat ng mga benepisyo para sa mga BHW,” Gaite said.

(I’ve been in service for 40 years. I was a volunteer who started with nothing. Every barangay health worker is praying for the Magna Carta to be realized, as it encompasses all benefits for BHWs.)

The Marcos administration previously included the proposed Magna Carta of BHWs as a priority measure of the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council in 2023.

The bill was nearing approval before the 19th Congress ended, but failed when the House of Representatives withdrew its version’s transmittal.

“In 2023, the President gave renewed hope to hundreds of thousands of BHWs when he publicly committed to supporting our Magna Carta. Today, BHWs are humbly appealing to the President to fulfill his promise,” NCBHWP president Khonan Cerial said.

BHWs, the primary healthcare providers at the barangay level, are left with a heavy workload and additional responsibilities not in their job description, all while being compensated poorly as volunteers.

The Magna Carta bill at the Senate, which has been approved on second reading as of writing, promises to institutionalize the employment of BHWs and give them permanent government positions. Instead of just honoraria and flexible benefits, they would be entitled to receive pay equivalent to Salary Grade 1.

Lyma Rico, Marikina BHW Federation president, said: “Ito na ang pagkakataon ng barangay health workers na maipasa ang Magna Carta. Sa tagal-tagal na lumipas na panahon, hindi man lang maipasa. Siguro ito na ‘yung pagkakataon na ibigay niya sa amin ito.”

(This is the opportunity for the Magna Carta of BHWs to be finally enacted into law. It has languished for so long. Perhaps the President will now grant our plea.)

Marcos is set to deliver his fifth SONA on Monday, July 27. – Rappler.com

World.title: Future Kiyapo? Incoming LPA has high chance of becoming tropical depression
World.content:
LPA. Satellite image of the low pressure area outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of July 21, 2026, 3 pm.

The low pressure area might enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Wednesday, July 22

MANILA, Philippines – A low pressure area (LPA) outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) has a high chance of developing into a tropical depression within 24 hours, the weather bureau said on Tuesday afternoon, July 21.

The LPA had formed outside PAR on Monday, July 20. As of 3 pm on Tuesday, it was located 1,505 kilometers east of Eastern Visayas.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said the LPA might enter PAR within 12 to 24 hours, or by Wednesday, July 22.

If it becomes a tropical cyclone inside PAR or enters PAR as a tropical cyclone, it would be given the local name Kiyapo — the Filipino word for water cabbage or water lettuce. Manila’s Quiapo district got its name from this plant.

The potential Kiyapo would be the Philippines’ 11th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the fourth for July.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Benison Estareja said the incoming weather disturbance could reach tropical storm intensity. In this scenario, the highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal would be Signal No. 2.

Estareja added that the future Kiyapo could move toward Northern Luzon on Friday, July 24, or Saturday, July 25. This means Northern Luzon and even Central Luzon may be directly affected during the second half of the week.

For now, the trough or extension of the LPA could bring scattered rain and thunderstorms to Eastern Visayas on Tuesday evening.

PAGASA advised the public to regularly monitor updates on the potential tropical cyclone as forecasts can still change.

The weather bureau is also warning the public to watch out for rain from the southwest monsoon or habagat, especially on the western side of the country.

Mindanao, Western Visayas, the Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, and Palawan are seeing scattered rain and thunderstorms due to the southwest monsoon on Tuesday evening. At the moment, Metro Manila only has localized thunderstorms, which are not linked to the southwest monsoon.

Rain from the southwest monsoon is likely to worsen in the coming days, with PAGASA releasing the following outlook at 5 pm on Tuesday:

Wednesday afternoon, July 22, to Thursday afternoon, July 23

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Maguindanao del Norte, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani

Thursday afternoon, July 23, to Friday afternoon, July 24

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Negros Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Sultan Kudarat

Floods and landslides are possible. – Rappler.com

World.title: Iranian forces target Bahrain and Kuwait after US hits Iran’s south
World.content:
IRAN TARGET. Military equipment targeted at an unknown location, during what US Central Command (CENTCOM) says are strikes on Iran, in this screengrab taken from a handout video released on July 20, 2026.

Despite the escalating cycle of attacks that has all but wrecked an interim peace agreement signed in June, signs that Tehran and Washington want to resume diplomacy keep oil prices in check

DUBAI, UAE – US forces bombed targets in southern Iran overnight after President Donald Trump said Tehran would pay dearly for the deaths of American soldiers, while Iran targeted US sites in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan and a tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz.

The exchanges came a day after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, opening a potential new front in the war and raising the threat to global energy supplies and trade beyond the Gulf.

Despite the escalating cycle of attacks that has all but wrecked an interim peace agreement signed last month, signs that Tehran and Washington want to resume diplomacy kept oil prices in check.

US Central Command said it had completed its latest round of strikes on Iran, saying it hit Iranian military command centers, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites, and air defence systems.

Explosions were heard around the city of Shiraz in southern Iran, while Konarak and Chabahar on the southern coast also came under attack, according to state media.

Iran responded with renewed attacks across the Gulf, where recent strikes on desalination facilities have raised concerns about water shortages and underscored the growing threat to civilian infrastructure.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they targeted infrastructure in Bahrain belonging to US tech company Amazon in retaliation for what they described as a US strike on the construction site of Iran’s planned Darkhovin nuclear power plant.

Iranian state media reported that Iranian forces also targeted accommodation facilities used by US military personnel at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Air Base. There was no immediate comment from the US military, Bahrain or Amazon on the reported incidents, which Reuters was unable to verify.

The Iranian army said it launched drone attacks against three US military bases in Kuwait on Tuesday. The Revolutionary Guards said they attacked a US military site in Jordan, and Jordan said its forces intercepted and destroyed five Iranian drones.

Tankers struck

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Tuesday a tanker in the strait reported being struck by an unknown projectile, forcing its crew to abandon the vessel and board a lifeboat.

Also on Tuesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers had caught fire after explosions while attempting to transit the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz. It was not immediately clear when those incidents took place.

Iran had been pressing the Houthis to close the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea if the US continued to attack Iranian power infrastructure — putting two of the world’s most vital energy arteries at risk.

A full closure of Bab el-Mandeb would reduce global oil supply by 7% as it would leave most Saudi oil exports unable to leave the region. The disruption would add to the huge cut to oil flows from the war in the Gulf, which has already reduced shipments by 10% of global supply.

After the Houthis announced their blockade, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it began implementing protection measures for its ships moving through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Oil markets weighed the threat to shipping against reports of diplomatic efforts to contain the conflict, with benchmark Brent crude prices easing slightly in early trading.

Diplomatic push to restore ceasefire

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday that Tehran had received a proposal from mediators for a 10-day ceasefire in efforts to salvage the interim deal, intended to pave the way to a lasting agreement to end the war that began on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni had asked Pakistan to resume its mediation role in the conflict. He later arrived in Islamabad for further talks.

The latest phase of fighting has proved to be among the deadliest of the conflict for US forces. US troop deaths rose to 17 over the weekend.

Trump, under mounting pressure at home over rising gasoline prices since the war began, said the latest US strikes on Iran were honoring the deaths of American service members.

“Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over! This directive has been passed on to Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Daniel Caine, and every Leader in the Military,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

The war has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon. Parts of Lebanon remain under Israeli occupation following attacks on Israel by Hezbollah fighters, who said they were acting in solidarity with Tehran.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun is due to meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday to present a plan on how to disarm Iran-aligned Hezbollah and secure an Israeli withdrawal. – Rappler.com

World.title: US, China to hold AI talks in September – sources
World.content:
The AI talks, a significant outcome of the Trump-Xi summit in May, will likely take place before Chinese President Xi Jinping's planned September 24 visit to the US, although the dates have not been finalized, sources say

BEIJING, China – The United States and China are planning to hold talks over AI in September, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, as the superpowers confront how to regulate the risks posed by their increasingly powerful rival frontier models.

The AI talks, a significant outcome of the Trump-Xi summit in May, will likely take place before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned September 24 visit to the US, although the dates have not been finalized, said the sources, who asked not to be named as the information is not public.

The talks would be led on the US side by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, four of the sources said. The identity of other participants on the US and Chinese side, as well as the agenda and location of the discussion, are still under deliberation as preparations are at an initial stage, three of them said.

The White House, US State Department and US Treasury did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. China’s National Development and Reform Commission, cyberspace regulator, industry and foreign ministries, and the State Council did not immediately respond to faxed requests for comment. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Romualdez did not ‘dare’ Senate to investigate him; video is AI-generated
World.content:
While the former House speaker has denied allegations that he masterminded a corruption scheme in the government, he did not make the statements shown in the video

Claim: In a video, former House speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez denied being the central figure in corruption scandals in the government and challenged the Senate to invite him to its probe.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The video was posted by a Facebook page named PolPolitika on July 15. As of writing, the video has garnered more than 2,100 reactions, 1,700 shares, and 700 comments.

The video appears to show Romualdez being interviewed onboard a ship, where he says, “Sa mga Pilipinong hindi bumibitaw, hindi niyo ba naisip? Imposible talaga na ako ang nag-approve ng budget. Common sense na lang talaga.”

(To the Filipinos who aren’t letting this issue go, haven’t you thought about it? It’s impossible that I approved the budget. It’s just common sense.)

“Bakit ako palagi ang puno’t dulo ng lahat ng ito? Imbitahan nila ako sa Senado. Hindi ako natatakot kahit kanino,” he added.

(Why am I always the one tagged as the central figure in all of this? Invite me to the Senate. I’m not afraid of anyone.)

Romualdez also allegedly calls out Senators Vicente Sotto III, Panfilo Lacson, and the Tulfo brothers while challenging the upper chamber to invite him to their hearings on alleged corruption in flood control projects.

Many social media users believed the post, with some urging the former House speaker to appear before the Senate while others called on Romualdez to drop the names of those involved in the system of corruption.

The facts: The video is AI-generated. Results from the AI video detection tool detectvideo.ai showed a 64% likelihood of use of AI generation tools with high confidence level. Humantext.pro also flagged it as AI-generated with a rating of 72%.

There are no reports from credible media outlets citing Romualdez as making the statements shown in the video.

‘Central figure’ in corruption scandal: Romualdez has been implicated in corruption allegations, particularly the flood control ghost projects and budget insertion scheme.

In November 2025, former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co released a video accusing Romualdez and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of being the masterminds behind insertions in the 2025 national budget.

The Office of the Ombudsman also tagged the Leyte representative as a “central figure” in the flood control corruption scandal.

“Our investigation identifies former speaker Romualdez as the central figure in a scheme built on the diversion of public funds meant for flood control projects — funds that were supposed to shield Filipino communities from the very floods that, year after year, take their homes, their livelihoods, and too often, their lives,” Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said on Monday, July 20.

The former House speaker, however, has repeatedly asserted his innocence. While he did not attend Senate hearings on the budget corruption controversy, he has denied the allegations against him and insisted that he won’t allow himself to be a “fall guy.” (WATCH: Breaking down Romualdez’s response to corruption claims)

Romualdez is currently placed under a precautionary hold departure order along with other individuals allegedly involved in the corruption scandal. The US government also canceled Romualdez’s diplomatic and tourist/business visas.

Earlier this year, the Court of Appeals ordered the freezing of assets linked to Romualdez. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Landbank, Visa launch government credit card with spending controls
World.content:
CREDIT CARD. Visa Philippines country manager Jeffrey Navarro (4th from left), Landbank executive vice president Marilou Villafranca (5th from right), and first vice president Kristine Marie Cuevas (4th from right) pose with other representatives of various government agencies.

Landbank's government credit card also comes with an expense management system that captures transactions, matches expenses with receipts, and facilitates approval processes

MANILA, Philippines – Land Bank of the Philippines (Landbank) and Visa have launched a customizable government credit card, which they assert will give agencies tighter control over public funds and provide a better audit trail.

The Landbank Visa Government Purchase Card (GPC) works much like a corporate credit card issued to agency heads and authorized officers. Agencies can set a credit limit for each cardholder and restrict transactions to approved merchant categories, such as travel, fuel, representation expenses, and low-value purchases.

Landbank executive vice president and branch banking group head Marilou Villafranca said the card would reduce the need for employees to request cash advances, spend their own money, and later submit documents for reimbursement or liquidation.

“This will cut the manual processes or paper-based cash advances as well as liquidation,” Villafranca said. “Because it works like a credit card, you just use your card and then, upon the billing cycle, the agency will have to pay the entire amount.”

Expense management system for government

Purchase cards have long been offered to companies, but Visa Philippines country manager Jeffrey Navarro said the main differentiator in the Landbank program is its accompanying expense management system.

The platform will automatically capture transactions, match expenses with receipts, facilitate approval processes, and generate reports showing how much was spent, by whom, and under which department or spending category.

Transactions outside an employee’s approved limit or spending rules may be rejected or flagged for further approval.

“By providing accurate data, it can allow more financial control and better governance by the implementing institution,” Navarro said. “It’s not just a card na all of a sudden you can just spend digitally.”

The platform is scheduled to become fully operational by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Villafranca said the system could also be made accessible to the Commission on Audit, allowing state auditors to view spending information using the same data available to the agency.

“From the time you use your card, that’s already transparent in the expense management system,” she said.

The Bureau of the Treasury is among the first government institutions to adopt the Visa-backed program, which has an expense management system component.

Landbank clarified that its wider government purchase card program had already onboarded 107 agencies since 2023. Around 773 cards have so far been issued, mostly to agency heads and senior officers.

What is new in the latest rollout is the Visa expense-management system, which 17 government offices are initially set to use.

The bank eventually wants to expand the program beyond national government agencies to state universities, government corporations, local governments, and possibly barangays. – Rappler.com

World.title: A transplant is no longer out of reach for children with cancer at PGH
World.content:
Sheila Romero, founder of the I Want To Share Foundation, with First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and British donor Jonathan Sterling at the Opening of PGH Stem Cell Transplantation and Cellular Therapy Center.

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine General Hospital has opened the country’s first charity bone marrow transplant unit, built so that a child’s survival no longer depends on what their family can pay.

First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos led the inauguration of the facility at PGH’s Stem Cell Transplantation and Cellular Therapy Center in Manila on Friday, July 10.

The unit was funded by the I Want To Share Foundation (IWTS), the childhood cancer charity founded by Sheila B. Romero, and will be operated by the PGH.

Article continues after this 

According to the foundation, more than 600 Filipino children with blood-related disorders need the procedure.

READ: Child cancer in PH: When inequality decides who lives or dies

The unit will offer it for free or subsidized, with priority for charity patients.

Its rooms are built for patients with extremely fragile immune systems, following strict infection-control protocols that include HEPA-filtered air systems.

Foundation legacy

“This is a legacy that the foundation would like to leave,” Romero said. “It’s our promise, our commitment, to continue to help these children every step of the way.”

Article continues after this 

The stakes are stark. The survival rate of children with cancer in the Philippines is only about 20 percent, Romero said.

Behind that figure is poverty, not medicine. Most of PGH’s young cancer patients are indigent, she said, many traveling from the provinces for treatment they cannot always continue. Some families stop coming back.

Article continues after this 

“It’s a choice between five children with no food or one child with cancer,” Romero said. “We hope that it’s no longer a choice later on — because there is an available facility, there is available financial help.”

In her speech, Marcos lauded the health workers, donors, and partners behind the facility, calling it a lasting beacon of hope for vulnerable Filipino families.

Self-sustaining ward

The ward is designed to sustain itself. Costs will be shared with the hospital, Romero said, and paying patients will help subsidize charity patients, who will have priority.

The unit was completed and turned over in about six months, she added.

The inauguration caps a decade of work. Since 2015, IWTS has supported PGH with second opinions, chemotherapy, MRI access, nurses’ salaries, and transportation home for patients and their families.

In 2024, the foundation renovated the hospital’s pediatric infectious ward, and a leukemia ward is set to follow.

Beyond the wards, the foundation runs survivorship programs, including hearing aids for children whose hearing was damaged by chemotherapy, in partnership with a Manila hearing foundation.

Its Childhood Cancer Helpline is training barangay health workers and physicians in Bacoor, Cavite, and Santa Rosa, Laguna. Patient navigators at PGH help arriving families land a slot with the right doctor the first time.

For children who cannot be saved, the foundation funds palliative care and burial expenses.

“We want to give them the dignity of life,” Romero said.

None of it happens alone, Romero stressed, thanking the benefactors behind the project — among them British donor Jonathan Sterling — “for the trust that has been given by all of these people.”

READ: Jonathan Sterling: Sometimes, hope begins with one generous heart

In August 2025, the foundation’s charity gala raised ₱88 million, earmarked for the ward’s second phase and 50 pieces of medical equipment for PGH’s Cancer Institute.

World.title: Highlights: Day 8 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | July 21, 2026
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court opened Day 8 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial on Tuesday by admonishing National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag, with Presiding Officer Francis Escudero telling him to “kindly avoid statements pertaining to individual members of this impeachment court” as soon as Matibag was called to the witness stand.

Matibag had been at the center of a public dispute with some senator-judges before his testimony.

READ: Highlights: Day 7 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | July 20, 2026

Article continues after this 

Despite defense objections to prosecution questions about the NBI’s special task force, Escudero overruled most of the challenges and allowed Matibag to proceed.

Testifying under Article IV on Duterte’s alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, Matibag told the court that the NBI aimed to establish a “pattern of violence” against Duterte.

The prosecution presented a video of Duterte, when she was Davao City mayor, punching a sheriff as supporting evidence of that pattern.

Matibag also testified that the similarity between threats made by Duterte and those later made by her brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, suggests possible collusion against the president’s life.

When Senator-judge Bam Aquino asked about the probability that Duterte had spoken to a hitman, Matibag replied that based on the vice president’s own statements, he was “100 percent” certain she had spoken to someone.

Article continues after this 

At the close of the session, the court granted a defense motion for a continuance, giving the defense team more time to examine documents the prosecution presented during Matibag’s testimony.

As a result, the cross-examination of Matibag will continue on Wednesday, July 22, and Article I on Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds will not be taken up that day.

Article continues after this 

Presiding Officer Escudero also announced that Week 4 of the trial will consist of only one session day, running from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., to accommodate President Marcos’s State of the Nation Address on July 27 and the Kontra-Sona on July 28.

Off the witness stand, House prosecutors held a press conference to address several controversies. Rep. Chel Diokno and lawyer Jay Tolosa denied that Duterte was impeached before evidence was gathered, arguing the Senate trial is the proper forum for full presentation of evidence.

Diokno described the subpoena order as “a big step forward” for the prosecution of Article II on unexplained wealth, while stressing the case is still in its early stages.

The defense team, for its part, said lawyers were “shocked” that much of the financial-records ruling had been prepared before the trial formally began on July 6, though defense spokesperson lawyer Michael Poa said the team respects the decision.

Meanwhile, Duterte herself was in The Hague, Netherlands during Day 8, according to her defense team. /dp
