Tech.title: The Best Smart Home Accessories to Boost Your Curb Appeal (2026)
Tech.content:
If this is a common problem at your house, our resident bird-gear tester Kat Merck has a solution: a smart nesting box. Birdfy makes a few different smart bird feeders we like for bird-watching, and the Nest Duo is a birdhouse that lets you watch the birds while they nest inside of it. It's a slim, attractive box that will add to your front yard's style while also packing two solar-powered cameras (one facing the entrance, one focused inside) so you can bird-watch from multiple angles. It comes with different hole sizes to appeal to different species, metal predator guards to prevent chewing around the hole, and a remote control to reset or recharge the camera without disturbing your feathered neighbors.

Stylish Smart Lights

I've liked Govee's smart outdoor string lights before, usually for my holiday decor, and have previously recommended something similar with a bistro-light-like look that happened to be smart. These clear bulb string lights are part of Govee's current lineup and have a contemporary twist with a triangle in the center instead of the wire filament. These are a fun option for outdoor lights you can enjoy on warm nights, and they can do every color and shade of white without looking as bulky as permanent outdoor lights. (Added bonus, these lights are also Matter compatible!)

Fresh Bulbs

If you have light fixtures you want to remote-control, add an outdoor smart bulb. There are tons to choose from, and you can usually find one from any brand you already have at home. The only downside is that outdoor-rated smart bulbs are usually 4.75-inch-diameter PAR38-style bulbs, so they're best for downward-facing floodlights on your porch or balcony. They'll likely be too big to fit in a wall fixture as a replacement for a normal-sized bulb. Don't just grab any smart bulb—not all are outdoor-rated. Check for mentions of outdoor use and waterproof ratings to make sure they're safe to use. I'm a big fan of Cync bulbs, and the brand has an outdoor version of the Cync Full Color bulbs I like to use indoors. You'll be able to add fun colors as well as shades of white, so you can turn the porch a spooky orange or red for Halloween, pink for Valentine's Day, or the colors of your favorite sports team on game day.

A Clean Pool

I'll never forget the gorgeous Airbnb I stayed at once that had a pool right in the front yard. Most pools aren't really something you need to worry about for official curb appeal, but if you can spot your pool from anywhere outside of your home, you'll want it looking pristine. My parents’ pool was one you could see from the road behind their house, for example, and while we didn't have that many trees, it still needed a ton of cleaning. If you're sick of trying to keep your pool clean, there's a handy gadget that can help: a robotic pool cleaner. It's like a robot vacuum but for your pool, working autonomously to scrub the floors, walls, and waterline. Beatbot makes a few different robot pool cleaners we like, but WIRED reviewer Christopher Null says the AquaSense 2 is a great option for under $1,000. It has three cleaning modes and a run time of four hours, and will return to its docking station to wirelessly recharge after it cleans.

Remote-Controlled Garage

If your garage is the centerpiece of your home's curb appeal, you can control it as easily as a smart door by adding a smart controller. You can do two different styles: I have the Chamberlain MyQ professionally installed smart garage opener, which means the device that controls my garage has these smarts built into it (plus a camera, but I find it doesn't work great with how far the device is from my Wi-Fi router), or you can get a smart garage controller that can add smart features onto an existing garage door. Both let you check whether the garage is open or closed and operate it remotely, and you can add a video keypad that doubles as a video doorbell and can let you open or close the garage without your phone.

Smart Shades

The front of my home faces west, so it's absolutely baking at the end of the day. What I need to add are some of our favorite smart shades to automate closing the shades on that side of the house at the right time of day. These also give your home a nice, cohesive look and immediate, controllable privacy from the outside world. Tech.title: Abdul El-Sayed Is an Epidemiologist Running for Senate. His State Is a Public Health Disaster
Tech.content:
Michigan is ground zero for the twin public health crises wreaking havoc in the US. The state has had some of the most polluted air on Earth due to Canadian wildfire smoke last week while it also has the highest number of cyclosporiasis cases in the country.

These in-your-face (and sometimes in-your-gut) problems, says senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, help make a complex topic—the need to invest in public health infrastructure—extremely easy to talk about with voters. And he has unique qualifications to do so as a MD-PhD who’s served as the health officer for Detroit.

“Do you like eating lettuce? I do. I don’t like the idea because we DOGE’d our whole service that keeps the lettuce safe,” El-Sayed says, referring to how the Department of Government Efficiency downsized the federal lab that tests for cyclosporiasis last year. “Now, everybody’s trying to dodge the lettuce. And if you don’t, then you’re stuck on a toilet for the next five days. That sucks.”

El-Sayed is locked in a tight Democratic primary for Michigan’s open senatorial seat. He’s received support from big-name progressives: Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rallied with him in Grand Rapids over the weekend, while Senator Elizabeth Warren endorsed him on Monday. In her endorsement, Warren said El-Sayed was someone who would fight “the same billionaires and special interests that have rigged our economy against working people.” For El-Sayed, that includes addressing election spending.

“A lot of this, in the end, comes back to getting money out of politics,” he says. “A lot of these changes in regulations are about massive food companies being like, well, those regulations are too much. We can enforce them ourselves. I’m like, can you? How come you didn’t fix the poop lettuce?”

WIRED caught up with El-Sayed to chat about how he’d fix the public health problems facing his state and why we shouldn’t accept that “poop lettuce” is our new normal.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

WIRED: How have the past few weeks been for you personally, with this one-two punch of public health crises?

Abdul El-Sayed: I don’t know what happened, but for four days I got taken out—I didn’t get tested, because I was on the campaign trail, but I think it was [cyclosporiasis]. If you can imagine campaigning, it was miserable. It was actually my wife who was like, you probably got this.

And then for the past week or so, we’ve been really worried about air quality. I try to stay active—I do a lot of biking—and I’ve been choosing to stay inside. You do more harm than good exercising outside with this kind of air quality.

You shouldn’t have to be dodging lettuce everywhere you go and then unknowingly getting the runs because you didn’t dodge the lettuce. Step back and ask yourself if any of this is normal.

You’ve had a lot of experience handling crises like these at the local and state level. What would you do in the Senate, especially given an administration that has been taking away funding and staff and the basic tools of public health, like peer-reviewed science and public data?

I’d love to be able to haul up leaders at the EPA, the CDC, and the FDA [to testify before Congress]. I want to investigate exactly how our food supply got compromised, how decisions were made at the CDC. Why are their counts so far behind? For the vast majority of people, cyclosporiasis is not a deadly outcome—but imagine what happens when the same infrastructure has to deal with something that really is. What are we going to do then?

Tech.title: ‘It’s a Modern-Day Draft’: Why Stanford Students Walked Out on Sundar Pichai’s Commencement Speech
Tech.content:
Are the kids all right? The answer to that question probably depends on your criteria. At the very least, I can tell you that some of them are most definitely very mad.

The anger percolating among America’s youth was on display this graduation season, as college students across the country booed and jeered several high-profile commencement speakers who dared discuss—let alone extol the benefits of—artificial intelligence. While AI use among college kids is widespread, so too is the fear and mistrust about what the technology might mean for the future. A recent Gallup poll found that Gen Z sentiment toward AI has significantly declined, with only 22 percent of respondents expressing excitement about the tech—and anxiety around AI affecting 42 percent of them.

Among the commencement speech chaos, though, one school stood out to me: Stanford University. The California-based institution, long a key hub for Silicon Valley recruiting and a pipeline into elite tech gigs, this year saw more than a hundred students walk out of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s remarks to graduates. Ironically, Pichai didn’t explicitly mention AI in his address at all. But for the organizers of the Stanford walkout, AI is only a tangential concern: More than any specific technology, their demonstration was designed to raise awareness of Google’s contracts with the US and Israeli governments, as well as ICE.

The walkout organizers may not have convinced Google to change its ways, but they did manage to create an international news event. Media outlets including CNN and the BBC ran with the story, and videos of the walkout have amassed millions of views online. I wanted to know more about how the coordinated effort came to be, what student organizers hoped to accomplish, and how it feels to be newly graduating—from a school as Silicon Valley–aligned as Stanford, no less—into a world that’s now arguably run by Big Tech.

Two of the Stanford walkout organizers, Eva Jones and Amanda Campos, traveled to New York and sat down with me in person earlier this month. Our conversation is below.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Eva Jones and Amanda Campos—welcome, both of you.

AMANDA CAMPOS: Thank you so much, Katie. Thank you for having us.

I'm delighted that you're here. Thank you for making the trip. First of all, congratulations on graduating. What did you study in school? Why did you choose Stanford four years ago when you were thinking about where to go to undergrad?

Campos: I studied environmental policy at Stanford, and I am currently working in the environmental justice activism and advocacy space in California.

I quite literally came to Stanford because I knew I wanted to take action, to solve the environmental crisis. I grew up in Brazil, and since I was little it was the huge issue I saw as being able to take action towards.

But arriving at Stanford, I quickly realized [the school] just had so much fossil fuel money and bias, and I quickly became an organizer as a result. As a sophomore, when October 2023 came, I quite quickly realized how intertwined the environmental justice movement and the movement for Palestinian liberation are.

It goes back to the corporate ties Stanford has, and choosing a Google CEO is indicative of such a tie and of such a bias, really. I was a lead organizer with Stanford SJP, Students for Justice in Palestine, and as soon as we heard about Sundar Pichai being chosen as the commencement speaker, we knew we had to do something.

Eva, what about you? What did you go to Stanford to study?

Tech.title: Stop Saying Kids Can’t Read
Tech.content:
It’s three weeks until Mississippi’s standardized test season begins, and Candace Hamberlin is feeling the pressure.

Evidence of what’s at stake hangs all around Jefferson County Middle School, where Hamberlin is in her first year teaching eighth-grade English. Inside her classroom, a large piece of black polyester with clear pouches labeled “Data Wall” shows the current reading level of each student. The school hallways are lined with posters listing schoolwide scores on an earlier practice test. One prominently displays the grade Mississippi would assign their school if that practice test had been the real thing: 175 out of 700 points, an F.

Jefferson County is one of the smallest in Mississippi; 6,800 people spread across 527 square miles along the Mississippi River. It’s also one of the poorest, with 32 percent of the population living below the poverty line. Fayette, where the only public elementary, middle, and high school are all based, is the only city in the county, home to about a dozen churches but not a single stoplight. The county is 13 percent white, but most of those families send their kids to private or parochial schools; 98 percent of the school district’s students are Black.

Inside Hamberlin’s classroom, it’s time for test-prep drills. This period has 20 eighth graders enrolled, but only 10 are present; six have been pulled out for remedial work with a consultant the district has hired to boost test scores, and the remaining four are absent for unclear reasons. The students in the room each grab a Chromebook and log in, at speeds ranging from feet-dragging to actively resistant. They open the StudySync software program, which shows them each a series of questions tailored to their weaknesses. Their faces look like they’re being marched to the guillotine.

Much of literacy instruction at Jefferson County Middle School now begins and ends with screens. In fact, Hamberlin doesn’t lecture at all on Wednesdays and Thursdays; students spend those class periods with StudySync and i-Ready, another adaptive software program, so each can focus where they need the most help.

Kids These Days The youngs are facing problems that didn't even exist half a generation ago. They’re handling it better than you think.

Their teacher can’t blame them for being sick of these exercises. The students’ lives, and hers, are dominated by the looming Mississippi Academic Assessment Program (MAAP), the set of annual standardized exams that measure their progress in language arts as well as science and math. Test prep is a year-round activity. Her students must learn how to decode the meaning of unfamiliar words, make inferences, identify the central idea of a passage, analyze tone and point of view. Every Friday brings a practice test.

Before moving to eighth grade, Hamberlin logged 25 years as an elementary school teacher. Eighth grade appealed to her because it’s all about analyzing texts, not just consuming them. That’s her idea of a good time. She remembers reading the first chapter of the first Harry Potter book four times just to make sure she didn’t miss a single detail. As she talks a group of students through a reading passage by Sojourner Truth, her passion is palpable—for the material, but even more for the puzzle-solving that reading comprehension requires.

“A lot of them think they’re studying the story,” she says afterward. “You’re not studying the story, that’s just the sprinkles on top. It’s what was she thinking, why did she say it, how did she convey her message?”

Tech.title: A Device Hidden in Cars Across the US Leaves Them Vulnerable to Hacking and Paralysis. Patch It Now
Tech.content:
As modern cars have evolved into multi-ton computers on wheels, drivers are beginning to learn they need to install security updates for their vehicles' code, just as they would for a phone or laptop. Yet not even the most tech-savvy car owners would expect they'd need to install a patch for an insecure third-party component they never installed or requested—and likely aren't even aware of—that's been wired into some of the most sensitive systems of their vehicle, leaving it vulnerable to stealthy hacking, tracking, and even roadside paralysis.

That's the disturbing discovery of a team of security researchers at UC San Diego, who found that a model of aftermarket car alarm known as the KARR Security System, installed in more than 2 million vehicles across the US by their estimate, can let any hacker within Bluetooth range send radio commands to silently unlock the car at will, turn off its alarm, honk the car's horn or flash its lights, or even disable its ignition and leave a driver stranded.

The KARR alarm devices are typically installed by car dealers, not manufacturers or owners, and used as a measure to prevent auto theft from dealer lots. Yet when the cars are sold, the alarms typically aren't removed, even if the buyer declines to pay for it as an additional feature. That means car owners across the US have a hackable device under their hood whose code they'll need to update to protect their vehicle—but one that, in many cases, they never purchased and have no idea is there.

The KARR Security System has been wired into the critical systems of more than 2 million vehicles by UCSD's estimate, all of which need the patch to protect them from hacking techniques that can track, unlock, and paralyze cars. Photograph: Courtesy of David Baillot/University of California San Diego

"This is a system added to cars by dealers, and unfortunately it has a severe vulnerability that allows anyone to gain access to any of these cars," says Aaron Schulman, the UCSD computer science professor who led the research. “It's designed to make cars more secure, but ultimately it's created a vulnerability that needs to be patched immediately across millions vehicles. We're trying to get the word out that you need to check your car for this device and manually patch it now.”

The company that sells the KARR Security System, Acrisure Protection Group, today rolled out a firmware update for the vulnerable Bluetooth model of its aftermarket KARR alarm to fix the security issues UCSD uncovered. Car owners who already have the KARR Security smartphone app installed should receive an alert about the firmware update, the UCSD team says. Those who don’t have it installed will need to download the KARR Security System smartphone app (Android, iOS), connect it to their vehicle's KARR alarm, then tap “customer service” and “firmware update.”

Given that at least half of car owners who have the KARR device installed didn't ask for it to be in their vehicles, according to UCSD's estimate, you can check if your car has the device by looking for a KARR sticker on your car's driver-side window—or in some cases a sticker reading, “SWDS” for SouthWest Dealer Services, a subsidiary of Acrisure Protection Group—as well as a small button with a blinking light attached to the underside of your car's dashboard. Car owners in Southern California are most likely to have the device installed due to its popularity among car dealers in the region, but the UCSD researchers warn that they've found the devices installed in vehicles across the US and even in other countries.

Tech.title: This Wearable Aims to Improve Your Blood Pressure. It’s Now in the US, and I Got a First Look
Tech.content:
The Hilo Core blood pressure system comes with a wireless cuff and a thin wristband that can continuously track your blood pressure. Giselle Castro-Sloboda/ CNET

Swiss health tech brand Aktiia announced Tuesday that its blood pressure health system, Hilo Core, is now available in the US. Backed by 22 years of research, the device delivers long-term blood pressure insights so users can better understand their heart health, which is especially significant considering that about half of US adults have high blood pressure (also known as hypertension).

According to the company, Hilo is also the world’s first blood pressure health system that combines an FDA-cleared cuff, which helps establish a baseline blood pressure reading, with a lightweight wearable wristband that provides ongoing blood pressure readings between cuff measurements.

“What we’re doing here is redefining completely the experience of blood pressure from a one-graph reading with a cuff on the arm to something that is embedded into your life,” Josep Solà, Aktiia co-founder and chief technology officer, told CNET during a Zoom call.

Ahead of its US launch, I’ve spent the last few days testing Hilo. This is what I’ve learned.

How Hilo works

Hilo focuses on your diastolic and systolic numbers, which are used to measure blood pressure. Systolic, the number on top of your reading, measures the maximum pressure in your arteries when your heart pumps out blood, while the bottom diastolic number shows the minimum pressure in your arteries when your heart is at rest and refills with blood.

Monitoring your blood pressure numbers can help prevent strokes and heart attacks.

An example of how Hilo reads your blood pressure trend over the course of a week. Hilo/Giselle Castro-Sloboda/CNET

I got to try Hilo firsthand and found it simple to use and set up. The Hilo Core kit includes a thin, screenless wristband wearable with a 15-day battery life and an FDA-cleared cuff that connects to a mobile app. Cuff measurements are required only during the first four days of activation for calibration, and thereafter on a monthly basis. This approach aims to give you a more comprehensive picture of your blood pressure fluctuations over time, rather than focusing on a single reading.

I took my cuff readings first thing in the morning after waking up and before eating or drinking coffee because certain foods and beverages can affect your readings.

After an initial four-day calibration, the Hilo cuff is used to measure your blood pressure monthly. Giselle Castro-Sloboda/CNET

The cuff reading felt similar to when I have my blood pressure taken at a doctor’s office, so it wasn’t anything out of the ordinary. The only difference is that the cuff is wireless and controlled by the app. The app recommends sitting still and relaxing to get the most accurate readings.

As for the Hilo band, it can capture up to 35 blood pressure readings per day. It also uses your sleep, heart rate and step count to provide contextualized insights.

To collect this data from the wrist, Hilo relies on optical blood pressure monitoring technology: photoplethysmographic — or PPG — light sensors, typically found in wearables, that can estimate blood pressure without requiring frequent cuff inflation.

The Hilo band is thin and includes light sensors that estimate blood pressure without a cuff. Giselle Castro-Sloboda/CNET

After you’ve calibrated your wristband, all you need to do is wear it like any other wearable. It’s lightweight, so you barely feel it, and it continuously reads pulse waves of your arteries every 90 minutes.

Setup was fast, and within minutes of the three inflating-and-deflating cycles performed by the cuff, I was able to view the cuff readings sent to the app. You can use the cuff for spot checks monthly or to validate the wearable’s readings.

For individuals who need to check their vitals regularly, I can see this device making it easy for them to track their blood pressure daily with minimal effort.

Is Hilo medical-grade?

In Europe, both the Hilo cuff and band are certified as medical devices. In the US, the Hilo cuff is FDA-cleared as a medical device, while the Hilo band is considered a wellness product and has not yet received FDA clearance. Just keep in mind that the system is meant to make you more aware of your daily blood pressure and isn’t meant to replace your doctor.

As always, consult with your practitioner before making any lifestyle changes or if you have questions. Before purchasing any health monitoring device like this one, you may also want to ask your doctor whether it’s right for your specific health condition.

However, Hilo is working toward getting approved to be included in a regulated medical platform used by healthcare professionals.

Hilo vs. other wearables that monitor blood pressure

There are already wearables, such as the Apple Watch and Oura Ring, that use their own tech to detect blood pressure changes to provide users with blood pressure awareness, but they aren’t currently approved for medical use, either. Now, there’s also the Signal Ring, which claims to replace a blood pressure cuff in providing accurate readings. Unlike Hilo, these wearables don’t come with a cuff that can establish a baseline reading or be used for monthly spot checks.

Previously, there was the Omron HeartGuide, a blood pressure monitor that used an inflatable cuff built into the wearable. It’s since been discontinued, but according to Hilo, its system differs from the HeartGuide because its wearable band doesn’t have a screen and uses optical sensors rather than an inflatable cuff. Hilo comes with a separate cuff for extra assurance that its readings have a baseline and are correct. With the HeartGuide, you’d chose when you’d take your blood pressure measurements, while Hilo automatically conducts readings every 90 minutes, including overnight.

Past success in Europe

Hilo already exists in Europe and has found success in helping people monitor blood pressure. According to a press release, a study conducted by the company from 2022 to 2025 with about 30,000 European participants found that, compared to people who didn’t regularly use a similar EU version of the Hilo app, those who consistently used it reduced their systolic blood pressure by up to five times over six months.

Solà told CNET that Hilo Core is generally used by people who have been diagnosed with high blood pressure, and those in their 50s and 60s.

How Hilo is different from traditional blood pressure cuffs

What the Hilo calibration process looks like during the first four days. Hilo/Giselle Castro-Sloboda/CNET

Normally, the recommended method to track blood pressure readings at home via a blood pressure cuff or monitor, but Solà wanted an easier approach: “I realized that they could shift this pain [of repeatedly using a blood pressure monitor] to a wearable device that does everything automatically.”

According to Solà, Hilo observed that those who were most engaged with the app saw greater improvement in their blood pressure readings over time.

“Normally, anyone who is diagnosed with high blood pressure has to measure it at least two times a day,” Solà explained. “What we’re seeing is that the average number of times that our users open the app to get their blood pressure numbers is up to three times a day.”

Having this knowledge at your fingertips can make you feel more in control and motivated to change your lifestyle habits, allowing you to see improvement in your blood pressure readings. It also gives you a clearer picture of your blood pressure health, which you can share with your doctor.

“We’re the companion to help them control blood pressure because we empower them with the data that they need,” Solà said.

The Hilo band makes it possible to continuously track your blood pressure. Hilo

What Hilo hopes to achieve in the US

Hilo’s goal with this launch is to help Americans with hypertension lower their blood pressure, as it did in Europe.

“This has the potential to help these patients resolve this hypertension problem,” said Solà. “The sooner you become aware of being hypertensive, the sooner you can start managing your blood pressure to help make it go down.”

Hilo’s privacy policy

Concerns about privacy are always at the forefront when someone chooses to monitor their health with a wearable. Hilo says that user data collected by the system is only used to improve Hilo’s products and services. The company doesn’t sell health data to third parties, and any data used for research or similar purposes is anonymized or aggregated.

An annual subscription is required

The Hilo Core kit is available for $90 at Amazon and Hilo.com. There is also a $150 annual subscription fee, which could be a barrier for those seeking an affordable way to regularly monitor their blood pressure. You can get pre-approved for HSA and FSA eligibility through your health insurance.

Tech.title: Don’t Wait for iOS 27, You Should Download iOS 26.5.2 Now for These Security Fixes
Tech.content:
Cole Kan/CNET/Apple

Apple is preparing to release iOS 27 this fall, but before that, you should download iOS 26.5.2 to your device to ensure it has the most up-to-date software. Apple released that update on Monday, June 29, and the company wrote online that iOS 26.5.2 brings over two dozen security fixes to your device, including one found with the help of Anthropic’s AI model Claude.

You can download iOS 26.5.2 now by going to Settings and tapping General. Next, select Software Update, tap Update Now and follow the prompts on your screen.

Apple wrote in the update’s release notes that this update offers security fixes, many of which are related to malicious web content vulnerabilities.

A closer look at the update’s common vulnerabilities and exposures report shows that many of the patches address issues in WebKit, the engine that powers Safari and other third-party browsers on iOS. Anthropics’ AI model Claude is credited for assisting in the discovery of one particular issue, which was related to a potential memory corruption exploit.

That discovery is the latest development in a busy few months for Anthropic’s AI models. In April, the company delayed the release of its Claude Mythos model to the public because its ability to find vulnerabilities represented a significant cybersecurity threat. It then released Fable 5 and Mythos 5 in June, before taking them down about a week later in the wake of government restrictions. Mythos 5 was then cleared for use on Friday, June 26, though only for a group of select companies and agencies.

As a result of that developing technology, we could start seeing Claude’s name appear more often on these CVE reports in the future.

For more on iOS, here’s what to know about iOS 27 before its fall release. Before that, here’s everything you need to know about iOS 26.

Tech.title: Judge Orders Temporary Block of Paramount Warner Bros. Merger
Tech.content:
A US District Judge has issued a temporary restraining order barring Paramount from closing its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery, NBC reports.

US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California has paused the merger after attorneys general from 12 states filed a lawsuit last week against Paramount Skydance, which is run by David Ellison. Martínez-Olguín said the restraining order would remain in effect for 14 days and scheduled a hearing on Aug. 3 for the states’ motion for a preliminary injunction.

The original lawsuit, filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, claimed the merger would create a monopoly and reduce competition across the film and cable industries. The deal cleared the US Department of Justice in June, with that agency stating that the merger would likely not cause harm or “raise actionable antitrust concerns.”

Under the proposed deal, CNN and CBS News, streaming services HBO Max and Paramount Plus, and film and television studios would be combined into a single media giant. That makes the lawsuit especially significant because it could reshape the media landscape if the deal is ultimately allowed to move forward. David Ellison’s father, billionaire Oracle founder Larry Ellison, is a high-profile donor and supporter of President Donald Trump.

A Paramount representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, the European Union is still vetting the transaction and is set to issue an approval or denial this month.

Tech.title: PS Plus July 2026 Games Are Packed With Zombies, Aliens and Nostalgia
Tech.content:
It’s officially the second half of 2026, which is going to be all about Grand Theft Auto 6. Until then, Sony has a new selection of games coming to PS Plus in July that includes Avatar: Frontier of Pandora, Dying Light and a couple of classic PlayStation 2 games.

PS Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 a month, the plans give subscribers access to games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can play a handful of new games at no additional charge.

If you’re a PlayStation Plus Extra or Premium subscriber, you can grab these games starting July 21.

Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora

Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora came out in 2023, a year after Avatar: The Way of Water released in theaters. Developed by Massive Entertainment – a division of Ubisoft – the open-world action-adventure puts players in the role of a Na’vi raised by the Resources Development Administration, or RDA, before returning to defend Pandora. Set in the previously unseen Western Frontier, the game emphasizes exploration, aerial traversal on an ikran and combat using both traditional Na’vi weapons and human firearms. While its gameplay shares many similarities with the Far Cry series, its lush environments and faithful recreation of Pandora earned praise from critics.

Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting July 21.

Rise of the Ronin

Team Ninja went a different direction than its usual Ninja Gaiden style with 2024’s Rise of the Ronin. Set during Japan’s turbulent Bakumatsu period in the late 19th century, the open-world action RPG lets players shape the story by siding with competing political factions. Combat combines fast-paced swordplay with firearms and other period weapons with the challenging gameplay the studio is known for. Its blend of historical events, exploration and player-driven choices helped distinguish it from Team Ninja’s previous action games.

Rise of the Ronin is now available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers.

Firefighting Simulator: Ignite

Firefighting Simulator: Ignite puts players in the role of a firefighter responding to emergencies across a large fictional city in the American Midwest. Whether playing solo with AI teammates or cooperatively with up to three friends, players battle dynamic fires, rescue civilians and use authentic firefighting equipment to contain increasingly dangerous blazes. Powered by Unreal Engine 5, the game features real-time fire, smoke and heat simulation designed to create a more realistic firefighting experience.

Firefighting Simulator: Ignite will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting July 21.

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Rita’s Rewind

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Rita’s Rewind is a true nostalgia bomb of a game. The side-scrolling beat-’em-up reimagines the classic 1990s TV series with pixel art visuals, cooperative multiplayer and familiar villains, including a robotic version of Rita Repulsa. Players battle through stages inspired by the show before piloting Dinozords and the Megazord in 3D action sequences that break up the traditional brawler gameplay.

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Rita’s Rewind will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting July 28.

Dying Light

It’s been more than a decade since Dying Light was released, but it’s still a title that gamers fawn over. Players explore the zombie-infested city of Harran using a fast-paced parkour system that makes traversing rooftops as important as combat. Scavenging for supplies, crafting weapons and surviving a dynamic day-night cycle keep the tension high as more dangerous infected emerge after dark. Its fluid movement and intense survival mechanics helped make it one of the most acclaimed zombie games of its generation.

Dying Light will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting July 21.

Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector

Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector builds on its predecessor by sending players across a lawless star system as an escaped android searching for freedom. Rather than focusing on traditional combat, the game emphasizes dialogue, dice-based skill checks and resource management as players assemble a crew and take on dangerous contracts. Its choice-driven storytelling and tabletop-inspired mechanics make every decision feel meaningful, with multiple paths that shape how the story unfolds.

Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting July 28.

Snow Bros. Wonderland

Snow Bros. Wonderland revives the long-running arcade franchise with a fresh 3D isometric look while staying true to its classic action-platforming roots. Players freeze enemies into snowballs before kicking them across each stage to defeat other foes and rack up combos. Cooperative play, colorful environments and larger-than-life boss battles help modernize the series without losing the charm that made the original games fan favorites.

Snow Bros. Wonderland will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting July 28.

Psi-Ops: The Mindgate Conspiracy

Psi-Ops: The Mindgate Conspiracy was first released for the PS2 in 2004 and had a mix of interesting physics gameplay that was a big trend in gaming at the time. Players control Nick Scryer, a secret agent who combines traditional gunplay with psychic abilities like telekinesis, mind control and pyrokinesis to take down enemies. The game’s physics-based powers encouraged creative problem-solving and helped it stand out from other action shooters of its era, earning it a cult following years after its release.

Psi-Ops: The Mindgate Conspiracy will be available for PS Plus Premium subscribers starting July 21.

Indigo Prophecy

Before it made a name for itself with the games Heavy Rain and Detroit: Become Human, developer Quantic Dream first experimented with making the point-and-click adventure gameplay style a bit more action-oriented with Indigo Prophecy. The supernatural thriller follows several interconnected characters as they investigate a string of mysterious murders while uncovering a conspiracy that threatens humanity. Its cinematic presentation, branching narrative and quick-time events helped lay the foundation for the studio’s later interactive dramas.

Indigo Prophecy will be available for PS Plus Premium subscribers starting July 21.

Tech.title: These Are the Best and Worst Letters to Guess in Wordle
Tech.content:
We’ve got all the best Wordle strategies here for your convenience. NurPhoto/Getty Images

Your Wordle opener can have a bigger impact than you might think. While plenty of players stick with familiar starting words like “TRAIN” or “CLOSE,” relying on the same guess every day isn’t necessarily the most effective strategy. With years of Wordle data now available, we know that some letters appear far more frequently than others. Prioritizing common letters like E, A and R gives you a better chance of uncovering useful clues early, helping you solve the puzzle more efficiently instead of relying on habit or luck.

In order to get the absolute best starter words, you should know which letters turn up the most in English. I reached out to the big brains at the Oxford English Dictionary – you know, the whopping, multivolume dictionary that no one actually owns, but that your school librarian adored. An OED representative sent me a list prepared by staff that analyzed all the main entries in the concise version of the dictionary.

“It’s worth noting that the piece is pretty old,” the OED representative said apologetically. “It mentions that the stats are from Concise Oxford English Dictionary in 2004, although current colleagues aren’t sure when the piece itself was written, and I’m afraid we don’t have any newer analysis of this sort.”

The list may be 22 years old, but I’m going with it. The alphabet isn’t like ice cream flavors or musical acts – no new, trendy letters have been introduced in that time. So whether you’re just getting into Wordle, or you want to shake up your starter words and make sure they’re still hitting the most common letters, this list is for you.

S begins the most English words

The most common letter is no surprise to most people: It’s E, and it’s immediately followed by another vowel, A. And those letters are much, much more popular than the final two letters in the OED’s list, which are J and Q. (Anyone else surprised that J is used less than X and Z?)

“The letter E is over 56 times more common than Q in forming individual English words,” the OED analysis found.

It notes that “there are more English words beginning with the letter S than with any other letter.”

Tech.title: FDA Still Investigating Diarrhea-Causing Parasite, as Cyclospora Outbreak Continues
Tech.content:
Cooking produce is the only 100% effective way to kill cyclospora, which is why raw salads are such a gamble right now. wildpixel/Getty Images

After weeks of “produce paranoia,” with people clearing out their fridges and swearing off salads, there’s been another hiccup in the investigation into the multistate cyclospora outbreak. On Sunday, the US Food and Drug Administration appeared to flip-flop on claims that the foodborne pathogen had been found in iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms, a global fresh produce company based in Salinas, California.

Cyclospora, which causes the gastrointestinal illness known for “explosive diarrhea,” has historically been linked to fresh produce such as berries and salad greens but is notoriously hard to trace. For several weeks, no specific food, brand, grower or supplier was conclusively identified as the source of the outbreak, which has led to panicking and a whole lot of memes on social media.

Last week, health officials announced they were investigating a link to Taylor Farms’ shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia. As a result, Taylor Farms said it was voluntarily pulling iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the US market. There seemed to be, momentarily, a collective sigh of relief.

Then, on Sunday, when the FDA said that a lettuce sample that tested positive for cyclospora was actually a “false positive,” the search for the outbreak’s source appeared to reset to square one. Taylor Farms wrote in a July 19 statement on its website: “To be clear, at this moment, FDA has not identified a single positive product test result for cyclospora. ” Nonetheless, the recall of Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce grown and processed in central Mexico remains in place across 27 states.

A new twist came on Monday, when the FDA clarified on social media that the agency was still confident of a link to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms locations in central Mexico. The FDA said in a post on X that the false-positive lab finding doesn’t alter the substantial epidemiological data backing Taylor Farms’ voluntary recall. Laboratory tests are just one piece of evidence, but not the decisive factor in the larger investigation of the current outbreak.

To clarify, this false-positive lab sample DOES NOT change the basis for FDA’s ongoing outbreak investigation or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the current voluntary recall by Taylor Farms.



Over the weekend, FDA alerted Taylor Farms that a new sample of… https://t.co/hedRwhPLd8 — U.S. FDA (@US_FDA) July 20, 2026

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that more than 7,000 cyclospora cases have been either confirmed or are under investigation nationwide since May 1, with over 100 hospitalizations and no deaths to date. Cases have been reported across 34 states, with Michigan among the hardest-hit regions.

After what seemed to be a step toward resolution, the source of the nation’s worst cyclosporiasis outbreak remains something of a mystery, leaving more uncertainty about which foods to avoid. With any health scare, bad advice and myths spread just as fast as the actual illness. So we turned to health care experts to learn the facts.

“I wouldn’t necessarily suggest that people avoid produce,” said Dr. John Openshaw, an infectious disease physician and medical epidemiologist at Stanford University. “Even though the number of people involved in the current outbreak or outbreaks seems large, overall the risk remains very low to most people.”

What is cyclosporiasis?

Cyclosporiasis is caused by cyclospora cayetanensis, a microscopic parasite transmitted through fecal matter that infects the small intestine. According to infectious disease experts at Johns Hopkins, it takes only a few microscopic cyclospora eggs to hijack your gastrointestinal tract.

In the US, previous cyclospora outbreaks have frequently been associated with fresh produce, including bagged salad mixes, cilantro, basil, raspberries, snow peas and green onions. Any food that’s contaminated and eaten uncooked can theoretically transmit cyclospora.

Unlike some stomach illnesses, such as the norovirus, cyclosporiasis is unlikely to spread directly from one person to another. After the parasite leaves an infected person’s body, it generally needs at least one to two weeks in the environment before it becomes infectious.

Stomach cramps are a common sign of cyclosporiasis, an infection caused by the cyclospora parasite. Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty Images

What are the symptoms of cyclosporiasis?

The most common symptom is watery diarrhea that can be frequent and, according to the CDC, sometimes “explosive.” Other unpleasant symptoms can include stomach cramps, nausea, loss of appetite, bloating and gas, fatigue, vomiting and a low-grade fever.

Unlike deadlier foodborne illnesses such as listeria or E. coli, cyclosporiasis isn’t usually life-threatening. The biggest risk right now during the hot summer months is dehydration. “People who are sick and are having trouble keeping hydrated should talk to a doctor,” Openshaw said.

Symptoms typically begin about one week after exposure, although they can appear anywhere from two days to two weeks or longer afterward. Dr. Timothy Henrich, professor of medicine at UCSF, said it’s typical for people to have “waxing and waning symptoms” over weeks to months. Others who are infected might have minimal or even no symptoms, he said.

Because symptoms can come and go, it’s important to get tested for cycolosporasis and talk with a doctor about treatment, which is generally well-tolerated and “may reduce the chances of further local fecal-oral spread,” Henrich said.

How high is the risk?

While cyclosporasis cases span a lot of the country, the outbreak’s highest concentration is in a small cluster of states, mostly in the Midwest. Jessica Steier, a public health scientist and CEO of Unbiased Science, said the risk remains low outside those areas, but that anyone who is “pregnant or immunocompromised might consider erring on the side of caution.”

The CDC says that only about 9% of people who contract the parasite require hospitalization, but the risk of severe illness and lasting complications is significantly higher for seniors, young children and others with weakened immune systems.

Health officials says it’s best to avoid bagged greens or precut mixes to stay safe during the current cyclospora outbreak. Al Drago/Getty Images

How can you reduce your risk?

Although the voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms, sourced from central Mexico, remains in effect across 27 states, there is still no nationwide recommendation to throw away lettuce. However, Michigan health officials have issued more specific guidance for lettuce during the current investigation, including buying whole heads of lettuce instead of bagged lettuce or premixed salad kits (then discarding the outer three layers of leaves) and cooking leafy greens when practical.

Though washing fresh produce might reduce your exposure to cyclospora and other foodborne contaminants, it can’t guarantee the parasite will be completely removed.

“Washing produce does not meaningfully decrease the risk of cyclospora, and heat remains the gold standard for risk reduction,” Steier said. Cooking vegetables at an internal temperature of 158 degrees Fahrenheit or higher is the only surefire way to kill the parasite.

Experts also warn against using soap, bleach or household disinfectants on produce. Fruits and vegetables can absorb soap and detergent, which may make you sick, and the CDC says routine chemical disinfection is unlikely to kill cyclospora.

Household tools or countertop items such as UV produce washers, ultrasonic cleaners or ozone devices won’t make contaminated food safe to consume, either. Steier confirmed that none of those methods have sufficient real-world evidence to support their use in killing the parasite.

What should you do if you have symptoms?

Experts advise contacting a health care provider if you develop persistent watery diarrhea, especially if it is severe, lasts longer than a week or goes away and then returns. Drinking fluids is also important because prolonged diarrhea can cause dehydration.

Diagnosing cyclospora requires special lab testing, and the parasite isn’t included in routine stool testing. The CDC says patients sometimes need to provide multiple samples because cyclospora can be difficult to detect.

The standard treatment is the prescription antibiotic combination trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, commonly sold under the brand names Bactrim and Septra. People who are allergic to sulfa drugs should discuss other options with a medical professional.

The CDC hasn’t found a single source linking the outbreak. sshepard/Getty Images

Why is it so hard to identify the source of an outbreak?

It often takes weeks or longer to identify the source of a parasitic outbreak because investigators have to compare what sick people ate, then trace the foods back through the supply chain. For cyclospora, that process is especially difficult because symptoms often begin days after exposure.

Public health agencies have also faced staffing cuts and funding reductions in recent years, making it harder to identify outbreaks quickly and to tell people which foods to avoid. A recent study found that states with more CDC support reported more outbreaks than those without those programs, suggesting that federal funding improves detection and management.

“Tracing any outbreak like this requires trained staff and resources – any cut to those elements of a public health response would impede efforts to trace an outbreak to a specific food item and identify how a pathogen like cyclospora got into the food supply,” Openshaw said.

Tech.title: The Pickle Is In, the Squint Is Out: Here Are the Newest Approved Emoji
Tech.content:
It’s official: We’re getting a pickle emoji next year. On Tuesday, July 14, the Unicode Consortium announced the nine new emoji you’ll see on your device in 2027. One new emoji is the pickle, and that means the eggplant’s reign as the go-to emoji for male anatomy could be coming to an end.

Here are the nine new emoji you will see on your device next year.

A cracking face

A leftward thumb sign gesture

A rightward thumb sign gesture

A monarch butterfly

A pickle

A lighthouse

A meteor

An eraser

A net with a handle

The Unicode Consortium originally proposed a squinty face emoji in 2025. However, the Unicode Emoji Standard & Research Working Group recommended changing that emoji to a cracking face in January.

Honestly, the cracking face emoji feels more relevant to today than the squinty face emoji. The squinty face read as suspicious while the cracking face emoji screams, “I’m putting on a brave face in these trying times.” If that’s not the most relatable sentiment these days, I don’t know what is.

While the Unicode Consortium approved these emoji, companies like Apple and Samsung still need to design and then implement their versions of the emoji. Those companies usually add the emoji to devices as part of a software update in the spring, so you likely won’t see these emoji on your phone until 2027.

Before these emoji land on your device, the Unicode Consortium will begin fielding proposals for the next round of new emoji. Anyone can submit an idea for a new emoji, and the Unicode Consortium usually uploads proposed new emoji to a public document late in the year. For example, the upcoming emoji were originally accepted in October, 2025.

For more on emoji, here’s how to decipher every emoji and the newest emoji on your iPhone and Android.
